chunks.text: Lalla was an Indian astronomer who lived in the southern part of Gujarat. Only two of his works are currently extant. In the Lunar Eclipse chapter of Śiṣyadhīvṛddhida Tantra (Chatterjee, 1981) the following verse is found: Subtract from the Moon’s longitude the longitude of the ascending node. Find RSine of the result, multiply it by 15, and divide by 191. The result is the latitude of the Moon. Since Lalla used the standard Indian radius of 3438 units, Eq. 1 becomes: $$L = \frac{Sine (ab) \times L{max}}{3438}$$ Or, $$\frac{L{max}}{3438} = \frac{15}{191}$$ Thus, $L_{max} = 3438 \times 15/191 = 270 \text{ min} = 4.5^{\circ}$.

chunks.text: Though the astronomer Mañjula’s location is not known for certain, he is thought to have lived in northern India, possibly near Patna in modern Bihar. In his Laghu-Mānasa we find the following reference to the Moon’s latitude (Shukla, 1990): Subtract the longitude of the ascending node from that of the Moon; Find the RSine of the result and multiply it by 36. The result is the latitude of the Moon in minutes. Mañjula’s system employed the unusual radius of 8' 8'', so Eq. 1 becomes: $$L = \frac{Sine (ab) \times L{max}}{8.133}$$ Or, $$\frac{L{max}}{8.133} = \frac{36}{1}$$ Therefore, $L_{max} = 8.133 \times 36 = 292.8 \text{ min} = 4.88^{\circ}$.

In his astronomical treatise, the Graha-Gaṇita (Arka Somayaji, 1980), within the section on Lunar Eclipses, is found the expression to calculate the latitude of the Moon: $$L = \frac{RSine (ab) \times 270}{R}$$ Thus, the maximum latitude will be 270 min = $4.5^{\circ}$, which will occur when $RSine = R$, that is, when the argument of latitude is $90^{\circ}$.

chunks.text: Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī was an astronomer and mathematician who belonged to the Kerala School of Mathematics and flourished during medieval times. His most influential astronomical work, the Tantrasaṅgraha, was completed in 1501 CE (Ramasubramanian, 2011). <<<CONTINUE>>> In the Lunar Eclipses chapter are found the following verses: The RSine of the longitude of the node subtracted from the Moon is multiplied by 270 and divided by the Radius, which gives the latitude of the Moon. This multiplied by the Moon’s orbital radius and divided by the actual distance between the Earth and the Moon gives the true value of latitude. While the first verse appears to suggest that 270 min ($4.5^{\circ}$) is the maximum latitude of the Moon, the second verse clarifies, in line with the general concept of the Sūryasiddhānta, that $4.5^{\circ}$ is only the Mean-Max latitude. Nīlakaṇṭha proclaims the actual latitude of the Moon as: $$L{\text{max}} = \frac{L{\text{Indian - mean - max}} \times D{\text{mean}}}{D{\text{actual}}} \text{,}$$ (2) where $D{\text{mean}}$ is the mean distance of the Moon, and $D{\text{actual}}$ is the actual distance. According to modern data, the mean distance of the Moon from the Earth is 239,000 miles, while the minimum and maximum are 226,000 and 252,000 miles, respectively. Plugging these values into Eq. 2 gives us the range of maximum latitude for the Moon as $4.27^{\circ}–4.76^{\circ}$ according to Nīlakaṇṭha.

chunks.text: Finally, to round off our analyses of ancient savants, we must make a mention of the Greeks. Claudius Ptolemy was the greatest among the astronomers of Greek descent who lived in Alexandria, Egypt during the second century CE. His works represent the culmination of Greco-Roman science, particularly his work on astronomy, the ‘Mathematical Syntaxis’, known among the Arabs as the Almagest (Ptolemy, 1952). In Book-V of the Almagest, he provides a lookup table for lunar latitudes, which presents the maximum latitude of the Moon as $5.0^{\circ}$ exactly.

chunks.text: Table 1 shows a summary of information from ancient literature with regard to the maximum latitude of the Moon. We have added an extra column at the end that shows the obliquity of the ecliptic according to these ancient astronomers, which may have a bearing on the topic at hand, as will be explained later. From the third column of the table, we note that all Indian astronomers of yore have misconstrued the Sūryasiddhānta where it is explicitly stated that $4.5^{\circ}$ is only a sort of mean value for the Moon’s maximum latitude and not the absolute maximum. In addition, all of them, except for Nīlakaṇṭha, have also assumed this supposed maximum of $4.5^{\circ}$ (or near about) to be a constant as well. This appears to indicate, quite shockingly, that none of these Indian or Greek savants of old ever made any actual observations of the Moon’s latitude themselves, or else they would have been aware that the maximum latitude is about $5.3^{\circ}$. Figure 4 shows the Moon at $4.5^{\circ}$ and $5.3^{\circ}$ latitudes in a typical landscape, which indicates the magnitude of the error. It is seen that the difference between the two values amounts to more than 1 and $1/2$ full-Moon widths; large enough to be easily perceived with the naked eye, and certainly not a trivial error. Yet, it appears that these leading lights of Indian and Greek astronomy have not noticed the substantial difference between their assumption and actuality. The beginnings of modern European astronomy can be traced back to the 16th century when the Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe, vexed by the inaccurate astronomical tables of his time, decided to create a good observational data set for himself. His efforts over the years yielded an extensive collection of very accurate observational data, which eventually paved the way for significant discoveries by himself and others. This was the pre-telescope era, in which all observation was done with the naked eye. From his observations of the Moon, Tycho discovered, among other things, that the maximum inclination of the Moon’s orbit to the ecliptic was not $5^{\circ}$ as stated by Ptolemy, but about $5.25^{\circ}$. Thus, we are confronted with the startling realization that no Indian or Greek astronomer of old was able to determine by observation what Tycho Brahe found easily, namely, that the maximum latitude of the Moon is about $5.25^{\circ}$, and that this maximum varies from month to month. Note that the Moon attains its maximum latitude 2 times every month (north and south), therefore this is not one of those rare phenomena for which an astronomer must wait many years for a chance of observation. A similar situation also occurs with the obliquity or tilt of the ecliptic. The tilt was $24^{\circ}$ at about 3000 BC, and it has been decreasing slowly over the years, its current value Table 1 Maximum lunar latitude according to various authorities | Author | Date | Max lunar latitude | Obliquity | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Āryabhaṭa | 495 CE | $4.5^{\circ}$ (constant) | $24^{\circ}$ | | Varāhamihira | 530 CE | $4.5^{\circ}$ and $4.67^{\circ}$ (constant) | $24^{\circ}$ | | Brahmagupta | 630 CE | $4.5^{\circ}$ (constant) | $24^{\circ}$ | | Lalla | 760 CE | $4.5^{\circ}$ (constant) | $24^{\circ}$ | | Mañjula | 935 CE | $4.88^{\circ}$ (constant) | $24^{\circ}$ | | Bhāskara-II | 1150 CE | $4.5^{\circ}$ (constant) | $24^{\circ}$ | | Nīlakaṇṭha | 1500 CE | $4.27^{\circ}–4.76^{\circ}$ (variable) | $24^{\circ}$ | | Ptolemy | 140 CE | $5.0^{\circ}$ (constant) | $23.86^{\circ}$ | --- Fig. 4. Margin of Error for the Moon's Maximum Latitude being $23.44^{\circ}$. The obliquity is a parameter that can be determined easily by observation, and it is seen from the fourth column of the above table that 350 years before Āryabhaṭa, the Greek astronomer Ptolemy had determined this parameter to be $23.86^{\circ}$. Yet, like the Moon’s maximum latitude, all Indian astronomers have simply assumed the obliquity to be a constant $24^{\circ}$ as stated in the ancient Sūryasiddhānta, without making any observational verification for themselves. Summarizing our three findings thus far: (i) While the oldest extant Indian text, the Sūryasiddhānta, clearly indicates that $4.5^{\circ}$ is only a sort of mean value for the Moon’s maximum latitude, the text does not provide a way to determine this maximum latitude; (ii) All Indian astronomers of old appear to have assumed the stated mean-max value of $4.5^{\circ}$ to be the maximum latitude of the Moon, without making any observational verification themselves; (iii) These astronomers also appear to have assumed the obliquity of the ecliptic to be $24^{\circ}$, once again, without making any observational verification. Let us take up the first item, and make a detailed study of the actual variation of the Moon’s maximum latitude from month to month, to see if we can perchance discover the missing algorithm in the Sūrya siddhānta.

chunks.text: The first variable we will examine is the Moon’s anomaly. As depicted in Fig. 5, the anomaly ($\theta$) is the angular distance of the Moon ($m$) from its apogee ($a$) as observed from the Earth ($e$). Note that when the anomaly is $0^{\circ}$ the Moon is at its greatest distance from the Earth while at $180^{\circ}$ it is the closest. Recall from the previous section that the Indian astronomer Nīlakaṇṭha, unlike his compatriots, had stated that the Moon’s maximum latitude is not a constant but varies inversely with its distance from the Earth. Fig. 5. Moon's anomaly Figure 6 shows the variation of the Moon’s maximum latitude with respect to its anomaly over 600 consecutive months, starting from January 1, 2020. It is seen that the data is quite dispersed, with no perceivable linkage between the anomaly and maximum latitude, though we do observe a slight upward shift of the dataset when the anomaly is near $90^{\circ}$.

chunks.text: Finally, we examine the variation of the Moon’s maximum latitude with its separation from the Sun, known as the Elongation, over 600 consecutive months starting January 1, 2020. As seen in Fig. 8, we appear to have hit the jackpot with this parameter. $L{\text{max}}$ is observed to have a direct relation to the elongation, almost a simple sinusoidal variation. We note that $L{\text{max}}$ is a minimum when the elongation is $0^{\circ}$ or $180^{\circ}$, and a maximum when it is $90^{\circ}$ or $270^{\circ}$, and the entire variation closely resembles a sine wave. Figure 9 depicts a physical summary of this finding. In Fig. A on the left, we see that when the separation between the Sun ($s$) and the Moon ($m$) is $90^{\circ}$ or $270^{\circ}$, that is, first or third quarter Moon phase, and when the Sun is at either node, the Moon’s maximum latitude will be greatest (around $5.3^{\circ}$). Fig. 8. Variation of the Moon’s maximum latitude with elongation Conversely, as shown in Fig. B, when the Sun is aligned to the Earth-Moon axis, that is, at full Moon or new Moon, and the Sun is $90^{\circ}$ from either node, the Moon’s maximum latitude will be least (around $5^{\circ}$).

chunks.text: With these results, we are now in a position to make a broad-based proposal for the missing algorithm of the Moon’s maximum latitude in Indian astronomy. Figure 10 shows two views of the standard Indian epicycle model for the Moon. The 2-D view depicts the Moon ($m$) revolving clockwise around the epicycle center, while the epicycle itself revolves counter-clockwise around the larger deferent circle, which has the Earth ($e$) at its center. The Mean Moon ($m^{\prime}$) is located at the center of the epicycle. Note that the radius of the epicycle varies in time, as shown by the dashed line. In the 3-D view, we see that the deferent circle, on which the mean Moon revolves, is inclined to the ecliptic at $4.5^{\circ}$. This is the mean-max latitude ($L{\text{indian-mean-max}}$) specified in the Sūryasiddhānta. Further, we note that the epicycle plane, in its turn, is inclined to the deferent plane. According to the Sūryasiddhānta, the nodes act upon both the Mean Moon (deferent) as well as the True Moon (epicycle), hence both will have separate inclinations of their own. Note that in this paper our focus is on the maximum latitude of the Moon, and Fig. 10 is only a general schematic representation to indicate that the deferent and epicycle circles have separate inclinations. This figure is not intended as a detailed model for the calculation of general latitude. The calculation of latitude in the epicycle model is an exceedingly complex affair. The interested reader can refer to available literature for further details (Swerdlow, 2005). --- Fig. 9. Configuration for Maximum and Minimum Lmax Fig. 10. The Moon's Epicycle In the Indian epicycle model for the calculation of longitudes, the angular velocity of the mean planet on the deferent is set equal to the angular motion of the true planet on the epicycle. We may conjecture that a similar condition is applied implicitly to the calculation of latitudes as well, that is, the lateral motion of the mean planet on the deferent is proportionately equal to that of the true planet on the epicycle. Now, while the Mean-Moon’s maximum latitude on the deferent is specified as $4.5^{\circ}$, how can we determine the maximum latitude of the True-Moon on the epicycle? We do that using the instruction in the Sūryasiddhānta (given in Sect. 5 above), which says that the maximum inclination equals an 80th part of the circumference. The Moon’s epicycle circumference ($C{\text{ep}}$) has been specified in the Sūryasiddhānta as approximately $32^{\circ}$, whose 80th part will be the inclination of the epicycle concerning the deferent, that is, $32/80 = 0.4^{\circ}$. Putting all this together, we can propose the following empirical expression for the maximum latitude of the Moon, which comprises a base mean value over which a variation is superimposed: $$L{\text{max}} = L{\text{Indian - mean - max}} + \frac{C{\text{ep}} \times (1 + \text{Sin}(E))}{80} \text{,}$$ (3) where, the elongation $(E) = (\text{Sun's Longitude}) - (\text{Moon's Longitude})$. The quantity $(1 + \text{sin}(E))$ can be regarded as a ‘pulsation factor’, which causes the circumference of the epicycle to vary (pulsate) in size from $C{\text{ep}}$ to $2C{\text{ep}}$. Substituting known values into Eq. 3, we will have: $$L{\text{max}} = 4.5 + 0.4 \times (1 + \sin(E))$$ (4) In the next section, we will compare the results of this proposed expression with actuality.

The proposed expression can no doubt be improved with some simple extensions to bring it closer to actuality, but we will not attempt any further enhancements in this paper. Using modern techniques such as the Fourier Transform, one can obtain a near-exact formula for the actual variation. However, that would likely result in very lengthy and complex expressions, which would be beyond what the ancient astronomer was capable of. Any future enhancements to the proposed expression for the missing algorithm should bear that in mind. --- Fig. 11. Variation of the proposed formula with actuality

9.1 Possible reasons for the missing algorithm
chunks.text: Having shown that the variation of the Moon’s maximum latitude can be captured using a simple mathematical expression that is well within reach of the ancient Indian astronomer, we have now to deal with the question of why such an easy algorithm is missing in the Sūryasiddhānta in the first place, especially when the text indicates that the maximum latitude is variable. And there is the related question of why no Indian astronomer of old was even aware that the Moon’s maximum latitude is not $4.5^{\circ}$ but $5.3^{\circ}$. Let us explore some possible answers to these questions.

chunks.title: On the calculation of the Moon’s latitude in Indian astronomy
heading_path: On the calculation of the Moon’s latitude in Indian astronomy
9.1 Possible reasons for the missing algorithm
chunks.text: It is, of course, quite inconceivable that no Indian astronomer ever made any actual observations. What is very likely, and practical moreover, is that the Moon’s latitude was not measured directly by the ancient astronomer, but only in an indirect manner, using the declination. As mentioned, the latitude of heavenly bodies is measured regarding the ecliptic (see Fig. 2). To make this measurement directly without sophisticated instruments is not a simple task since the exact location of the ecliptic is not easy to pinpoint in the sky. Instead, the ancient astronomer usually based his observations on four easy-to-use reference points, namely: (i) The cardinal directions (north, south, east, west); (ii) The horizon; (iii) The pole star; (iv) The zenith point (directly overhead). In Fig. 12, the observer is at $O$ and his zenith point ($Z$) is directly overhead. His geographical latitude ($Lo$) is, say, $40^{\circ}$ north, and therefore the north celestial pole ($P$) will appear to him $40^{\circ}$ directly above the north point of the horizon ($N$). The southern horizon point ($S$) is directly opposite $N$. The great circle containing $N, P, Z,$ and $S$ is called the meridian for our observer. It is observed from the figure that the celestial equator, which lies $90^{\circ}$ away from the pole, cuts the meridian at point $E$, which will be at a constant $40^{\circ}$ south of the zenith for our observer. Fig. 12. Determining the declination of the Moon The declination $(\delta)$ of a heavenly body is defined as its angular distance, north or south, from the celestial equator. An ideal time to determine the declination of a heavenly body (including the Moon) is when it arrives at the observer’s meridian since the location of the celestial equator on the meridian is known (point $E$). Referring to the figure, the Moon’s declination is then simply the arc $Em$. In practice, it is usual for the astronomer to measure either the altitude $h$ (arc $Sm$) or the polar distance (arc $Zm$) of the body, both of which can be determined easily using instruments like the meridian circle. Given $h$, the declination (arc $Em$) can be found by Eq. 5 given below. Note that the Moon is south of the equator in the figure, so its declination will be negative. $$\delta = (Lo + h) - 90^{\circ}$$ (5) Thus, we see that the Moon’s declination is a quantity that is fairly easy to determine. Coming to the latitude, its determination is a different matter altogether. As mentioned, the latitude of a heavenly body is its angular distance, north or south, from the ecliptic. Now, while the location of the celestial equator on the observer’s meridian (point $E$) is fixed and known, as explained earlier, where the ecliptic cuts the meridian (point $T$) is variable throughout the year. In standard works of spherical trigonometry (Smart, 1977), the relation between the latitude $(\beta)$ and the declination $(\delta)$ involves the right ascension $(\alpha)$ and the obliquity of the earth’s axis $(\eta)$. The full expression is as shown in Eq. 6. $$\sin (\beta) = \sin (\delta) \cos (\eta) - \cos (\delta) \sin (\eta) \sin (\alpha)$$ (6) Fig. 13. Variation of the Moon’s Maximum Declination in Time For the special case where $\alpha = 90^\circ$, that is, when the Moon is on the meridian and the equinox point is located on our observer’s horizon, Eq. 6 will become: $$\sin (\beta) = \sin (\delta) \cos (\eta) - \cos (\delta) \sin (\eta).$$ Applying standard trigonometric identities we will have: $$\sin (\beta) = \sin (\delta - \eta)$$ Therefore, $$\beta = \delta - \eta$$ Or, $$\delta = \beta + \eta \text{ (7)}$$ Thus, we see that for this special case, the declination, latitude, and obliquity have a simple relation among themselves. In general, the declination will be a maximum when latitude is a maximum since the obliquity of the ecliptic is a constant for a given epoch. However, the obliquity does change over longer periods, and it has been decreasing steadily for the past 8000 years. How does this affect the Moon’s maximum declination? The answer is shown in Fig. 13. The solid line in the figure, which has been computed per modern astronomy (Meeus, 2000), shows that the Moon’s maximum declination has been decreasing steadily over the centuries due to the decreasing obliquity. Its current value is the sum of the Moon’s maximum latitude ($5.3^\circ$) and the current obliquity ($23.44^\circ$), which comes to $28.74^\circ$. The dashed line in the figure shows the Indian value for the Moon’s maximum declination, which is a constant since both the Moon’s maximum latitude ($4.5^\circ$) and the obliquity ($24^\circ$) are deemed constants, their sum equating to $28.5^\circ$. Recall from the third and fourth columns of Table 1 that all Indian astronomers of old have assumed the obliquity to be constant at $24^\circ$ and the Moon’s maximum latitude as $4.5^\circ$ (or near about). Thus, we see the interesting circumstance in Indian astronomy where the negative error in the Moon’s maximum latitude compensates for the positive error in the obliquity, such that their sum (the maximum declination) comes to within $0.5^\circ$ of the actual maximum declination, as seen in Fig. 13. The relative size of the full Moon is depicted on the right in Fig. 13 to indicate the magnitude of the Indian error for the Moon’s maximum declination. The width of the full Moon is $0.5^\circ$, and it is noted from the figure that the actual and Indian maximum declinations fall within the Moon’s orb, at least since Āryabhaṭa’s time (500 CE), which may have contributed to the Indian astronomer being satisfied that his values for the Moon’s maximum latitude ($4.5^\circ$) and the obliquity ($24^\circ$) were correct. The important point being made here is that it is the declination that was of primary interest to the ancient astronomer, not the latitude.

chunks.text: Apart from the declination, there may have been other reasons that have contributed to the Indian astronomer’s lack of interest in the actual maximum latitude of the Moon. For the ancient astronomer, the three primary reasons to calculate the Moon were: (i) The regulation of months (new Moon); (ii) The calculation of eclipses; (iii) Calculation of the Moon’s phases. For the first item, the Moon’s latitude does not figure anywhere in the calculation of New Moon. For the second, in the calculation of eclipses, the Moon’s latitude does matter, but not her maximum latitude. Both Lunar and Solar eclipses occur when the Moon is close to her node, in other words, close to zero latitude. For the third, in the calculation of the Moon’s phases, only her declination is employed, not her latitude.

chunks.text: Some conclusions that may be drawn from this study on the missing algorithm for the Moon’s maximum latitude in Indian astronomy are as follows: (1) The expression to calculate the Moon’s latitude, as given in various Indian texts, is precisely correct per modern spherical trigonometry. (2) One of the terms employed in the expression for latitude is the Maximum Latitude. Though the oldest extant Indian text, the Sūryasiddhānta, clearly indicates that the maximum latitude of the Moon is variable, it does not explicitly present a way to calculate this maximum latitude, providing instead only a mean value of the maximum latitude. (3) The analysis conducted in this paper discovered that the missing algorithm for the Moon’s maximum latitude may have had a simple form based on the elongation between the Sun and the Moon. (4) It is speculated that the missing algorithm may have been expunged from the Sūrya siddhānta due to long disuse since the Moon’s maximum latitude is not an essential parameter in any other calculations. (5) On the question of why the ancients were unaware that the Moon’s maximum latitude is not $4.5^\circ$ but $5.3^\circ$, it is conjectured that these astronomers were primarily concerned with the Moon’s maximum declination, and not the maximum latitude per se. Since the maximum declination is a combination of the maximum latitude and the obliquity, it is shown in this paper that the negative error due to assuming a maximum latitude of $4.5^\circ$ is compensated by the positive error in assuming an obliquity of $24^\circ$, resulting in the summed maximum declination of the Moon to be close to the actual observed maximum declination. More research is needed before anything material can be established on the subject. The discovery of any ancient documents containing an algorithm for the maximum latitude would certainly be a fortuitous development in this regard and is eagerly awaited. In the meantime, one area to explore further is the possibility of improving upon the simple expression presented in this paper for the Moon’s maximum latitude to bring it closer to actuality. chunks.text: The conceptualisation of negative numbers represents a fascinating aspect of mathematical development, characterised by its evolution over time and its multifaceted applications across various disciplines. This paper embarks on a scholarly exploration of this intriguing subject, focusing on a salient segment from Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava, a detailed commentary of Bhāskarācārya’s Bījagaṇita. It situates the discussion within its historical and scholarly context by examining the complexities inherent in understanding ‘negative’ quantities. While briefly referencing the evolution of negative numbers by notable mathematicians such as Brahmagupta and Bhāskara, the primary focus remains on dissecting a section of the “dhanarṇaṣaḍvidha” excerpt from Bījapallava, thereby shedding light on significant aspects of the discussion on negative numbers. Keywords dhana · ṛṇa · dhanarṇaṣaḍvidha · Bījapallava · Kṛṣṇa Daivajña · Negative numbers · Indian mathematics

chunks.title: The conception of negative numbers: A study of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava
chunks.author_display: Lalitha S R, Nagendra P R N, K Ramasubramanian
heading_path: The conception of negative numbers: A study of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava
chunks.text: The concept of numbers is one of the most ancient, important, and fascinating inventions of the human mind. The representation of numbers using different systems across various civilisations over the ages is an amusing and engaging story in itself.1 Typically, the concept of numbers is introduced to a child by using physical objects or their sketches on paper. Therefore, we generally understand a number to denote the count or measure of something. Consequently, the notion of negative numbers and the notion of negativity inherent in numbers would have been intriguing to people for centuries. In the textbooks on mathematics, negative numbers are generally denoted by positioning them to the left of zero on a numerical line. Despite the commonplace usage of phrases such as “negative thinking,” the precise connotation of negativity as an attribute of or adjective for numbers may not be immediately apparent to those encountering it for the first time. Upon observing the number line, one may intuit that negative numbers denote quantities lesser than zero. However, a more thorough investigation is necessary to fully ascertain their conceptual significance. This paper aims to explore the conceptualisation of negative numbers by delving into a salient textual excerpt from Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava, focusing on the conceptualisation of negative numbers. To provide a comprehensive understanding, it situates this investigation within a broader historical and scholarly context, emphasising the complexities inherent in grappling with the concept of negatives. Drawing on a rich lineage of mathematical thinkers including Brahmagupta and Bhāskara, the paper traces the trajectory of negative numbers in Indian mathematics. It discusses how negative numbers were applied in diverse fields such as accounting, algebraic expressions related to spherical trigonometry, and astronomy. Given that Bījapallava is a prominent commentary of Bījagaṇita, the paper also examines the significance of commentarial traditions in shaping mathematical discourse in ancient India. By closely scrutinising a specific excerpt from the “dhanarṇaṣaḍvidha” of Bījapallava, the paper aims to illuminate how the complex concept of negative numbers was elegantly introduced, highlighting the practical applications associated within the Indian mathematical tradition. 1: Ifrah (2000). ***

2 Precursor to the notion of negative quantities
chunks.text: The terms that are generally used for the positive (+ve) and negative (−ve) quantities in the Indian mathematical treatises are dhana (wealth) and ṛṇa (debt) respectively. One of the earliest references for the use of the word ṛṇa can be traced back to the Vedic corpus. We have the following passage in the Kṛṣṇa-yajurveda: जायमानो वै ब्राह्मणस्त्रिभिरृणवा जायते ब्रह्मचर्येण ऋषिभ्यो यज्ञेन देवेभ्यः प्रजया पितृभ्य एष वा अनृणो यः पुत्री यज्वा ब्रह्मचारिवासी तदवदानैरेवाव दयते तदवदानानामवदानत्वम् । (तै.सं. ६.३.१०.५) jāyamāno vai brāhmaṇastribhirṛṇavā jāyate brahmacaryeṇa ṛṣibhyo yajñena devebhyaḥ prajayā pitṛbhya eṣa vā anṛṇo yaḥ puttrī yajvā brahmacārivāsī tadavadānairevāva dayate tadavadānānām avadānatvam | (Taittirīyasaṃhitā 6.3.10.5) The above passage essentially states that an individual is born with three debts, namely: 1. the debt towards the seers and scholars of the past, whose wisdom has provided us with a vision to shape our lives and build a harmonious atmosphere around us, 2. the debt to the nature around us (personified as divine forces), whose blessings have provided us with a conducive environment to live, and finally 3. the debt towards the ancestors in our family, to whom we completely owe our existence today. This passage was cited primarily to draw readers’ attention to the use of the the word ‘ṛṇa’ in one of the most ancient literatures that has survived intact to date. Since further discussion on this topic is not germane to this paper, without much elaboration, we will proceed to highlight other ancient texts that discuss negative quantities.

3 Brahmagupta’s rule for dealing with negatives
chunks.text: By the 7th century CE, one of the most prominent Indian mathematicians, Brahmagupta, discussed the application of negative numbers in detail. It has been generally accepted among the historians of mathematics that he was the first to provide a detailed explanation of operations involving both positive and negative numbers. His contributions include the conceptualisation of zero as the result of subtracting a number from itself and the formulation of rules governing arithmetic operations on negative and positive numbers, as well as surds. Negative numbers feature prominently in Brahmagupta’s treatise, Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta (628 CE). The following verses from the 18th chapter illustrate the arithmetic of zero, positive and negative numbers and it is noteworthy that, with the sole exception of zero divided by zero being zero, these are identical to their counterparts in modern algebra:2 धनयोर्धनमृणमृणयोर्धनर्णयोरन्तरं समैक्यं खम् । ऋणमैक्यं च धनमृणधनशून्ययोः शून्ययोः शून्यम् ॥ १८.३० ॥ शून्यविहीनमृणमृणं धनं धनं भवति शून्यमाकाशम् । शोध्यं यदा धनमृणादृणं धनाद्वा तदा क्षेप्यम् ॥ १८.३२ ॥ ऋणमृणधनयोर्घातो धनमृणयोधनवधो धनं भवति । शून्यर्णयोः खधनयोः खशून्ययोर्वा वधः शून्यम् ॥ १८.३३ ॥ धनभक्तं धनमृणहृतमृणं धनं भवति खभक्तं खम् । भक्तमृणेन धनमृणं धनेन हृतमृणं मृणं भवति ॥ १८.३४ ॥ खोध्दृतमृणं धनं वा तच्छेदं खमृणधनविभक्तं वा । ऋणधनयोर्वर्गः स्वं खं खस्य पदं कृतिर्यत्तत् ॥ १८.३५ ॥ dhanayor dhanam ṛṇam ṛṇayor dhanarṇayor antaraṃ samaikyaṃ kham | ṛṇam aikyaṃ ca dhanam ṛṇadha naśūnyayoḥ śūnyayoḥ śūnyam ||18.30|| śūnyavihīnam ṛṇam ṛṇaṃ dhanaṃ dhanaṃ bhavati śūnyam ākāśam | śodhyaṃ yadā dhanam ṛṇād ṛṇam dhanād vā tadā kṣepyam ||18.32|| ṛṇam ṛṇadhanayor ghāto dhanam ṛṇayor dhanavadho dhanaṃ bhavati | śūnyarṇayoḥ khadhanayoḥ khaśūnyayor vā vadhaḥ śūnyam ||18.33|| dhanabhaktaṃ dhanam ṛṇahṛtam ṛṇam dhanaṃ bhavati khabhaktaṃ kham | bhaktam ṛṇena dhanam ṛṇaṃ dhanena hṛtam ṛṇam ṛṇaṃ bhavati ||18.34|| khoddhṛtam ṛṇaṃ dhanaṃ vā tacchedaṃ kham ṛṇadhanavibhaktaṃ vā | ṛṇadhanayor vargaḥ svaṃ khaṃ khasya padaṃ kṛtir yat tat ||18.35|| ... [The sum of] positive (dhana) and negative (ṛṇa), if they are equal, is zero (kha). The sum of a negative and zero is negative, of a positive and zero is positive and of two zeros, zero (śūnya). ... Zero subtracted from negative is negative, from positive is positive, and from zero is zero (ākāśa). ... The product of zero and a negative, of zero and a positive, or of two zeroes is zero. ... A zero divided by zero is zero. ... A positive or a negative divided by zero is that with zero-denominator.3 The treatise presents precise guidelines for the arithmetic of negative numbers, with positive and negative integers denoted by the terms dhana and ṛṇa: literally meaning “wealth/ fortune” and “debt” respectively. It is, therefore, evident that the practice of accounting is highly likely to have facilitated the natural integration of negative numbers into arithmetic computations. 2: Brāhmasphuṭasiddhānta of Brahmagupta, Ed. with his own commentary by Dvivedi (1902, verses 18.30–35, pp. 309–310). 3: Ramasubramanian and Srinivas (2010, p. 204). ***

chunks.title: The conception of negative numbers: A study of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava
chunks.author_display: Lalitha S R, Nagendra P R N, K Ramasubramanian
heading_path: The conception of negative numbers: A study of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava
4 Compelling contexts for the evaluation of negatives
chunks.text: The conjecture that it was the highly developed tradition of accounting in India which led to a fuller understanding of negative numbers has some scholarly endorsement from Mattessich.4 However, David Mumford, in his eminently readable historiography entitled “What’s So Baffling About Negative Numbers?” muses as to “what considerations led Indian mathematicians in the late centuries BCE or the early centuries CE to these conclusions—especially for the multiplication of negative numbers” and points out how the introduction of negative numbers paved the path for deeper explorations in algebra:5 Perhaps the deepest of these was the Indian work on Pell’s equation $x^2 - Ny^2 = m$ — especially finding solutions for $m = 1$: Brahmagupta himself made the first huge step, discovering the multiplication law arising from the factorization $$x^2 - Ny^2 = (x + \sqrt{N}y)(x - \sqrt{N}y).$$ More exactly, he showed how from solutions of the equation for $m1, m2$, one gets one for their product $m = m1 \dots m2$. Additionally, early contributions to Indian mathematics were closely interwoven with advancements in astronomy, calendrics, and time reckoning. Mathematical inquiry, as well as the development of mathematical concepts and techniques, served, at least initially, as an auxiliary discipline to facilitate and aid the practical needs of understanding celestial phenomena and maintaining accurate time measurements. The conceptualisation of the negatives was also applied in Indian astronomy.6 In the tradition of astronomical scholarship of specifying variables pertaining to astronomical measurements, negative numbers find yet another application in the realm of coordinates, particularly in measuring celestial latitude (separation along a great circle, perpendicular to the ecliptic) or declination (separation along a great circle, perpendicular to the celestial equator) of celestial objects such as planets and stars. The conception of these physical quantities measured in opposite directions as positive and negative becomes evident from the exposition provided by Kṛṣṇa Daivajña (see Sect. 7.4.2). Despite the natural fit for negative numbers in these contexts, tradition often dictates the use of north/south designations rather than positive/negative, posing a challenge to altering this convention. However, in the context of converting a pair of values specifying the position of the planets in one coordinate system to the other and when calculating the rising times of the Sun, etc., positives and negatives frequently need to be incorporated into formulas. They are also employed in the calculation of the duration of lagnas, as well as in determining sine values themselves. Thus, we find compelling contexts where rules for negatives are used.

chunks.text: Usually, the source texts in the Indian tradition, particularly in ancient times, have been composed adopting a terse style of versification. This is true irrespective of the discipline—be it philosophy, aesthetics, astronomy or mathematics. Consequently, in order to fully appreciate the content of these texts, we need to resort to commentaries authored at much later times, sometimes even a millenia later. Within Indic scholarship, commentaries serve a significant function not only in understanding the content of the text, but also in appreciating the epistemic structure of knowledge systems. Consistent with the customary practice, we encounter multiple commentaries on a single text, be it in philosophy, literature, music, astronomy or mathematics. For instance, Līlāvatī of Bhāskara II, undoubtedly one of the most elegant and foundational texts in the genre, has several extant commentaries, such as Buddhivilāsinī, Kriyākramakarī, Līlāvatīvivaraṇa, Līlāvatīvāsanā, Gaṇitāmṛtalaharī and so on. Likewise, his Bījagaṇita garnered considerable scholarly attention in the commentatorial tradition. This prominence prompted numerous scholars to produce commentaries on the text, including Bālabodhinī (also known as Bījodāharaṇa, Bījagaṇitavivṛti, or Bījagaṇitavyākhyā), Bījapallava (alternatively titled Bījavivṛti-kalpalatāvatāra or Kalpalatāvatāra), Bījavivṛtikalpalatā, Bījaprabodha, Bījagaṇitatīkā, and Sūryaprakāśabījavyākhyā.7 Of these, Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava seems to have been the most popular one. 4: Mattessich (2000, Chap. 7, pp. 129–143). 5: Mumford (2010, p. 124). 6: See Mumford (2010, p. 124). 7: See Footnote 21 of Chapter 1 in Ram (2012) that refers to Sen (1966). ***

chunks.text: Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava is an extensive commentary on Bhāskarācārya’s Bījagaṇita, written during the late sixteenth century. We can comprehend how elaborate this commentary is from a succinct note provided by the author himself. At the end of the commentary, after presenting a brief account of his academic lineage—just as Bhāskara himself does—Kṛṣṇa Daivajña notes that his commentary altogether has about 4500 granthas: एवमादितो ग्रन्थसंख्या ४४५८ । evamādito granthasaṃkhyā 4458 | Thus, the number of the granthas from the beginning is 4458. Though the word grantha has various connotations, in this context, it means 32 syllables, which is essentially what a verse composed in anuṣṭubh metre has. Bhāskara at the end of Bījagaṇita notes: अत्रानुष्टुप् सहस्रं हि ससूत्रोद्देश्यके मितिः । atrānuṣṭupsahasraṃ hi sasūtroddeśyake mitiḥ | In this (book), including sūtra and uddeśya, the measure is one thousand anuṣṭups [32000 syllables]. Thus we see that the commentary, Bījapallava, is approximately 4.5 times larger in size than the text Bījagaṇita, along with his own vāsanā by Bhāskara.8 Fig. 4. 6.1 Lineage of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña and his work
chunks.text: Kṛṣṇa Daivajña, a distinguished scholar of his era, belonged to a venerable lineage of astronomers and mathematicians. His academic and genealogical lineage, detailed at the end of his work Bījapallava, reveals a rich heritage of scholarly excellence and devotion. His ancestor Śrīkeśava, a master of the discipline of gaṇita, passed down his extensive knowledge to Gaṇeśa, whose virtuous fame and mastery of jyotiṣaśāstra were highly celebrated. Gaṇeśa’s nephew, Nṛsiṃha, carried this tradition of excellence forward, and his disciple Viṣṇu further advanced their scholarly lineage. It was under Viṣṇu’s guidance that Kṛṣṇa Daivajña studied all the three branches of jyotiṣa and emerged as a preeminent scholar. Fig. 1 provides the academic lineage of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña over three generations. Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s familial lineage, delineated in Fig. 2, is equally illustrious. His ancestor Cintāmaṇi, known for his devotion and virtues, was revered to the extent that Goddess Gaurī herself is said to have appeared in response to his prayers. Cintāmaṇi’s lineage included Rāma, a highly esteemed figure whose foresight was sought by the King of Vidarbha. Rāma’s sons, Trimalla and Gopirāja, and subsequently Trimalla’s son Ballāla, continued to enhance the family’s scholarly reputation. Ballāla’s son, Kṛṣṇa Daivajña, maintained and elevated this legacy through his many notable contributions. Kṛṣṇa Daivajña produced the Chādakanirṇaya, an original piece on eclipse calculation, and several other scholarly commentaries, including those on Bhāskara’s Līlāvatī and Śrīpati’s Jātakapaddhati. Furthermore, he is said to have played a pivotal role among the cohort of scholars at the court tasked with the Sanskrit translation of Ulugh Beg’s astronomical tables.

6.2 The dedication in Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava
chunks.text: In Bījapallava, Kṛṣṇa Daivajña poetically describes the emergence of his work by invoking the metaphor of a seed sprouting from the earth. The following beautiful verse in vasantatilakā metre is embellished with two figures of speech, śleṣa (puns) and rūpaka (metaphors): यद्भास्करेण निजधामगुणातिरेकात् संपादितं सगुणवर्गघनं हि बीजम् । तत्कृष्णभूमिमधिगम्य विचारवारि- संसिक्तमाङ्कुरजनुष्यभवत् समर्थम् ॥ ६ ॥ yadbhāskareṇa nijadhāmaguṇātirekāt saṃpāditaṃ saguṇavargaghanaṃ hi bījam | tatkṛṣṇabhūmimadhigamya vicāravāri- saṃsiktamaṅkurajanuṣyabhavat samartham || 6 || The verse can be interpreted in two distinct ways due to the dexterous usage of certain words that have double meaning. 8: As these texts involve equations and numerical values, how exactly the count of syllables is made is a matter of investigation in itself and may be worth undertaking. ** Fig. 5. Family lineage of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña Fig. 5. Family lineage of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña The key phrase in the verse is ‘vicāravāri’. The word ‘vicāra’ means contemplation, and ‘vāri’ is water. These two words, independently connected with the rest of the words in the verse give rise to the two distinct interpretations because of the nimble choice of a few other words. Table 1 presents a list of such śliṣṭa words in the verse that provide the pun and enable us to have two layers of interpretation. With one set of interpretation of the words (column 2 in the table), clubbed with an eloquent metaphor for the creative process that led to the writing of the text, we get the following meaning: The seed (bīja), dense with a set of virtues (saguṇavargaghanam), which was nourished by the Sun (yad bhāskareṇa), having found the [fertile] black soil (kṛṣṇabhūmi), sprinkled with water (vārisaṃsiktam), became capable of producing a sprout. A more nuanced reading in the context of algebra and the tradition of Indian mathematics choosing the other set of interpretation, we device the following meaning: Algebra or bījagaṇita, involving intricate discussions of scalar multiples, including exponents such as squares and cubes (sa-guṇa-varga-ghanam), curated originally by Bhāskarācārya [in his work Bījagaṇita] and nourished by the contemplative intellect of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña, led to the birth of the commentary [Bījapallava]. In another verse, the commentator, without shying away from openly admitting, articulates that enormous efforts have been invested in composing the commentary. यैर्यैः श्रमौर्विचितोऽस्ति नवाङ्कुरोऽसौ तेषामभिज्ञ इह कः परमात्मनोऽन्यः । इत्थं विचिन्त्य जगदीेश तवैव तुष्ट्यैै सर्वज्ञ ते चरणयोर्नििहितस्ततोऽयम् ॥ ७ ॥ yairyaiḥ śramair viracito’sti navāṅkuro’sau teṣāmabhijña iha kaḥ paramātmano’nyaḥ | itthaṃ vicintya jagadīśa tavaiva tuṣṭyai sarvajña te caraṇayor nihitas tato’yam || 7 || Who, other than God, is aware of the [stupendous] efforts involved in producing, i.e., composing this new sprout (navāṅkura) [namely the work Bījapallava]. Thinking along these lines, O the Omniscient (sarvajña) and the Lord of the universe, this work is placed at Thy feet in order to please Thee alone. The implication of what Kṛṣṇa Daivajña conveys in the above verse is:- Since the scholarly world, out of envy or jealousy, may not appreciate much the tremendous and sincere efforts that have been put by me in elucidating Bhāskara’s work, I am more than happy dedicating this work to Thee, as it has been successfully completed to my heart’s content by Thy grace!9 Modern scholars have particularly valued Bījapallava as this commentary features demonstrations and derivations of mathematical rules and relationships (referred to as upapatti) that include hypothetical dialogues between... | Śliṣṭa words | Literal reading | Interpretative variation | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | भास्कर | The Sun | Bhāskarācārya | | धाम | light or effulgence | brilliance or ability | | गुण | virtues, qualities or merits | a factor or a scalar multiple | | वर्ग | set or category | square or exponent of two | | घन | dense | cube or exponent of three | | बीज | seed | Bījagaṇita, the text, as well as algebra | | कृष्णभूमि | black soil | Kṛṣṇa Daivajña | Table 1 Meaning of some of the words with figurative usages such as śleṣa (pun) and rūpaka (metaphor) 9: It is typical in Indian tradition to not take pride in one’s accomplishments and to dedicate the effort and fruit of one’s endeavours to the Almighty. <<<CONTINUE>>> the commentator and an imagined interlocutor. It also analyses fundamental mathematical concepts that underpin the algorithms, such as zero, unknown quantities, negative numbers, explorations into issues of determinability and conditions for solvability, among other topics. It has sections dedicated to the six mathematical operations, the pulveriser (kuṭṭaka), indeterminate equations of the second degree, equations with one unknown, as well as equations with multiple unknowns. The text has undergone several editorial revisions, including those by Āpaṭe (1930), Radhakrishna Sastri (1958), and Vasisht (1982). The Bījapallava presents intricate mathematical problems and stands out for its incorporation of upapatti. Though, etymologically, the word upapatti has many a nuances in interpretation, in a broad sense, it can be understood as “explanation,” “reasoning,” “proof,” “demonstration,” or “derivation,” depending upon the context in which it is employed. We now move on to present the detailed upapatti* given by Kṛṣṇa Daivajña to drive home the concepts of negative numbers.

heading_path: The conception of negative numbers: A study of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava
7 Conceptualisation of negative numbers: textual analysis of the excerpt on dhanarṇaṣaḍvidha from Bījapallava
7.1 Introducing positive and negative through commonplace example
chunks.text: The section under consideration, a prose piece, commences with the sentence: एवं देवदत्तस्य मुद्रात्रयमेकं धनम् । अन्यदपि मुद्राचतुष्टयं धनमस्तीत्युक्ते अस्त्यस्य मुद्रासप्तकं धनमिति विलसति सार्वजनीनो व्यवहारः । evaṃ devadattasya mudrātrayamekaṃ dhanam | anyadapi mudrācatuṣṭayaṃ dhanamastītyukte astyasya mudrāsaptakaṃ dhanamiti vilasati sārvajanīno vyavahāraḥ | Thus, Devadatta has three mudrās. If you say that he has another four mudrās, then that he has [totally] seven mudrās in his possession is a common discourse among all people. The fundamental mathematical concept of addition is mentioned at the outset. The commentator uses an illustration featuring a character named Devadatta. Described as possessing three mudrās or coins10 initially, Devadatta is said to further have four additional mudrās [received as a gift]. It is then of common knowledge (sārvajanīno vyavahāraḥ) that Devadatta is now in possession of a total of seven mudrās. Taking the discussion further ahead, the commentator states that if Devadatta has three mudrās of wealth in his possession, and a debt or ṛṇa of four mudrās, then, again, the prevalent notion among all (sakalajanasādhāraṇo vyavahāraḥ) would be that he has a debt of one mudrā. Likewise, if he has a debt of three mudrās and has four mudrās with him, then he would be thought of as being debt-free and having a mudrā left with him. Here, the commentator is, in essence, evoking, illustrating and expatiating upon two quotes from Bījagaṇita that he employs to serve as the foundation for his subsequent conceptualisations and discussions: योगे युतिः स्यात् क्षययोः स्वर्वा धनर्णयोरन्तरमेव योगः । yoge yutiḥ syāt kṣayayoḥ svayorvā dhanarṇayorantarameva yogaḥ | When the two numbers are both positive (dhana) or negative (ṛṇa) then the sum (yoga) is obtained by addition. [If not] the difference of the positive and negative is the sum. It is well known in the world, that if the positive (wealth in one’s own possession) and negative (debt) are of equal magnitudes, they nullify each other leading to zero as net possession. On the other hand if they are of different magnitudes, then whichever is of greater magnitude is what remains positive or negative as the net possession. The basic idea is that two debts can be combined into a single debt of greater magnitude. This narrative introduction sets the stage for further explanation and exploring mathematical operations within a relatable framework.

7 Conceptualisation of negative numbers: textual analysis of the excerpt on dhanarṇaṣaḍvidha from Bījapallava
chunks.text: Following this introduction, the commentator goes on to mention, in passing, the fundamental arithmetic operations of addition and subtraction (saṃkalana and vyavakalana) of both fractions and whole numbers (bhinnānām abhinnānāṃ ca). He also justifies the inclusion and omission of certain operations for whole numbers or integers (rūpavarṇa) vis-à-vis surds (karaṇī). Then he notes that it is apt to introduce addition before other operations such as subtraction, as they are all dependent on addition (saṃkalanopajīvakatva). Subtraction as well as multiplication are based on addition. Here subtraction is visualised as the addition of a negative value: तथापि धनर्णताव्यत्यासमात्रविलक्षणस्य व्यवकलनस्य tathāpi dhanarṇatāvyatyāsamātravilakṣaṇasya Even then, it [the subtraction] is different [from the addition] only because of the nature of the quantities being positive and negative. Addition with a negative quantity gives the difference. When both quantities are negative, they are added using the mathematical operator of addition. The following verse from Bījagaṇita is quoted in this context to bring greater clarity: संशोध्यमानं स्वमृणत्वमेति स्वत्वं क्षयस्तद्युतिरुक्तवच्च । saṃśodhyamānaṃ svamṛṇatvameti svatvaṃ kṣaya-stadyutiruktavacca | A positive [number], that is being subtracted (saṃśodhyamānaṃ), becomes a negative [number],11 and, a negative [number] (kṣayaḥ) [becomes] positive. And their addition is as stated earlier. In providing the translation to the above verse, it may be noted that we have supplied that verb eti which means ‘becomes’ again. It is quite common in Sanskrit tradition to be highly conservative and unostentatious with respect to the use of words. That we are right, and have not taken any additional liberty in doing so, is evident from the commentary. It is said: तद्यदि धनमस्ति तर्हि ऋणत्वमेति । यदि क्षयोऽस्ति तर्हि धनत्वमेति । tadyadi dhanamasti tarhi rṇatvameti | yadi kṣayo'sti tarhi dhanatvameti | If it (i.e., the quantity to be subtracted) is positive, then it (positive) becomes negative. If it is negative (kṣaya), it becomes positive. Having succinctly summarised how to deal with the basic mathematical operations, the commentary proceeds to very systematically introduce the concept of negative quantities.

heading_path: The conception of negative numbers: A study of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava
7 Conceptualisation of negative numbers: textual analysis of the excerpt on dhanarṇaṣaḍvidha from Bījapallava
chunks.text: It was quite natural for Kṛṣṇa Daivajña to commence the discussion with positive quantity and first establish the fundamental and straightforward nature of the addition rule (saṃkalana), before elaborating extensively on subtraction (vyavakalana). This is because even in real-world scenarios such as borrowing money, the borrowed amount is, after all, a positive quantity. These descriptions may prompt the readers to embark upon thinking that negative quantities exist solely at a conceptual level; there are no real negative numbers. Whatever needs to be removed from one’s possession or deducted is conceived as negative. Again, when two quantities, both of the same nature positive or negative (kṣayayoḥ va svayorvā), need to be added, the operation is addition. So, shall we say that the negative numbers are mere mental constructs? From a certain viewpoint, yes we can say so and this can be appreciated too. However, negative numbers are as fundamental as positive numbers in mathematics! If negative numbers are mental constructs so too are positive numbers! In mathematical computations, we require negative notations to accurately represent situations such as debt or deficits. More often than not, it is such real-life needs, applications and observations that inspire specific modes of mathematical reasoning and abstraction, ultimately leading to the conceptualisation and creation of abstract yet highly useful entities such as negative numbers.

7.4 Categorisation of negative entities: spatial, temporal and possessional
chunks.text: In the ensuing portion, Kṛṣṇa Daivajña proposes a lucid categorisation of the concept of negative entities into three distinct types: ऋणत्वमिह त्रिधा तावदस्ति - देशतः, कालतः, वस्तुतश्चेति । ṛṇatvamiha tridhā tāvadasti - deśataḥ, kālataḥ, vastutaśceti | Negativeness is indeed of three types — pertaining to location (or space), time, and possession (or ownership) [of objects]. He also defines the negative [in each of these categories] as oppositeness or contrariety: tacca vaiparītyameva. The negative is thus characterised by polarity, antithesis, or possessing an opposite character. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the passage extends its exploration beyond basic arithmetic, delving into broader applications of negative values. The concept of the negative with respect to space is explained using three examples.

7.4 Categorisation of negative entities: spatial, temporal and possessional
7.4.1 Geometric demonstration of the negative in terms of directionality
chunks.text: The first demonstration or upapatti uses a geometric construction described in the text Līlāvatī. The case in point is verse 168, appearing in the chapter on geometry titled “Kṣetravyavahāra”. This verse is presented by Bhāskara as a problem to be solved in connection with finding the alititude (lambaka) of a triangle. This specific problem is entitled ṛṇābādhodāharaṇa which means an example when the ābādhā 12 is negative: दशसप्तदशप्रमौ भुजौ त्रिभुजे यत्र नवप्रमा मही । अबाधे वद लम्बकं तथा गणितं गाणितिकाशु तत्र मे ॥ १६८ ॥ daśasaptadaśapramau bhujau tribhuje yatra navapramā mahī | abadhe vada lambakaṃ tathā gaṇitaṃ gāṇitikāśu tatra me || 168 || In a triangle which has sides of measure 10 and seventeen and the base is measured nine, O mathematician, tell me immediately the altitude (lambaka), the two segments (abadhe) of the base and the area (gaṇita). The problem posed by Bhāskara can be understood with the help of Fig. 3. Here $ABC$ is the triangle whose two sides and the base are specified in the verse to be 10, 17 and 9 respectively. Now the problem is to find the altitude $BD$. It is evident that the triangle $ABC$ is an obtuse triangle. Hence, Bhāskara demonstrates how to find the solution to the problem. He indicates that the two ābādhās, $AD$ and $CD$, are 15 and 6 respectively. The foot of the perpendicular, $BD$, falls outside the base $AC$ of the obtuse triangle $ABC$, forming a negative ābādhā, $CD$. Of this excellent geometric demonstration of the conceptualisation of negative distance, Mumford remarks as follows:13 This is stated so casually, as if it were common wisdom, that one can only conclude that this way of thinking about negative distances was well-known in his time. Nonetheless, as we will see, it doesn’t occur in Europe before the work of Wallis near the end of 17th century. Kṛṣṇa Daivajña observes that, in terms of directionality, the ṛṇābādhā has the nature of reversal or viparītasya bhāva as is required by negative entities: ऋणगता आबाधा दिग्‍वैपरीत्येन इत्यर्थ इति । ṛṇagatā ābādhā digvaiparītyena ityartha iti | The ābādhā on the negative side is because of the opposition in direction. Fig. 8. Illustration of ṛṇābādhodāharaṇam in the Līlāvatī Fig. 8. Illustration of ṛṇābādhodāharaṇam in the Līlāvatī In the next upapatti, this notion of the negative in directionality is taken a step ahead.

heading_path: The conception of negative numbers: A study of Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s Bījapallava
7 Conceptualisation of negative numbers: textual analysis of the excerpt on dhanarṇaṣaḍvidha from Bījapallava
7.4 Categorisation of negative entities: spatial, temporal and possessional
7.4.2 The negative visualised with the aid of number line and directions
chunks.text: In the earlier geometric example, the concept of the negative in the context of directionality assumes that the two segments lying on either side of $C$ are designated as positive and negative. This suggests that the measurements are positive in one direction and negative in the other. This idea is neatly elucidated by Kṛṣṇa Daivajña as follows: तत्र एका रेखा स्थिता । द्वितीया दिक् विपरीता दिक् इत्युच्यते, यथा पूर्वविपरीता पश्चिमा दिक्, यथा वा उत्तरदिग्विपरीता दक्षिणा दिक् इत्यादि । तथा च पूर्वापरदेशयोर्मध्ये एकतरस्य धनत्वे कल्पिते तं प्रति तदितरस्य ऋणत्वम् । tatra ekā rekhā sthitā | dvitīyā dik viparītā dik ityucyate, yathā pūrvaviparītā paścimā dik, yathā vā uttaradigviparītā dakṣiṇā dik ityādi | tathā ca pūrvāparadeśayormadhye ekatarasya dhanatve kalpite taṃ prati taditarasya ṛṇatvam | There is [essentially] one line. [Having marked a point in that line], the other direction is said to be the opposite direction, much like how east is opposite to west, or south is opposite to the north and so on. Thus among the eastern and the western regions, if one is designated as positive, then the other is considered negative. Here, ṛṇatva (negativeness) is introduced by invoking the concept of displacement along the opposite (viparīta) directions in a line, by considering segments along the line in opposite direction, having chosen a point of reference in that line as ‘origin’. This, dating back to circa 1150 AD, could be deemed as “the first occurrence of the “number line”, of using positive and negative numbers as coordinates on either side of an origin.”14 Having discussed the notion of negativity in connection with the displacement along a line in the opposite directions, the commentator next proceeds to conceptualise the negative using observational astronomy (Fig. 4). 7.4 Categorisation of negative entities: spatial, temporal and possessional
7.4.3 Use of negatives in connection with the motion of celestial objects
chunks.text: The phenomenon of apparent retrogradation among planetary bodies in the solar system has long intrigued ancient astronomers. All the celestial bodies, the Sun, Moon, planets and stars have a certain uniform motion westwards.15 This motion (from east to west) is purely apparent and is due to the rotation of the Earth. However, the Sun, Moon and planets have their proper motion towards the east, and this causes their longitudes to increase. Of course, the rate at which the longitude increases is different for different celestial bodies. For the Sun and the Moon, the longitudes keep increasing continuously. On an average, the rate at which the Moon’s longitude is $\approx 13^\circ/\text{day}$ whereas for the Sun it is close to one degree per day. In the case of planets, as they keep traversing eastwards, something bizarre happens. During their orbital motion, at certain points in their orbits, the planets appear to take a momentary halt from their eastward drift. And in the subsequent days, it would appear as if they are moving westwards having taken a reverse course in their motion. This phenomenon could continue for a few days, a few weeks, or a few months (as in the case of Saturn) depending upon the planet. After this, once again they may halt momentarily and continue their eastward motion. In this manner, all the five planets, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn—that are visible to the naked eyes—seem to exhibit this kind of ‘strange’ motion called retrograde in English and vakragati in Sanskrit, of the planets noted by the observers on the Earth. This apparent reversal in direction of motion has to do with the relative positions of the planet, the Earth, and the Sun. Kṛṣṇa Daivajña invokes this particular planetary phenomenon called viparītasya bhāva to illustrate dhanaṛṇatva, the notion of positive and negative: पूर्वगतेर्धनत्वकल्पने यदा ग्रहः पश्चिमगतिर्भवति तदा ग्रहे गतितुल्यकला ऋणं भवति । यथा वा पश्चिमभ्रमस्य धनत्वे यावद् ग्रहः पूर्वतो गच्छति तावत् पश्चिमभ्रमे ऋणमिति । दक्षिणोत्तरदेशादिष्वप्येवमेव धनर्णत्वं बोध्यम् । pūrvagaterdhanatvakalpane yadā grahaḥ paścimagatirbhavati tadā grahe gatitulyakalā ṛṇaṃbhavati | yathā vā paścimabhramasya dhanatve yāvad grahaḥ pūrvato gacchati tāvat paścimabhrame ṛṇamiti | dakṣiṇottaradeśādiṣvapyevameva dhanaṛṇatvaṃ bodhyam | If movement towards the east is considered positive, when a planet moves towards the west, then that amount of motion in minutes (gatitulyakalā) is considered negative. Conversely, if the westward movement is regarded as positive, then as much as the planet moves eastwards, that much (tāvat) is conceived to be negative (ṛṇam) in [terms of] westward motion (paścimabhrame). It may be understood that this way of conceiving positive and negative is applicable to the regions in the north-south directions and so on.16 Here the commentator brilliantly makes use of the commonly observed phenomenon of apparent retrograde motion of planets to explain the concept of negativity. This choice could be based on two reasons: to facilitate the understanding that the system of positive and negative is not confined to describing things in the terrestrial frame, but also in the celestial frame. to indicate that what matters is the directionality that is invoked by us in describing the phenomenon and not whether the direction is conceived on the ground or in the space. Given that astronomy or jyotiṣa is essentially the science of time reckoning (kālavidhāna śāstra), it is fairly intuitive that the text next addresses time as a means to conceive of the notion of the negative.

7.5 The concept of the negative in temporal terms
chunks.text: Having introduced the concept of -ve numbers using spatial coordinates, Kṛṣṇa Daivajña moves on to explain the same by making use of the concept of travelling back in time. The negativity of earlier and later times may be exemplified in determining the day as well as through the organisation of the days of the week, where each day follows a sequential order from the beginning (Sunday) to the end (Saturday): एवं पूर्वोत्तरकालयोः अन्योन्यं ऋणत्वं वारप्रवृत्त्यादिषु प्रसिद्धम् । evaṃ pūrvottarakālayoḥ anyonyam ṛṇatvaṃ vārapravṛttyādiṣu prasiddham | Similarly, the relativity (anyonya) of the negativity of the previous and later times (pūrvottara kāla) is well known with reference to the passage of the day and so on. We know that the past was indeed present and the future is also going to be present. Thus, Kṛṣṇa Daivajña, by presenting this example, buttresses the notion of negativity by helping us think of the concept in multiple ways.

7.6 The concept of the negative in ownership
chunks.text: The concept of negative quantities is further elucidated in the context of ownership or possession. Here, the vaiparītya is demonstrated concerning the relationship of ownership (svasvāmibhāva-sambandha). An entity is considered to belong to someone only as long as one can assert possession over it according to prevailing norms. When wealth is lost or transferred, what is truly lost or transferred is one’s association or sambandha with the svāmibhāva or ownership. Hence, in the transfer of ownership, when one party gains possession, the other has to necessarily lose. This idea of reciprocal nature of ownership of wealth/ properties and its connection with declaring them as positive (dhana) and negative (ṛṇa) is beautifully brought out in the following passage: एवं यस्मिन् वस्तुनि यस्य स्वस्वामिभावः सम्बन्धः तस्य तद्धनमिति व्यवह्रियते । तस्मिन् वैपरीत्यं तु परस्य स्वस्वामिभावः सम्बन्धः । अतो देवदत्तस्वामिके धने यावति यज्ञदत्तस्वामिकत्वं तावत् देवदत्तस्य ऋणमिति व्यवह्रियते । evaṃ yasmin vastuni yasya svasvāmibhāvaḥ sambandhaḥ tasya taddhanamiti vyavahriyate | tasmin vaiparītyaṃ tu parasya svasvāmibhāvaḥ sambandhaḥ | ato devadattasvāmike dhane yāvati yajñadattasvāmikatvaṃ tāvat devadattasya ṛṇamiti vyavahriyate | Similarly, when an entity is considered as belonging to a person, it is deemed as his wealth; [and, therefore, positive]. The converse [i.e., ṛṇa] is the case when the ownership of that entity shifts to another person. Therefore, that portion of Devadatta’s wealth over which Yajñadatta acquires ownership [by property transfer] is to be declared as Devadatta’s debt [and, therefore, negative]. Similarly, an entity is described to be the wealth (dhana) of a person as long as he possesses ownership over it.

7.7 Upapatti using “deśa”—a geographic example to elucidate the concept of the negative
chunks.text: Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s discussion on negative numbers using geographical locations to elucidate the concept is indeed captivating. The discussion explores the geographical relationship between three cities, all considered holy and pilgrimage spots. Of the three cities, two of them, Vārāṇasī and Prayāga are mentioned by names. The third one is simply described by the term ‘pattana’ and is stated to be on the banks of the Gaṅgā. Furthermore in this discussion, Vārāṇasī is thought of as the centre or origin. The ‘pattana’ is 15 yojanas towards the east from Vārāṇasī and to the west of Vārāṇasī, in eight yojanas, is Prayāga. So, the distance of separation (antara) between the pattana and Prayāga is 23 yojanas. As the description presented by Kṛṣṇa Daivajña is quite elaborate, discursive and self-explanatory, with this brief introduction, we straight away present the original passage along with the translation without making any further remarks or attempts to paraphrase it at this stage: श्रीविश्वेशितुः शम्भोः आनन्दकाननात् पुरन्दरदिशि पञ्चदशसु योजनेषु स्वर्गतरङ्गिणीतीरविलासि वरीवर्ति किलैकं पत्तनम् । वरुणदिशि वा अष्टसु योजनेषु इन्दीवरदलश्यामलापतङ्गतनयातङ्गचुम्बिभिः शरच्चन्द्रिकाधवलैः सुरनदीकल्लोलैः स्मृतहरिहरमूर्तिः आनन्दलहरीरनुभवन् जागर्ति तीर्थराजः प्रयागः ॥ śrīviśveśituḥ śambhoḥ ānandakānanāt purandaradiśi pañcadaśasu yojaneṣu svargataraṅgiṇītīravilāsi varīvarti kilaikaṃ pattanam | varuṇadiśi vā aṣṭasu yojaneṣu indīvaradalaśyāmalapataṅgatanayātaraṅgacumbibhiḥ śaraccandrikādhavalaiḥ suranadīkallolaiḥ smṛtahariharamūrtiḥ ānandalaharīranubhavan jāgarti tīrtharājaḥ prayāgaḥ | तयोस्तु उच्चावचसकलजनव्यवहारसिद्धमस्ति त्रयो-विंशति-योजनात्मकम् अन्तरम् । तच्च योगं विना नोपपद्यते । अतो विजातीययोरन्तरे साध्ये योगः कर्तव्यः । परं स योगः पश्चिमः पूर्वो वा ? तत्र पत्तनात् प्रयागः कस्यां दिशीति विचारे तावत् आनन्दकाननात् प्रयागपर्यन्तम् अष्टयोजनात्मको देशः यथा पश्चिमः, तथा पत्तनादपि पश्चिम एव । किन्तु आनन्दकाननात् पत्तनपर्यन्तं पञ्चदशयोजनात्मको यः पूर्वदेशः स भवति पत्तनात् पश्चिम एव । एवं पत्तनात् प्रयागपर्यन्तं देशविचारे आनन्दवनपर्यन्तं पञ्चदशयोजनात्मकमेकं शकलं, ततः प्रयागावाधि द्वितीयम् अष्टयोजनात्मकं शकलद्वयस्य पश्चिमतवाज्जातः त्रयोविंशतियोजनत्मकः पश्चिमो देशः । एवं प्रयागात् पत्तनं कस्यां दिशीति विचारे प्रयागादानन्दवनपर्यन्तं देशशकलं विपरीतदिक्कं भवति । 10: The word mudrā refers to coins with emblems, generally used for transactional purposes. These could be of gold, silver or any other metal. 11: In our translation, we have consciously rendered the term ‘ṛṇatvameti’ as ‘becomes a negative [number].’ A more literal translation would be ‘gains negativeness.’ This nuanced translation choice is significant, as it reflects the typical usage found in Sanskrit literature. 12: The word ābādhā is a technical term in Indian geometry for segments formed by the foot of the perpendicular drawn to the base of the triangle. This word ābādhā is also referred to by other terms such as abadhā, avabadhā, kukhaṇḍa, bhūkhaṇḍa, etc. in the literature. For instance, in the verse quoted above, it is called abadhā. Elsewhere in Līlāvatī Bhāskara uses the term ābādhā. 13: See Mumford (2010, pp. 126–127). 14: See Mumford (2010, p. 126). 15: In fact, all the clocks (digital or otherwise) have been designed to work in accordance with this apparent westward motion of the celestial sphere along with the celestial objects. 16: What the author indicates subtly here is the way the declination of the celestial bodies is conceived and specified in astronomy for the purpose of calculation.

7.7 Upapatti using “deśa”—a geographic example to elucidate the concept of the negative
chunks.text: तयोस्तु उच्चावचसकलजनव्यवहारसिद्धमस्ति त्रयोविंशतियोजनात्मकम् अन्तरम् । तच्च योगं विना नोपपद्यते । अतो विजातीययोरन्तरे साध्ये योगः कर्तव्यः । परं स योगः पश्चिमः पूर्वो वा ? तत्र पत्तनात् प्रयागः कस्यां दिशीति विचारे तावत् आनन्दकाननात् प्रयागपर्यन्तम् अष्टयोजनात्मको देशः यथा पश्चिमः, तथा पत्तनादपि पश्चिमो भवति । किन्तु आनन्दकाननात् पत्तनपर्यन्तं पञ्चदशयोजनात्मको यः पूर्वदेशः स भवति पत्तनात् पश्चिम एव ॥ एवं पत्तनात् प्रयागपर्यन्तं देशविचारे आनन्दवनपर्यन्तं पञ्चदशयोजनात्मकमेकं शकलं, ततः प्रयागावधि द्वितीयम् अष्टयोजनात्मकम् । शकलद्वयस्य पश्चिमत्वाज्जातः त्रयोविंशतियोजनात्मकः पश्चिमो देशः । एवं प्रयागात् पत्तनं कस्यां दिशीति विचारे प्रयागादानन्दवनपर्यन्तं देशशकलं विपरीतदिक्कं भवति ॥ Fifteen yojanas east of (purandaradiśi) Vārāṇasī (ānandakānanā), wherein dwells Lord śiva (śambhu), the Controller of the Universe, indeed lies a city (pattana), nestled along the banks of the Gaṅgā (svargataraṅgiṇī). To the west (varuṇadiśi), in eight yojanas, at the confluence is the king of (i.e., foremost among) pilgrim sites, Prayāga, revelling in the reminiscences of Hari and Hara, evoked by the confluence of the waves of Yamunā (pataṅgatanayā: daughter of the Sun) with her deep complexion resembling the blue lotus (indīvaradalaśyāmala), [as she] mingles with the celestial Gaṅgā (suranadī), whose hues are as white as the autumnal moon (śaraccandrikādhavalaiḥ). It is a commonplace knowledge established through the discourse of people of all classes (uccāvacasakalajanavyavahārasiddham) that the distance of separation (antara) between these cities (i.e., Prayāga and pattana) is $23\text{ yojanas}$. This would not be possible without the addition of [two] values. Thus to find the separation (antara) between [entities of] two genres (vijātīyayoḥ), addition must be performed. But is that addition eastward or westward? In discussing the direction of Prayāga from pattana, it is evident that as much as it is eight yojanas west from Vārāṇasī to Prayāga, so too, it is west with respect to pattana. However, [it is to be noted that] the distance of $15\text{ yojanas}$ eastwards from Vārāṇasī to pattana is to be considered westwards in relation to pattana. Similarly, when discussing about the intervening space between pattana and Prayāga, there is a segment (śakala) of $15\text{ yojanas}$ that extends to Vārāṇasī, and another segment of eight yojanas that extends to Prayāga. Because both these segments are westwards, the entire stretch of $23\text{ yojana}$ is westwards. Similarly, when we discuss about which direction pattana is from Prayāga, the segment from Prayāga to Vārāṇasī is in the opposite direction. The concepts described above can be better depicted as a figure to assist easy understanding. In Fig. 5, with respect to an observer $O$ at Vārāṇasī ($V$), there is a segment of $15\text{ yojanas}$ extending to pattana ($Pa$) in one direction and another segment of eight yojanas extending from Vārāṇasī to Prayāga ($Pr$) in the opposite direction. For the observer $O$, $OPa$ is $+15$ and $OPr$ is $-8$ (since it is in the opposite direction). The distance between $Pa$ and $Pr$ is obtained by finding the antara or difference between these two segments: $$OPa - (-OPr) = Pa Pr.$$ That is, $$15 - (-8) = 23.$$ To further elucidate Kṛṣṇa Daivajña’s exposition on negative numbers, it is essential to understand the dual meaning of the term ‘antara’ in Sanskrit. Antara signifies both the difference and the distance between two locations. This duality is fundamental in comprehending how Kṛṣṇa Daivajña conceptualises the subtraction of distances and the application of negative numbers. When he describes the distance between the pattana and Prayāga, he clarifies that the movement in opposite directions from a central point $O$ (Vārāṇasī) necessitates assigning one direction as positive and the opposite as negative. Thus, when determining the separation between these locations, the concept of subtracting a negative value naturally leads to a positive outcome, effectively illustrating the principle that subtracting a negative is equivalent to addition. This mathematical operation is not merely abstract but grounded in the physical reality of traversing distances in opposite directions. Therefore, when one moves $15\text{ yojanas}$ east from Vārāṇasī to the pattana and then $8\text{ yojanas}$ west to Prayāga, the total distance covered is $23\text{ yojanas}$, derived from the calculation $15 - (-8) = 23$. This explanation further underscores the practical application of negative numbers in ancient Indian mathematics, demonstrating how theoretical concepts are seamlessly integrated with tangible experiences.

7.8 Why subtracting a negative is equivalent to adding a positive?
chunks.text: Normally we learn in schools that two negative signs next to each other turn into a positive sign. This is usually learned as a mathematical rule without much of an explanation. The explanation that is at times offered is—think of removing a negative thought or reversing a loss that was incurred. However, having illustrated how the direction of travel impacts the perception of distance (as positive and negative), the commentator here strives hard to drive in the point why $-(- \text{number} ) = + \text{number}$. Proceeding with the finale of the discussion, he brilliantly elucidates why and how finding difference with a negative turns out to be a positive in the following para commencing with “tathā ca”, which means “therefore”. It is to be noted that this finale is purely based on the physical geographical description given above. In fact, it is to give this final punch such a detailed discussion was undertaken by Kṛṣṇa. Summarising the discussion he notes: तथा च, यस्मादनन्तरं साध्यते तदवधिशकलं विपरीतदिक्कं भवतीत्यत उक्तम् -- “संशोध्यमानं स्वमृणत्वमेति स्वत्वं क्षयः” इति । एवं धनर्णयोरन्तरं प्रतिपादितम् । एवं धनयोरपि । तद्यथा -- एकः किल काशीतः पूर्वदिग्भागे दश योजनानि गतः, इतरोऽपि तस्मिन्नेव भागे सप्त योजनानि गतः । तयोश्चान्तरं योजनात्रयं सर्वजनसिद्धम् । तच्च दशयोजनगात् पश्चिमम् । सप्तयोजनगात् पूर्वम् ॥ tathā ca yasmādanantaraṃ sādhyate tadavadhiśakalaṃ viparītadikkaṃ bhavatītyata uktam “saṃśodhyamānaṃ svamṛṇatvameti svatvaṃ kṣayaḥ” iti | evaṃ dhanarṇayorantaraṃ pratipāditam | evaṃ dhanayorapi | tadyathā - ekaḥ kila kāśītaḥ pūrvadigbhāge daśa yojanāni gataḥ, itaro’pi tasminneva bhāge sapta yojanāni gataḥ | tayoścāntaraṃ yojanatrayaṃ sarvajanasiddham | tacca daśayojanagāt paścimam | saptayojanagāt pūrvam | Therefore, the segment up to that reference point, beyond which the direction is determined from a different point to the first reference point, is in the opposite direction. Hence, it is said “saṃśodhyamānaṃ svamṛṇatvameti svatvaṃ kṣayastadyutiruktavacca.” Thus is the difference between positive and negative (dhanarṇayorantaraṃ) explained. This is the same for the positive as well. One travels $10\text{ yojanas}$ from Kāśī, and the other travels seven yojanas. It is known to all that their difference is three yojanas. And it is westward from the one who has travelled $10\text{ yojanas}$, and eastward from the one who has travelled seven yojanas. This operation applies equally to positive directions. In Fig. 6 consider Vārāṇasī ($V$), also famously known as Kāśī, to be the initial point. If two travellers, $A$ and $B$, cover a distance of 10 and seven yojanas eastwards from Kāśī, then the difference in the magnitude of distance covered by them, $VA$ and $VB$ respectively, is clearly three yojanas. It is to be noted that these three yojanas is westward from the point of view of traveller $A$ who covered $10\text{ yojanas}$, and eastward from the point of view of traveller $B$ who covered seven yojanas. 7.9 Conjecture and evidence on identifying the ‘pattana’ of Bījapallava as modern-day Patna
chunks.text: Though not germane to the paper, it was a matter of curiosity for us to determine the identity of the city referred to as “pattana” in the upapatti.17 Based on preliminary analysis, we surmise that this city could possibly be Pāṭaliputra or modern-day Patna. The basis for this argument is as follows. According to the text, the distance between Prayāgrāj and Vārāṇasī is stated as $8\text{ yojanas}$. Today we know that their distance is approximately $120\text{ km}$. This essentially means one yojana is estimated to be approximately $15\text{ km}$ according to Kṛṣṇa Daivajña. Additionally, the text mentions that the pattana is located $15\text{ yojanas}$ eastward of Vārāṇasī. The shortest distance (aerial) between Vārāṇasī and Pāṭaliputra is approximately $227\text{ km}$ and it aligns closely with the estimation of $15\text{ yojanas}$. The text also describes that all three geographical locations are pilgrimage centres situated on the banks of the Gaṅgā. Fig. 7 depicts a route map of the river Gaṅgā, while Fig. 8 illustrates the positions of the three cities of Prayāgrāj, Vārāṇasī, and Patna on Google Maps. Additionally, Table 2 displays the coordinates of the three cities, further supporting our conjecture. Assuming the radius of the earth to be approximately $6371\text{ km}$, the circumference of the earth at the equator is $\approx 40,030\text{ km}$. The circumference at the latitude of $25.5$ is $36,107\text{ km}$. Thus the distance between the two cities from Vārāṇasī based on the longitudinal separation is: ![Route map of the Gaṅgā [Courtesy: Google Earth]](media/p13fig01.jpg) ![Rail route from Prayāgrāj to Patna via Vārāṇasī [Courtesy: Google Maps.]](media/p13fig02.jpg) | Name of the city | Its coordinates | | :--- | :--- | | Prayāgrāj | $25.43^\circ\text{N}, 81.84^\circ\text{E}$ | | Vārāṇasī | $25.32^\circ\text{N}, 82.97^\circ\text{E}$ | | Patna/ Pāṭaliputra | $25.59^\circ\text{N}, 85.13^\circ\text{E}$ | Vārāṇasī and Prayāgrāj $\approx 100.297 \times 1.13 = 113.34\text{ km}$ Vārāṇasī and pattana $\approx 100.297 \times 2.16 = 216.64\text{ km}$ The values obtained above are also consistent with the description given in the text. Thus, the “pattana” referred to by Kṛṣṇa Daivajña in the Bījapallava is most likely to be modern-day Patna. Moreover, throughout its rich history, Patna has had various nomenclatures, including Pāṭaliputra or Pāṭalipattana, Pāṭaligrāma, Kusumpura, Pāṭliputra and more. Another legend suggests that it was originally known as Pattan or Patthan. In conclusion, based on these conjectures and supporting evidence, we feel that the “pattana” referred to in the text is indeed Patna.
