This is a rite which follows the motion of the sun, with its middle of the viṣuvant day. Yajurveda (38.20) says that the āhavanīya or the sky altar is four-cornered since the sun is four-cornered, meaning thereby that the motion of the sun is characterized by four cardinal points: the two solstices and the two equinoxes. The āhavanīya altars described in the ŚB are also four-cornered. With respect to the motion of the sun, ŚB 2.1.3 divides up the year into two halves in two different ways : vasanto grīṣmo varṣāḥ, te devā ṛtavaḥ. śaraddhemantaḥ śiśiraste pitaro ya eva. sa yatrodagāvartate, deveśu tarhi ......; yatra dakṣiṇāvartate pitṛṣu tarhi. The spring, the summer, and the rains, these seasons (represent) the gods; and the autumn, the winter, and the dewy season represent the fathers. When he (the sun) moves northwards, then he is among the gods .....; and when he moves southwards, then he is among the fathers. The first classification divides the year from equinox to equinox, whereas the second classification does so from solstice to solstice. The year-long rites list a total of 180 days before the solstice and another 180 days following the solstice. Since this is reckoning by solar days, it is not clear stated how the remaining 4 or 5 days of the year were assigned. But this can be easily inferred. Note that the two basic days in this count are the viṣuvant (summer solstice) and the mahāvrata day (winter solstice) which precedes it by 181 days in the above counts. Therefore, even though the count of the latter part of the year stops with an additional 180 days, it is clear that one needs another 4 or 5 days to reach the mahāvrata* day in the winter. This establishes that the division of the year was in the two halves of 181 and 184 or 185 days. Corroboration of this is suggested by evidence related to an altar design from ŚB.

chunks.text: The description of the agnicayana, or the building of the fire-altar, begins in the sixth kāṇḍa (book). But rather than speak of the altar of bricks, the text begins with an account of the creation of the universe. The significance of this is that the bricks are just meant to illustrate certain astronomical facts. As we know, the numerical and the area equivalences with respect to the bricks and astronomical and the area equivalences with respect to the bricks and astronomical data used in the Vedic books are just a means for presenting the facts and it is not clear that the altars were actually constructed. Indeed some of the “bricks” are made out of water or sometimes just loose earth sprinkled on an altar could itself stand for a brick. 181 THE SUN'S ORBIT IN THE BRĀHMAṆAS Book 7 described the construction of a gārhapatya altar. Book 8 describes the construction of an altar in five layers. Out of these layers, the first represents the terrestrial world;17 the second layer is the near atmosphere;18 the third layer is the air or the middle atmosphere;19 the fourth layer is the high atmosphere below the heavens;20 and the fifth layer is the sky.21 Note that the first layer is round, which is the usual figure for the earth; the second layer is square; the third shows the cardinal directions; the fourth is square; and the fifth represents the orbit of the sun. The whole altar is just an expansion of the tripartite system of the world:22 “the first layer is this very (terrestrial) world; and the uppermost (layer) is the sky; and those three (intermediate layers) are the air”. These layers are shown in the Figures 1 through 5. Figure 1. Layer 1, the earth. Figure 1. Layer 1, the earth. 182 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Figure 3. Layer 3, the mid-atmosphere. Figure 3. Layer 3, the mid-atmosphere. 183 THE SUN'S ORBIT IN THE BRĀHMAṆAS Figure 5. Layer 5, the orbit of the sun. Figure 5. Layer 5, the orbit of the sun. 184 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE The fifth layer, being a representation of the sky, presents a most interesting overview of the understanding of the physical universe. The details of how the bricks of the fifth layer are to be laid are described in the fifth adhyāya of the 8th kāṇḍa. Note that there are some differences between our Figure 5 and that drawn by Eggeling,23 who has used incorrect sizes for many of the bricks that go inside the ring. When the size of each stomabhāgā brick is one unit square, the outer diameter of the ring should be 11 units rather than the 12 units which has been used by Eggeling. This becomes clear when Eggeling’s drawing for the fifth layer is compared to those of the first and third layers and we find that the viśvajyoti (V) bricks do not line up as they are supposed to. The outer rim of layer 5 consists of 29 stomabhāgā bricks. The rest of the layer consists of 5 nākasad upon which are placed 5 pañcacūḍā bricks; chandasyā bricks representing the metres of which three each of triṣṭubh, jagatī, and anuṣṭubh are within the ring of the stomabhāgā bricks. In the middle is the gārhapatya altar of 8 bricks upon which is placed a second layer of 8 bricks called the punaściti. Just within the ring on the east are 2 ṛtavyā, and the lone viśvajyoti (V). Finally, on top of the punaściti are placed two perforated bricks called vikarṇī and svayamātṛṇṇā.

chunks.text: ŚB 8.5.4.2 calls the stomabhāgās, that form the outer ring of 29 bricks, as “the yonder sun”. Note that the gārhapatya altar is placed right in the middle of this ring, and the gārhapatya altar represents the earth. So the layer 5 of Figure 5 represents the earth at the center with the sun going around in a circle. Figure 6 shows layer 5 with the layer 1 inscribed within. Figure 7 shows the earth with the center of the sun’s orbit at an offset. On top of the central gārhapatya altar, lie the two perforated bricks at an offset to the center. The lower one is at the center. ŚB 8.7.3.9-10 says: atha vikarṇīm ca svayamātṛṇṇām copadadhāti, vāyurvai vikarṇī dyauruttamā svayamātṛṇṇā vāyum ca taddivam copadadhātyuttame'upadadhātyuttane hi vāyuśca dyauśca .... tadasāvāditya imāṃlokānttsūtre samāvayate, tadyattatsūtram vāyuḥ sa sa yaḥ sa vāyureṣā sa vikarṇī .... He then lays down the vikarṇī and svayamātṛṇṇā (bricks), — the vikarṇī is Vāyu (the wind), and the svayamātṛṇṇā is the sky: he thus sets up both the wind and the sky. He lays them down as the last (highest), for wind and sky are the highest...... [The] yonder sun strings these worlds [the earth and the atmosphere] to himself on a thread. Now that thread is the same as the wind; and that wind is the same as this vikarṇī ..... 17: ŚB 8.2.1.1 18: ŚB 8.3.1.1 19: ŚB 8.4.1.1 20: ŚB 8.5.1.1 21: ŚB 8.6.1.1 22: ŚB 8.5.4.12 23: see page 98 of Part 4 of item 5 above. That Eggeling was aware that there was a discrepancy in his figures and the descriptions in the text is shown by his Note 2 on page 128 where he says, “Bricks would seem, in the fifth layer, to lie by half a foot further away from the central point ...” THE SUN’S ORBIT IN THE BRĀHMAṆAS 185 Figure 6. Layer 5, with the design of layer 1 inscribed within. Figure 6. Layer 5, with the design of layer 1 inscribed within. ** 186 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Figure 7. The earth and the centre of the sun’s orbit. Figure 7. The earth and the centre of the sun’s orbit. THE SUN’S ORBIT IN THE BRĀHMAṆAS 187 It is possible, indeed likely, that the meeting point of these two bricks, which is offset from the center of the circle, was taken to be the center of the motion of the sun. The vikarṇī, as the binding force of the sun, will then reach right down to the earth. This inequality would have been easy to discover. The Indians used the reflection of the noon-sun in the water of a deep well to determine the solstice days. Now note that the number of bricks placed in the four quadrants of the circle is not identical. This suggests that the two halves of the year were taken to be unequal. If one assumes that the two halves of the year are directly in proportion to the brick counts of 14 and 15 in the two halves of the ring of the sun, this corresponds to day counts of 176 and 189. This division appears to have been for the two halves of the year into counts of 181 and 184. The apparent motion of the sun is the greatest when the earth is at perihelion and the least when the earth is at aphelion. Currently, this speed is greatest on January 3. Figure 8 presents the current dates for the perihelion and the aphelion. The interval between successive perihelia, the anomalistic year, is $365.25964$ days which is $0.01845$ days longer than the tropical year on which our calendar is based. In 2000 calendar years, the date of the perihelion advances about 36 days. Or it advances about 185 days, a half-year, in 10000 years. The perihelion cycles, therefore, in about 20000 years. It is this relative shrinking of the summers and winters which causes ice ages with a period of about 20000 years.24 It is interesting to observe that the Greeks discovered the asymmetry in the quarters of the year around 400 BC. Euktemon is supposed to have discovered this asymmetry and beginning with the winter solstice he found the four intervals to be 92, 93, 90 and 90 days. Kallippos (c. 370 BC) is supposed to have improved upon these numbers by proposing 90, 94, 92 and 89 days. Modern calculations show that at this time, the four quarters of the year starting with the winter solstice were 90.4, 94.1, 92.3, and 88.6 days long. The period from the winter solstice to the summer solstice was then 184.5 days and the perihelion occurred more than a month prior to the winter solstice.25 Considering the rites of the Brāhmaṇas it is best to assume that the insistence that there were exactly 180 days from the winter to the summer solstice was some kind of an idealization. Apparently the basis of this count was the observation that the period from the winter to the summer solstice was shorter than the corresponding period from the summer to the winter solstice. The approximate equality of these two halves of the year would occur when the perihelion is at either of the two solstices. Now, the perihelion was at the winter solstices in 1200 AD, but that is too late to have been the basis of the observations. The other possibility is that during the rites the perihelion occurred prior to June 21, but this would be true only before about 8800 BC. But this gives periods which will be considered to be too early for the rites described in the Brāhmaṇas. There is no reason to doubt that the ancient Indians had found that 24: J. Imbrie and K.P. Imbrie, Ice Ages. Harvard University Press, Cambridge (1986). 25: W.M. O’Neil, Early Astronomy*. Sydney University Press, Sydney (1986), pages 56-57; but note that there is a typographical error in the book regarding the period of the perihelion cycle.

chunks.text: *** 188 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE the two halves of the year were asymmetric in a certain sense. From the observations of the Greeks it is clear that this asymmetry between the two halves of the year during the 1st millennium BC. was just the opposite of what we find in the Brāhmaṇas. These texts describe rites which should thus belong to a much earlier age. How much earlier we cannot be certain of at this time given the confusion regarding the chronology of early India. A distinction should be made between the period of the rites and the time that these rites were written down. It is common for a religious tradition to be practised even after the astronomical basis for it ceases to have any meaning. For example, the biblical account of the creation of the universe in seven days may have been true in a metaphorical sense where each day represents the creation of the planets but three thousand years after the origin of this myth there are people who believe in it literally. It is natural to assume that the myths of the ancient people were already very old when they were written down. This is a point which has been very powerfully made and substantiated by de Santillana and von Dechend before.26 What we obtain from the analysis presented in this paper is that the Vedic tradition was already as ancient as the archaeological record which has been traced back to at least 8000 B.C. in Mehrgarh in the unbroken tradition.27 We can be certain that the first millennium B.C. for the rites of the Brāhmaṇas, as was assumed by the colonial historians of the 19th century, is absolutely ruled out. We have proposed that, being as conservative as possible, one may assign the 2nd millennium BC. as representing the period when the Brāhmaṇas were written down. This is supported by other evidence in these texts which refers to the 3rd and the 2nd millennia BC. This dating has the virtue of being supported by recent archaeological findings.28 Once the idea of the non-uniform motion of the sun had taken root, the idea of the apogee exercising a slowing force would be a natural development.

chunks.text: This paper on the orbit of the sun, together with the earlier work of Yājñavalkya on harmonizing the solar and the lunar years by means of the 95-year intercalary cycle, provides an explanation for the legend that Yājñavalkya was inspired by the sun. This “inspiration” here suggests Yājñavalkya’s development of a theory related to the motion of the sun and its reconciliation with the motion of the moon. The evidence from the design of the altar of layer 5 confirms that the year was divided into two parts: winter solstice to summer solstice being equal to 181 days, and midsummer-to-midwinter of 184 or 185 days. This means that the Brāhmaṇa rites could definitely not belong to the first millennium BC. This conclusion is of the greatest 26: Santillana, G. de and H. von Dechend, Hamlet’s Mill: An essay on myth and the frame of time. Gambit, Boston (1969). 27: Feuerstein, G. , Kak, S.C., Frawley, D. In Search of the Cradle of Civilization. Quest Books, Wheaton 91995). 28: See Note 4, or see above. ** THE SUN’S ORBIT IN THE BRĀHMAṆAS 189 significance for the chronology of the Vedic texts and it invalidates the chronology popularized by Max Müller. The theory that the sun was the “lotus” [the central point] of the sky and that it kept the worlds together by its “strings of wind” gave rise to a heliocentric tradition in India. The offset of the sun’s orbit evolved into the notion of mandocca and the motions of the planets around the sun were transferred to the earth’s frame through the device of the śīghrocca. The continuing analysis of the astronomical references in the Brāhmaṇas has made it clear that the theory that the Siddhāntic astronomy was somehow derived from the Babylonians and the Greeks is wrong. What is emerging from texts, that are anterior, by any reckoning, to the eras of astronomical advance in Babylonia or in Greece is that astronomical ideas developed in India in stages and these stages can be seen in the different layers of the Vedic texts, the Brāhmaṇas, and the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa. chunks.title: Sriyantra – A Study of Spherical and Plane Forms
heading_path: ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS
chunks.text: C.S. RAO (Received 24 February 1998) Śrīyantra is an ancient geometrical form with great traditional significance and current interest in scientific studies and architectural applications. It consists of a complex network of intersecting triangles in its central region. The construction of the plane figure from traditional literature is adequate for small objects for worship. Errors at intersections of certain lines becomes significant for large sizes of the figure. These errors occur due to the incompatibility of the redundant measurements in the specifications. Accurate measurements from recent literature are available for specific configurations of plane form. This paper presents a comprehensive study of the geometrical properties of the triangular network of spherical and plane forms of Śrīyantra. A general formulation of the triangular network for the spherical form is presented using spherical trigonometry. Geometrical relationship observed in specimens of plane figures from different sources are expressed as mathematical equations. The resulting system of simultaneous nonlinear equations is solved by numerical methods for each set of selected relationships for obtaining the parameters required for drawing the figure. Figures with closest resemblance to the traditional figure are obtained by non-linear optimization. The formulation for the plane form is derived as a simplification of the formulation of spherical form. The figure of Śrīyantra of both plane and spherical forms can be constructed to any required size ranging from miniature objects of worship to temple structures with a high degree of accuracy from the results of this study. Keywords : Kurma-prishtha, Meru, Non-linear optimization, Numerical methods, Simultaneous non-linear equations, Spherical trigonometry, Śrīyantra, Śrīcakra.

chunks.title: Sriyantra – A Study of Spherical and Plane Forms
heading_path: ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS
chunks.text: The development of various architectural forms through centuries of history is well known. Definite shapes and patterns of pyramids, Churches, Monuments, Temples and also Modern structures can be distinctly recognised. In recent structures, the Meru temple in Devipuram near Visakhapatnam in Andhra Pradesh uses Śrīyantra as the plan view for its multi-storeyed structure. --- Associate Professor, Civil Engineering Department, Indian Institute of Technology, Powai, Mumbai-400076. \pagebreak 204 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Fig.1 Śrīyantra—The Tantra Figure \pagebreak ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS 205 The manifestation of the world process, the experiences of the universe and the individual are explained in the introduction of Sivasutras.1 The essence of the universe is Siva. His power of action is Sakti. The essence in every individual is is called Jiva. Siva is unlimited in all his attributes whereas Jiva is limited in all respects. The central point in the Śrīyantra called Bindu is identified with the unified Siva and Sakti. The whole of Śrīyantra shown in Fig. 1 considered as the expanded form of the Bindu consists of 9 regions called enclosures. The Inner Sector is a triangle complex consisting of a network of triangles circumscribed by a circle. It is composed of five primary triangles called Sakti triangles with vertices downward and four primary triangles called Siva triangles with vertices upward. These triangles have parallel bases with symmetric left and right sides. The mutual intersection of these 9 primary triangles results in the formation of 43 secondary triangles. The central point of the figure is considered as the first enclosure. The innermost secondary triangle is counted as second. Enclosures from third to sixth consist of 8, 10, 10 and 14 secondary triangles respectively. The outer sector consists of 3 enclosures. The 7th enclosure consists of an eight petalled lotus around the circum circle of the triangle complex and lying within a second circum circle. The 8th enclosure consists of a sixteen petalled lotus around the second circum circle and lying within a third circum circle. A triplet of closely spaced circles are used in the place of the third circum circle. The 9th enclosure consists of a set of three concentric squares outside the outermost circum circle. Openings on all four sides of the squares called gateways are provided. A popular description and construction of the complete plane figure having its origin from tantra literature is given in the commentary on Saundarya Lahari.2 The triangle complex consists of spacings of 6, 6, 5, 3, 3, 4, 3, 6, 6, 6 units of distance between successive parallel base lines of the primary triangles. The radius of the circum circle is 24 units. This figure corresponding to the above construction is called tantra figure. There are three major versions of the yantra in popular use. The plane form contains all the enclosures in a single plane where triangles and squares are formed by straight lines. In the Meru form, different enclosures lie in different horizontal planes at different elevations. The square at outermost enclosure is at the base level and successive enclosures are at progressively higher levels with the central point placed at the highest elevation. In the spherical form, the triangular complex of the first 6 enclosures is formed by spherical triangles on a spherical surface. The sides of the triangles are taken as arcs of great circles on the spherical surface. The outer sector is placed either in a single plane or in a stepped form. This form is known as Kurma-prishtha Meru. Photographs of Śrīyantra of spherical form made of rock crystals are given by Madhu Khanna.3 A figure of Śrīyantra on a copper plate with elliptical arcs as sides of the triangles is given by Ajit Mookerjee.4 \pagebreak 206 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE The significance of Śrīyantra as an abode of the presiding deities of the cosmic organisation is indicated in Atharva veda.5 A detailed exposition of these principles correlating these powers in the cosmic organisation and the organisation within a human individual is given in Bhavanopanishat.6 A symbolic representation of the hierarchical principal and powers operating in the organisation of the cosmos in Śrīyantra based on a thorough study of various Tantras is given by Sir John Woodroff.7 One of the greatest applications of Śrīyantra is the traditional worship8 where the goal is to realise the identification of the individual with entire universe. A treatment of procedures of the worship and their significance is given in Srividya Saparya Vasana.9 Fig. 2.1 : Spherical Triangular Complex \pagebreak ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS 207 Kulaichev and Ramendic10 investigated the visual influence of Śrīyantra on the psycho-physiological states of man. They studied the influence of visual stimulus of gazing at the figure of Śrīyantra on the response of Electroencephalograms of several individuals. They concluded that Śrīyantra is a unique composition to concentrate on for achieving certain states of consciousness. Raj Bapna11 states that the original purpose of Śrīyantra was to develop mind power. It is stated that gazing at the central dot of the Śrīyantra increases the communication between left brain and right brain by which the power of concentration is enhanced. The errors of intersection of the lines in the tantra figure are shown by Kulaichev.12 He gives a mathematical formulation for drawing the triangle complex of a plane figure. A set of 5 geometric properties were used. The required parameters were obtained by solving a set of non-linear algebraic equations by nested iterative procedures. Diagrams of spherical form of Śrīyantra* were given without any mathematical formulations.

chunks.text: The formulation of the geometry of construction is based on spherical trigonometry. The spherical triangular complex is shown in Fig. 2.1. The upper part of the hemisphere above horizontal plane is shown. The radius of the sphere is R with centre at point O. The vertical circle arc containing the points $P{11}$, $Pc$ and $P{12}$ forms the arc of symmetry of the triangular complex. The centre of the triangular complex $Pc$ is vertically above the centre of the sphere. The horizontal base circle of radius $Rc$ passing through points $P0-1-2-P{10}$ forms the circum circle around the triangular complex. The great circle arc "r" is the angle subtended by the arc $P0 Pc$ or $Pc P{10}$ at the centre of the sphere. The altitude "h" is angle subtended by arc $P{11} P{10}$ or $P{12} P{10}$ at the centre of the sphere. These parameters can be ralated as follows. $$r + h = \frac{\pi}{2} \tag{2.1a}$$ $$Rc = R \cos(h) = R \sin(r) \tag{2.1}$$ A spherical triangle is formed by three arcs of great circles intersecting at three points. A side is denoted by the angle subtended by the great circle arc at the centre of the sphere. The length of the side is obtained by the product of the angle in radians and the radius in linear units. The angle at the point of intersection of two sides is taken as the angle between the planes of the two great circle arcs forming the sides. The points $P0$ to $P4$ and $P7$ to $P{10}$ form the vertices of 9 root triangles. The base lines of the root triangles intersect the arc of symmetry at right angles at the base points $P1$ to $P9$. The variables in the spherical triangle complex are shown in Fig 2.2. The intercepts g, c and b mark the base points $P4$, $P3$ and $P1$ with respect to the centre $Pc$. on the arc of symmetry. The intercepts d and e locate the base points $P7$ and $P9$. The remaining base points $P2$, $P5$, $P6$, and $P8$ are obtained during the construction. The sequence of construction of the figure is described along with the expressions for several intermediate variables like $xi$, $Ui$ as follows. The base great circle arc $P31$ perpendicular to arc of symmetry $P{11}P{12}$ at $P3$ meets the circumscribing circle at point 1. The length of arc $P31$ is denoted by $x1$. The lengths of other base lines are similarly denoted by $xn$ where $n$ represents the number denoting the corner of the triangle. In the right angled spherical triangle $PcP31$ $\text{arc } P31 = x1 \quad \text{arc } Pc1 = r = \frac{\pi}{2} - h$ $\text{arc } P3Pc = c \quad \text{angle } PcP31 = \frac{\pi}{2}$ The arc $x1$ can be obtained from Napier's rules13 for right angled triangles as follows: $$\text{Cos } x1 = \frac{\text{Cos } r}{\text{Cos } c} \tag{2.3}$$ Similarly the base great circle arc drawn perpendicular to arc of symmetry at $P7$ meets the circumscribing circle at point 2. The arc length $P72 = x2$ is obtained from the spherical triangle $PcP72$ right angled at $P7$ as $$\text{Cos } x2 = \frac{\text{Cos } r}{\text{Cos } d} \tag{2.4}$$ Point 3 is the intersection of the transverse line $P02$ with the base line $P31$. Solution of the spherical triangles $P0P33$ and $P0P72$ right angled at $P3$ and $P7$ respectively and having a common angle at vertex $P0$ gives $$\sin(r - c) = \tan(x3) \cot(P0) \text{ and } \sin (r + d) = \tan(x2) \cot (P0) \tag{2.5a}$$ The arc $P33 = x3$ is obtained by eliminating $P0$ from eq(2.5a) $$\tan x3 = \frac{\text{Sin } (r - c)}{\text{Sin } (r + d)} \tan x2 \tag{2.5}$$ Point 4 is the intersection of the transverse line $P{10}1$ with the base line $P72$. Arc length $P74 = x4$ is similarly obtained from triangles $P{10}P74$ and $P{10}P31$ as $$\tan x4 = \frac{\text{Sin } (r - d)}{\text{Sin } (r + c)} \tan x1 \tag{2.6}$$ 210 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Point 5 is obtained by the intersection of transverse line $P14$ with the base line $P31$. Arc length $P35 = x5$ is obtained from the triangles $P1P35$ and $P1P74$ as $$\tan x5 = \frac{\sin (b)}{\sin (b + c + d)} \tan x4 \tag{2.7}$$ Point 6 is obtained by the intersection of the transverse line $P93$ with base line $P72$. The arc length $P76 = x6$ is obtained similar to $x5$ as $$\tan x6 = \frac{\sin (e)}{\sin (c + d + e)} \tan x3 \tag{2.8}$$ Point 7 is obtained by the intersection of the two transverse arcs $P75$ and $P46$. The base point $P5$ is located by drawing the great circle arc through point 7 which meets the arc of symmetry at right angles. The arc length $P57 = x7$ is obtained as follows. Let $S7$ be the arc length between $P4$ and $P7$. The Point $P5$ lies between $P4$ and $P7$ such that $P5P7 = U7$ and $P4P5 = V7$. It can be seen from the Fig. 2.2 that $$S7 = U7 + V_7 = d + g \tag{2.9}$$

The base point $P8$ is located by drawing the great circle arc through point 8 to meet the arc of symmetry at right angles. The following relations based on point 8 can be obtained similar to eq(2.9 to 2.14). $$S8 = U8 + V8 = r + g \tag{2.15}$$ $$\frac{\sin U8}{\sin (r + c)} = \frac{\tan x8}{\tan x1} \tag{2.16}$$ $$\frac{\sin V8}{\sin (d + g)} = \frac{\tan x8}{\tan x6} \tag{2.17}$$ $$Q8 = \frac{\sin V8}{\sin U8} = \frac{\sin (d + g)}{\sin (r + c)} \frac{\tan x1}{\tan x6} \tag{2.18}$$ $$\tan U8 = \frac{\sin S8}{Q8 + \cos S8} \tag{2.19}$$ The arc length $P88 = x8$ can be obtained from eq(2.16) as $$\tan x8 = \frac{\sin U8}{\sin (r + c)} \tan x1 \tag{2.20}$$ $$v8 = r - U8 - d \tag{2.21}$$ Point 16 is obtained by the intersection of the base line through $P9$ with the transverse line $P46$ extended. The base arc length $P916 = x{16}$ is obtained from triangles with common vertex at $P4$ as $$\tan x{16} = \frac{\sin (d + e + g)}{\sin (r + c)} \tan x6 \tag{2.22}$$ The transverse line $P75$ gives the points 11 and 17 by intersection with base lines through $P4$ and $P1$ respectively. The base arcs $P411 = x{11}$ and $P117 = x{17}$ are obtained as $$\tan x{11} = \frac{\sin (d + g)}{\sin (c + d)} \tan x5 \tag{2.23}$$ 212 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE $$\tan x{17} = \frac{\sin (b + c + d)}{\sin (c + d)} \tan x5 \tag{2.24}$$ The same transverse line $P75$ intersects another transverse line $P02$ to locate the point 9. The following relations for point 9 can be derived similar to eq (2.9 to 2.14) $$S9 = U9 + V9 = r + d \tag{2.25}$$ $$\frac{\sin U9}{\sin (r + d)} = \frac{\tan x9}{\tan x2} \tag{2.26}$$ $$\frac{\sin V9}{\sin (c + d)} = \frac{\tan x9}{\tan x5} \tag{2.27}$$ $$Q9 = \frac{\sin V9}{\sin U9} = \frac{\sin (c + d)}{\sin (r + d)} \frac{\tan x2}{\tan x5} \tag{2.28}$$ $$\tan U9 = \frac{\sin S9}{Q9 + \cos S9} \tag{2.29}$$ The arc length $P29 = x9$ can be obtained from eq(2.26) as $$\tan x9 = \frac{\sin U9}{\sin (r + d)} \tan x2 \tag{2.30}$$ $$v9 = r - U9 - c \tag{2.31}$$ Point 10 is obtained by extending the base line through $P4$ to meet the transverse line $P14$ which gives the arc length $P410 = x{10}$ as $$\tan x{10} = \frac{\sin (b + c - g)}{\sin (b + c + d)} \tan x4 \tag{2.32}$$ Point 18 is intersection of the base line through $P8$ with the transverse line $P14$ produced which gives the arc length $P818 = x{18}$ as $$\tan x{18} = \frac{\sin (b + c + d + v8)}{\sin (b + c + d)} \tan x4 \tag{2.33}$$ Point 12 is obtained by the intersection of the transverse arcs $P46$ and $P810$. The great circle arc through point 12 is drawn to meets the arc of symmetry at right angles at the base point $P6$. ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS 213 $$S{12} = U{12} + V{12} = d + g + v8 \tag{2.34}$$ $$\frac{\sin U{12}}{\sin (d + g)} = \frac{\tan x{12}}{\tan x6} \tag{2.35}$$ $$\frac{\sin V{12}}{\sin (d + g + v8)} = \frac{\tan x{12}}{\tan x{10}} \tag{2.36}$$ $$Q{12} = \frac{\sin V{12}}{\sin U{12}} = \frac{\sin (d + g + v8) \tan x6}{\sin (d + g) \tan x{10}} \tag{2.37}$$ $$\tan U{12} = \frac{\sin S{12}}{Q{12} + \cos S{12}} \tag{2.38}$$ Arc length $P6 12 = x{12}$ can be obtained from eq (2.35) as $$\tan x{12} = \frac{\sin U{12}}{\sin (d + g)} \tan x6 \tag{2.39}$$ $$v{12} = d + g - U{12} \tag{2.40}$$ Point 14 is the intersection of the base line through $P5$ with the transverse line $P8 10$ so that $P5 14 = x{14}$. chunks.text: Some of the geometrical relationships observed in available specimens of Śrīyantra are formulated as constraint functions. The value of the function defined must be equal to zero for the relationship to be satisfied. 1. Because of the sequence of construction adapted for drawing a third line through the earlier intersection point of a pair of lines, all intersections will be perfect except at point 11. The essential condition of concurrency at all points to be satisfied is that the two points of intersection 11 and $11a$ must be at the same location. This requires that the six intercepts b, c, d, e, g and h must be compatible such that $x{11} = x{11a}$. This may be stated as the error of intersection $F1$ defined as follows must be zero. $$F1 = x{11} - x{11a} \tag{3.1}$$ 2. The inscribed circle of the innermost secondary triangle viewed as a magnification of the centre point must be concentric with the circumscribing circle around the triangular complex. The distance between the centres of the two circles defined as function $F4$ represents the error in concentricity of the two circles. The centre $PT$ of the inscribed circle of radius $rT$ is at the intersection of the arc of symmetry $P4 P5$ and the bisector of the angle $P4 7 P5$. The transverse arc $P4 7$ and the base arc $P5 7$ are tangential to the inscribed circle at points T and $P5$ respectively (Fig. 2.2). In the spherical triangle $P4 P5 7$ right angled at $P5$ angle $P5 7 P4 = t$ and $P4 P5 = V7$ $$\sin x7 = \tan V7 \tan (\frac{\pi}{2} - t) = \frac{\tan (d + g - U7)}{\tan t} \tag{3.2a}$$ $$\tan t = \frac{\tan (d + g - U7)}{\sin x7} \tag{3.2b}$$ In the spherical triangle $PT P5 7$ right angled at $P5$ angle $P5 7 PT = \frac{t}{2}$ and $PT P5 = rT$ $$\tan rT = \sin (x7) \tan (\frac{t}{2}) \tag{3.2c}$$ The concentricity error $F2$ defined as the arc $Pc PT$ is $$F2 = d - U7 - rT \tag{3.2}$$ 3. The root triangle with vertex at $P8$ is equilateral. Solving the triangle $P8 P4 10$ with the arc length $P8 10 = 2 x{10}$ gives ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS 215 $$\cos V8 = \frac{\cos(2 x{10})}{\cos(x{10})} \tag{3.3a}$$ $$F3 = \cos (d + g + V8) - \frac{\cos (2 x{10})}{\cos (x{10})} \tag{3.3}$$ 4. The root triangle with vertex at $P2$ is equilateral. The condition function is obtained similar to eq (2.48) as. $$F4 = \cos (c + d + g + v9 - v{12}) - \frac{\cos (2 x{13})}{\cos (x{13})} \tag{3.4}$$ 5. The base arcs $P6 13$ and $P4 10$ are equal. $$F5 = x{10} - x{13} \tag{3.5}$$ 6. The inner most secondary triangle with vertex at $P4$ is equilateral. The function is obtained similar to eq (2.48) as. $$F6 = \cos (d + g - U7) - \frac{\cos (2 x7)}{\cos (x7)} \tag{3.6}$$ 7. The base arcs $P8 18$ and $P2 19$ are equal. $$F7 = x{18} - x{19} \tag{3.7}$$ 8. Point 16 lies on the circumscribing circle of radius r. $$F8 = r - r{16} \tag{3.8}$$ where $r{16}$ is the arc $Pc 16$ of the triangle $Pc P9 16$ right angled at $P9$ $$\cos(r{16}) = \cos(d + e) \cos(x{16}) \tag{3.8a}$$ 9. Point 17 lies on the circumscribing circle. $$F9 = r - r{17} \tag{3.9}$$ where $r{17}$ is the arc $Pc 17$ of the triangle $Pc P1 17$ right angled at $P1$ $$\cos(r{17}) = \cos(b + c) \cos(x{17}) \tag{3.9a}$$ 10. The intercepts $P1 P4$ and $P4 P8$ are equal. $$F{10} = b + c - d - 2g - v8 \tag{3.10}$$ 11. The intercepts $P9 P6$ and $P6 P2$ are equal. $$F{11} = c + d + v9 - 2 v{12} - e \tag{3.11}$$ 216 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE 12. The base arc lengths $P9 16$ and $P1 17$ are equal. $$F{12} = x{16} - x{17} \tag{3.12}$$ 13. The transverse arcs $P8 10$ and $P2 13$ intersect at point 20. The base line passing through 20 intersects the arc of symmetry at $P{20}$. The condition is that $P5$ is the mid point of the arc $P6 P{20}$. By using relations similar to eq (2.9 to 2.14) we obtain $$F{13} = U7 - \frac{(U{20} - v8 + v{12})}{2} \tag{3.13}$$ where $\tan U{20} = \frac{\sin S{20}}{Q{20} + \cos S{20}} \tag{3.13a}$ $$Q{20} = \frac{\sin (c + d + v9 - v{12}) \tan x{10}}{\sin (d + g + v8) \tan x{13}} \tag{3.13b}$$ and $S{20} = c + d + v8 + v9 \tag{3.13c}$ 14. The transverse arcs $P9 19$ and $P1 18$ intersect at point 21. The base line passing through 21 intersects the arc of symmetry at $P{21}$. The condition is that $P6$ is the mid point of the arc $P7 P{21}$. Similar to condition 13, one can obtain $$F{14} = v{12} - \frac{(U{21} - e)}{2} \tag{3.14}$$ where $\tan U{21} = \frac{\sin S{21}}{Q{21} + \cos S{21}} \tag{3.14a}$ $$Q{21} = \frac{\sin (b + c + d) \tan x{10}}{\sin (c + d + e) \tan x{13}} \tag{3.14b}$$ and $S{21} = b + c + d + e \tag{3.14c}$ 15. The condition is similar to the previous one. The condition here is that $P4$ is the mid point of the arc $P3 P{21}$. Similar to condition 14, we obtain $$F{15} = g + \frac{(d + e + c - U{21})}{2} \tag{3.15}$$ 16. Points 16 and 17 are equidistant from the centre of the figure $Pc$ $$F{16} = r{16} - r{17} \tag{3.16}$$ ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS 217 17. Points 18 and 19 are equidistant from the centre of the figure $Pc$. $$F{17} = r{18} - r{19} \tag{3.17}$$ where the radial distances $r{18}$ and $r{19}$ derived similar to eq (3.8a) are. $$\cos (r{18}) = \cos (d + v8) \cos (x{18}) \tag{3.18a}$$ $$\cos (r{19}) = \cos (c + v9) \cos (x{19}) \tag{3.18b}$$ 18. Points 16 and 18 are equidistant from the centre of the figure $Pc$. $$F{18} = r{16} - r{18} \tag{3.18}$$ 19. Points 17 and 19 are equidistant from the centre of the figure $Pc$. $$F{19} = r{17} - r{19} \tag{3.19}$$ 20. The outer most root triangles with vertices at $P0$ and $P{10}$ are identical. $$F{20} = c - d \tag{3.20}$$

chunks.text: For generating the triangle complex on a spherical surface of radius R, the 6 basic variables b, c, d, e, g and h are required. The other parameters required can be found from the formulation of the construction. Each basic variable may be assigned any arbitrary value or may be fixed according to some specified geometrical property. Since there are 6 basic variables, any 6 constraints can be satisfied at a time in a figure. Among the constraints formulated, the concurrency condition in eq (3.1) and the concentricity condition in eq (3.2) are considered essential. Any other 4 constraints from $F3$ to $F{20}$ may be used along with the 2 essential conditions to form a set of conditions. The problem is to find the values of a set of basic variables which would give a figure satisfying the selected set of conditions. This requires that the 6 selected constraint functions must be equal to zero simultaneously. Newton-Raphson14 method is used for solving this system of simultaneous non-linear equations. A set of approximate initial values are selected for the basic variables. The numerical values of the 6 selected constraint functions are computed using these initial values. The partial derivatives of these functions with respect to the basic variables are numerically evaluated by forward finite difference approximations. Corrections to be applied to the initial values are obtained by solving the resulting system of linear simultaneous equations. The values of the 6 constraint functions are computed using the corrected values of the basic variables. If any one of the values is greater than a specified tolerance value, the corrected values of the basic variables are taken as new initial values and new corrections are found. The iterations are continued till the value of each of the 6 functions is less than the tolerance. 14: Scarborough, J.B., Numerical mathematical analysis, Chapter 10, Newton-Raphson Method for Simultaneous equations, Oxford & IBH Publishing Co., New Delhi, 1979, pp. 215-219. 218 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE TABLE 1. chunks.text: It can be seen from the results of the constrained figures that figures satisfying any 6 specified constraints can be obtained. Any given figure which may not be satisfying some essential conditions can be improved by eliminating the errors. The corrected figure with minimum changes from the given figure may be called an optimum figure. Let $L1, L2, \dots, Ln$ be the finite number of given lengths used to draw the reference figure. The corresponding values $H1, H2, \dots, Hn$ of the optimum figure can be computed in terms of of the basic variables of the present study. A measure of deviation of the optimum figure from the reference figure may be defined as the sum of squares of the deviations of the respective dimensions as follows. $$S = \sum{i=1}^{n} (Hi - Li)^2 \quad \dots (5.1)$$ The values of the reference lengths $L1, L2, \dots, L{10}$ representing the arcs $P{10}P9, P9P8, \dots, P1P0$ are chosen as 6, 6, 5, 3, 3, 4, 3, 6, 6, 6 units corresponding to the tantra plane figure. The corresponding arcs $H1, H2, \dots, Hn$ are related to the variables of the present formulation as follows. $$H1 = r - d - e \qquad H6 = d + g - U7$$ $$H2 = e - v8 \qquad H7 = c - g$$ $$H3 = v8 \qquad H8 = v9$$ $$H4 = v{12} \qquad H9 = b - v9$$ $$H5 = U7 - v{12} \qquad H{10} = r - b + c \quad \dots (5.2)$$ ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS 221 Fig. 5 SPHERICAL LOCAL OPTIMUM FIGURES: (a) ALTITUDE h = 80 deg. (b) ALTITUDE h = 60 deg. (c) ALTITUDE h = 40 deg. (d) ALTITUDE h = 20 deg. Fig. 5 SPHERICAL LOCAL OPTIMUM FIGURES 222 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE The above spherical intercepts in radians are scaled to thge radius of 24 units of the tantra figure by multiplying with a factor of $\frac{24}{r}$ The problem of finding the optimum figure is to find a set of values of the basic variables b, c, d, e, g and h such that the objective function S given in eq (5.1) is a minimum subject to the following equality and inequality constraints. $$F1 = 0, F2 = 0, F8 > 0 \quad \text{and} \quad F_9 > 0 \quad \dots (5.3)$$ The problem is solved by using the methods of general nonlinear optimization.15 It was observed that different sets of initial values tried for the basic variables converged to different solutions. Hence a systematic search was conducted by finding a local optimum solution for each selected value of "h" with b, c, d, e and g as the 5 basic variables. Values of "h" within the range $0$ to $\frac{\pi}{2}$ at intervals of $0.01$ radians were tried. The global optimum was obtained when the value of "h" was close to $\frac{\pi}{2}$. This may be due to the reference lengths being taken from the tantra plane figure. Optimum solutions of basic variables of some selected values of "h" are shown in Table 5. Plan views of some local optimum solutions are shown in Fig. 4.

chunks.text: The formulation of spherical form of earlier sections is simplified to obtain the formulation of plane form of Śrīyantra where the area occupied by the triangular complex is very small compared to the total area of the sphere. The length $P0P{10}$ of the arc of symmetry (Fig. 2.1) is given by $2Rr$. The length of the $P0P{10}$ forming the diameter of the circum circle is given by $2RC$. The length of the chord is equated to the length of the arc to reduce the spherical formulation to plane formulation as follows. $$RC = R \ r \quad \dots (6.1)$$ Substituting for $RC$ from eq (2.1) and simplifying one gets $$\sin(r) = r \quad \dots (6.2)$$ The following two relationship are also used which are valid when $r \ll 1$. $$\tan(r) = r \quad \text{and} \quad \cos(r) = 1 - \frac{r^2}{2} \quad \dots (6.3)$$ Similar substitutions are made for all the other variables representing the lengths of arcs having the same order of magnitude as "r". When terms of different orders of magnitudes are added, the terms of higher order are neglected. The angles between adjacent sides of triangles are retained without any change. The reduction of some typical equations is as follows. 15: Fletcher, R., Practical Methods of Optimization, 2nd ed, John Wiley & Sons, Chichester, New York, 1991, pp. 140, 144. ŚRĪYANTRA - A STUDY OF SPHERICAL AND PLANE FORMS 223 1. Equations of the form of eq (2.2) involving arcs only. $$r = a + b + c = d + e + f \tag{6.5}$$ 2. Replacing cosines of arcs from eq (6.3) in eq (2.3) and expanding $$1 - \frac{x1^2}{2} = \frac{1 - \frac{r^2}{2}}{1 - \frac{c^2}{2}} \tag{6.6a}$$ $$x1^2 = r^2 - c^2 \tag{6.6}$$ 3. Replacing sines and tangents using eq (6.2) and (6.3) in eq (2.5) $$x3 = \frac{(r - c)}{(r + d)} x2 \tag{6.7}$$ 4. The eq (2.10) which is similar to eq (2.5) with terms transposed is reduced to $$\frac{U7}{(c + d)} = \frac{x7}{x5} \tag{6.8}$$ 5. The eq (2.12) is reduced using eq (6.2) and (6.3) as follows $$Q7 = \frac{V7}{U7} = \frac{(d + g)}{(c + d)} \frac{x5}{x6} \tag{6.9}$$ 6. The eq (2.13) is reduced using eq (6.2) and (6.3) as follows $$U7 = \frac{S7}{Q7 + 1} \tag{6.10}$$ 7. Replacing tangents of arcs from eq (6.3) without changing "$\tan (t)$" in the eq (3.2b) $$\tan (t) = \frac{(d + g - U7)}{x7} \tag{6.11}$$ 8. Similarly eq (3.2) reduced as follows. $$\tan (rT) = x7 \frac{t}{2} \tag{6.12}$$ 9. The eq (3.3) is modified before reduction as follows $$F3 = \cos(d + g + v8) - \{ \cos(x{10}) - \sin(x{10}) \tan(x{10}) \} \tag{6.13a}$$ 224 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE $$F3 = -\frac{(d + g + v8)^2}{2} + \frac{3}{2} x{10}^2 \tag{6.13}$$ 10. The eq (3.9a) is similar to eq (2.3) with terms transposed which reduces to $$r{16}^2 = (d + e)^2 + x{16}^2 \tag{6.14}$$ It was also verified $^{16}$ that these reduced equations are the same as those obtained by a direct formulation using plane geometry. Only 5 independent variable b, c, d, e and g are required to define the figure with a given value of "r". The constrained solutions with 5 conditions inclusive of the 2 essential conditions are obtained. The results for some of the combinations of the constraints are given in Table 3. Some figures drawn are shown in Fig. 5. The figure for conditions, 1, 2, 8, 9, 20 in Fig. 5c matches exactly with the figure given by Kulaichev. $^7$ The formulation $^{16}$ of plane optimum figure can also be obtained similar to a spherical local optimum with only 5 basic variables. The intercepts $H1$ to $H{10}$ for the plane optimum solution corresponding to reference values of 6, 6, 5, 3, 3, 4, 3, 6, 6 and 6 of the tantra plane figure are given in Table 4. The basic variables b, c, d, e and g of this optimum figure are given in Table 3. The optimum figure is shown in Fig. 5d. TABLE 3. chunks.text: A general formulation of the spherical triangle complex of Śrīyantra is presented. It can be seen from the accurate figures drawn using computer graphics based on the solutions obtained that the constraints formulated are satisfied. Any other property may also be added to those formulated in the present work. A condition of the form F = h - k will constrain the parameter "h" to have any specified value "k". The incompatibility of conditions in some sets tried was indicated by some of the variables reaching values outside the permitted ranges during execution of the programms. Optimum spherical figures with reference to tantra plane figure were obtained for a range of values of altitude "h". The value of "h" obtained was close to $\frac{\pi}{2}$ for the global optimum. Similarly any other given figure can be used as a reference. Instead of the sum of squares of deviations used in the present work, any other measure of similarity may also be used to define an optimum figure. The validity of the formulation of the plane figures reduced from the spherical formulation shows the generality of the formulations. Detailed dimensions of all the components of the spherical figure as a structural form of braced dome and the plane form for a Meru can be computed to a high degree of accuracy by specifying the required tolerances of errors. It is interesting to observe that an unlimited number of figures with different proportions of components can be obtained which satisfy the general specifications of Śrīyantra from traditional literature. The significance of Śrīyantra with figures of different geometrical constraints in relation to the applications needs further study. The study has shown the effectiveness of the modern numerical methods of non linear programming applied to the study of the ancient geometrical form of Śrīyantra.

chunks.text: [ चन्द्रग्रहणे योगकालः : ] अर्कस्फुटं सचक्रार्धं भूच्छायास्फुटमुच्यते । सूर्यास्तमयकालोत्थौ छायाचन्द्रौ समीपगौ ॥ १ ॥ उदये वाथ विन्यस्य तद्योगोऽत्र निरूप्यताम् । चन्द्रेऽधिके गतो योगो, न्यूने चैष्य इति स्थितिः ॥ २ ॥ तदन्तरं तु षष्टिघ्नं गत्यन्तरहतं तयोः । योगकालो घटीपूर्वो गतो गम्योऽपि वा क्रमात् ॥ ३ ॥ [ रवीन्द्रोः पर्वन्तकालस्फुटः : ] तात्कालिकौ पुनन्नीत्वा मध्यार्केन्दुस्फुटावपि । उदयाद्योगकालेन नीयेते1 चेत् तदुक्तवत् ॥ ४ ॥ तात्कालिकार्कनिघ्नघ्नचरसंस्कार इष्यते । अस्तकालोक्तवत् तस्मात् चाल्येते2 चेत् चरोद्भवः ॥ ५ ॥ इष्टकालार्कतश्चैवं कार्यः3 प्राणकलान्तरात् । दोर्भेदाच्चापि संस्कारो रवीन्दू तौ स्फुटौ तदा ॥ ६ ॥ योगकालस्ततो नेयस्तत्त्रिघ्ना स्वा स्फुटा गतिः । षष्ट्याप्ता स्वस्फुटे योज्या गम्ये योगेऽन्यथान्यथा ॥ ७ ॥ समलिप्तौ भवेतां तौ पर्वन्तसमयद्भवौ ॥ ८a ॥ [ रवीन्द्रोः कक्ष्याव्यासार्धयोजनम् : ] दशाभ्यस्ता त्रिजीवेन्दोः4 कक्ष्याव्यासार्धयोजनम् ॥ ८b ॥ तच्चन्द्रभगणाभ्यस्तं भानोः स्वभगणोद्धृतम् ॥ ९a ॥ [ भू-रवि-शशीनां बिम्बयोजनव्यासाः : ] भूवृत्तादुदितात् प्राग्वद् व्यासस्तस्यापि5 नीयताम् ॥ ९b ॥ $4410$ $315$ दिग्वेदब्धिमितो भानोर्व्यासस्तिथ्यग्नयो विधोः ॥ १०a ॥ 1: C. नीयते 2: C. चाल्येते 3: C. कार्य 4: C. त्रिजीवेन्दोः 5: C. तत्रापि --- S 92 K.V. SARMA [ रविशशिनोः स्फुटयोजनकर्णः : ] कालकर्णहतं1 स्वस्वकक्ष्याव्यासार्धयोजनम् ॥ १०b ॥ त्रिज्याप्तं स्याद् भूगोलस्य मण्डलस्य च मध्ययोः । योजनेरन्तरालं स्यात् तत्कालोद्भवं स्फुटम् ॥ ११ ॥ [ रवीन्द्रोः द्वितीयस्फुटयोजनकर्णः : ] उच्चोनशशिकोटिज्यादलं पर्वन्तजं स्फुटम् । स्फुटयोजनकर्णे स्वं जह्यात् कक्ष्यादिजं ततः ॥ १२ ॥ स्वभूभ्यन्तरकर्णः3 स्यात् तेन बिम्बकलां नयेत्4 । स्फुटयोजनकर्णे स्वे मासान्ते शशिवद् रवेः ॥ १३ ॥ व्यस्तं पक्षान्तजं कार्यं रविभूभ्यन्तराप्तये ॥ १४a ॥ [ अर्केन्द्रोर्बिम्बकलाव्यसः : ] बिम्बस्य योजनव्यास5 विष्कम्भार्धहतं हरेत् ॥ १४b ॥ स्वभूभ्यन्तरकर्णेन लिप्ताव्यासः शशीनयोः ॥ १५a ॥ [ भूच्छायाबिम्बकलाव्यसः : ] $1050$ $3360$ रविभूभ्यन्तरं खेषु6पङ्क्तिघ्नं, खर्तुनिज्झरैः ॥ १५b ॥ हतं, भूगोलविष्कम्भाद् भूच्छायादैर्घ्ययोजनम् । चन्द्रभूभ्यन्तरं त्यक्त्वा शेषे भूव्यासताडिते ॥ १६ ॥ छायादैर्घ्यहृते व्यासः, चन्द्रवत् तमसः कलाः ॥ १७a ॥ [ चन्द्रविक्षेपः स्फुटभुक्तिश्च ] $270$ पातोनेन्दुर्भुजाजीवा ध्योमताराहता, हता ॥ १७b ॥ त्रिज्यया, सौम्ययाम्येन्दोः विक्षेपः, सा च स्फुटा गतिः । भूगोलचन्द्रकर्णेन भूचन्द्रान्तरयोजनैः ॥ १८ ॥ हते, स्फुटे इह ग्राह्ये विक्षिप्तिभुक्ती स्थितेर्दले ॥ १९a ॥ [ ग्रहणस्य सदसद्भावः : ] विक्षिप्तिः सा चन्द्रभूच्छायाबिम्बार्धाधिका यदि ॥ १९b ॥ ग्रहणं नैव चन्द्रस्य, हीना चेदस्य सम्भवः ॥ २०a ॥ 1: C. हतं 2: B. स्फुटे 3: C. स (wr.) 4: B. कला नयेत् 5: C. योजनं व्यासं 6: C. स्वेषु (wr.)

chunks.text: --- TANTRASAMGRAHA OF NĪLAKAṆṬHA SOMAYĀJĪ S 93 [ समस्तग्रहणम् ] चन्द्रबिम्बोन्नभूच्छाया बिम्बार्धादधिका यदि ॥ २०b ॥ सर्वग्रासो न चैव स्याद्, हीना चेद् ग्रस्यतेऽखिलम् ॥ २१a ॥ [ स्थित्यर्धस्पर्शमोक्षौ च ] सम्पर्कर्धकृतेस्त्यक्त्वा क्षेपवर्गं पदीकृतम् ॥ २१b ॥ षष्टिघ्नं भानुशीतांशोर्हृतं गत्यन्तरेण यत् । स्थित्यर्धनाडिकाद्यं तत्, पर्वन्ते तद्युतोनिते ॥ २२ ॥ मोक्षः स्पर्शश्च चन्द्रस्याप्यविशिष्टौ1 स्फुटौ तु तौ ॥ २३a ॥ [ स्थित्यर्ध-स्पर्श-मोक्षाणाम् अविशेषः : ] स्थित्यर्धघ्ने स्फुटे भुक्ती2 षष्ट्याप्ते भानुचन्द्रयोः ॥ २३b ॥ शोधयेत् समलिप्तेन्दोः3 सूर्याच्च स्पर्शिकावुभौ । स्वभुक्तिमन्यथा पाते सदा तात्कालिकीकृतौ ॥ २४ ॥ स्पर्शेन्दोश्च पुनः क्षेपस्थित्यर्धं तद्गती4 शशी । प्राग्वदेवासकृत् कार्या निश्चलत्वदिदृक्षुणा ॥ २५ ॥ स्थित्यर्धगतिकर्कन्द्वोः5 क्षिप्त्वा तौ मौक्षिको नयेत् । अन्यत् सर्वं समं मोक्षे स्थित्यर्धस्याविशेषणे ॥ २६ ॥ [ स्थित्यर्धाभ्यां स्पर्शमोक्षौ ] स्पर्शस्थितिदलं शोध्यं पर्वान्तादितरत् क्षिपेत् । स्पर्शमोक्षौ तु तौ स्यातां मध्ये स्यात् परमो ग्रहः6 ॥ २७ ॥ [ रव्युदयास्तमये स्पर्शमोक्षयोः दृश्यादृश्यत्वम् ] उदयास्तमयासन्ने स्पर्शे मोक्षे च संशयः । स्पर्शो दृश्य उतादृश्यश्चन्द्रस्यास्तमये त्विति ॥ २८ ॥ प्राग्वा पश्चाच्च मोक्षः स्यात् तद्देशोदयादिति ॥ २९a ॥ [ स्पर्शमोक्षयोः दृश्यादृश्यत्वनिर्णयः : ] स्पर्श रव्युदये कार्यो दृक्क्षेपः क्षिप्तिरिन्दवी ॥ २९b ॥ व्यासार्धघ्नः स्फुटः क्षेपः7 सम्पर्कर्धहतस्तु यः । तदृक्क्षेपधनुर्भेदो8 दिशोः साम्येऽन्यथा युतिः ॥ ३० ॥ 1: C. शिष्टौ तु तौ स्फुटो 2: C. (except 8) भुक्ति 3: C. समलिप्तेन्दोः 4: A. गतः; C. (edn.) गती 5: A. स्थित्यर्धे 6: C. परमग्रहः 7: A. स्फुटं क्षेपः ; C. स्फुटक्षेपः 8: A. तं दृक्क्षेप; C. तदृक्क्षेपाद् <<<CONTINUE>>> S 94 K.V. SARMA तदूनभत्रयजीवा तमोव्यासदलहता । त्रिज्याप्ता लम्बने योज्या भूच्छायाशङ्कुलब्धये ॥ ३१ ॥ द्वितीयस्फुटभाग्यस्य1 तिथ्यंशो लम्बनं त्विह । राशिप्रत्ययाधिके क्षेपदृक्क्षेपानीतकार्मुके ॥ ३२ ॥ अधिकस्य गुणात् प्राग्वत् लब्धं शोध्यं तु लम्बात् । शेषस्तस्य तमःशङ्कस्त्रिज्याकृत्या2 हतः स च ॥ ३३ ॥ हतो3 घातेन सूर्यस्य द्युज्याया लम्बकस्य च । लब्धा: प्राणा: क्षपाशेषे यदि रव्युदयात् ततः4 ॥ ३४ ॥ स्पर्श: प्रागेव, तर्ह्येव दृश्य: स्यान्न ततः परम्5 । एवं रव्यस्तकालोत्थक्षेपाप्ताप्टेन शङ्कुना ॥ ३५ ॥ सिद्धै: प्राणैर्यदा मोक्षो रव्यस्तमयत: परम् । तदैव दृश्यतामेति तत: प्राङ्मोक्षणेन च ॥ ३६ ॥

chunks.text: बिम्बान्तरसमेनादौ लिखेत सूत्रेण मण्डलम् ॥ ४६b ॥ बिम्बान्तरं तु सम्पर्कदलं स्यात् स्पर्शमोक्षयो: । शलाकाङ्कितमध्या2 या वलनद्विगुणायता ॥ ४७ ॥ प्राग्रेखागतमध्याङ्कनेमिस्पृष्टोभाग्रया । वलनं नीयतां स्पष्टं यथादिशमथानया ॥ ४८ ॥ प्रत्यग्रेखास्थ3 मध्याङ्कन्यस्तया व्यस्तमेव च । रेखां पूर्वापरां कुर्यात् तद्वशादपि चेतराम् ॥ ४९ ॥ छायामार्गोंऽनयो: पूर्वो विक्षेपान्तरिता विधो: । रेखाविक्षेपदिक्स्थतो4 मार्गौ तत्कालजौ तु तौ ॥ ५० ॥ लिप्ताव्यासदलेनेन्दो: स्वमार्गे परिधौ लिखेत । पौर्णमास्यां प्रतीच्यां तु प्रागेव प्रतिपद्यपि ॥ ५१ ॥ वृत्तममध्ये तमोबिम्बं स्वमार्गे सर्वदा लिखेत् । तमोबिम्बाद बहिर्भूतं दृश्यमिन्दौ न तद्गतम् । हनुपार्श्वादिभेदादि दृश्यतामत्र सुस्फुटम् ॥ ५२ ॥ ॥ इति तन्त्रसंग्रहे चन्द्रग्रहणप्रकरणं नाम चतुर्थोऽध्याय: ॥ 1: C. घातत्रिज्याप्त तस्य 2: C. मध्याया 3: C. प्रत्यग्रेखास्त 4: A. विक्षेपान्तरितं --- S 96 V. S. NARASIMHAN

chunks.text: द्रष्टुर्भूपृष्ठगस्येन्दुबिम्बोऽर्कच्च महान् भवेत् । नानात्वात् प्रतिदेशं तन्नेयं बिम्बं स्वदेशजम् ॥ ३४ ॥ मध्यकालभुजाज्याया: प्राग्वद् दृक्क्षेपमानयेत् । भानोर्दृक्क्षेपलग्ना ज्या हता दृक्क्षेपशङ्कुना ॥ ३५ ॥ त्रिज्याप्ता दृग्गतिभानोर्यत्तद्वत् दृक्क्षेपवर्गयो: । योगात् पदं तदैवैक्यं त्रिज्वागाञ्च्च यत् पदम् ॥ ३६ ॥ 1: C. 1-5, 8, 10 काले विशेषत: 2: B. तद्युक्तो <<<CONTINUE>>> TANTRASAMGRAHA OF NĪLAKAṆṬHA SOMAYĀJĪ | S 99 छायाशङ्कू रवेस्ताभ्यां भूव्यासार्धस्य योजनैः । हताभ्यां त्रिज्यया लब्धे दोःकोटी योजनात्मिके ॥ ३७ ॥ रविभ्यन्तरतः कोटि त्यक्त्वा तद्बाहुवर्गयोः । योगात् पदं भवेद् भानोर्दृक्कणों योजनात्मकः ॥ ३८ ॥ क्षेपदृक्क्षेपचापैैक्यं नतिः साम्येऽन्यथान्तरम् । राशित्रयं यदूनं यत् तज्ज्या शङ्कुः पराभिधः ॥ ३९ ॥ चन्द्रोन्नलग्रबाहूना त्रिज्या जूकादिजान्विता । क्षेपकौट्या हता भक्ता त्रिज्यया बाण उच्यते ॥ ४० ॥ ततो दृक्क्षेपकोटिघ्नं त्रिज्यातं परतस्त्यजेत् । शेषः शङ्कुः शशाङ्कस्य ततो दृग्ज्या च पूर्ववत् ॥ ४१ ॥ भूव्यासार्धहते2 ते च त्रिज्याप्ते कोटिदोःफले । दृक्कणोंऽर्कवदिन्दोस्तु स्वभूभ्यन्तरयोजनैः ॥ ४२ ॥ त्रिज्याघ्नाद् योजनव्यासात् तेनाप्ता बिम्बलिप्तिकाः । इष्टेन्दुः समलिप्तेन्दोर्दृग्गीत्यस्फुटभोगतः ॥ ४३ ॥ इष्टकेवलपर्वान्तद्युगतन्तरकालजात् । विक्षेपः केवलाच्चन्द्रात् प्राग्वत् त्रिज्याहतो हतः ॥ ४४ ॥ योजनैर्विवरे चन्द्रभगोलघनमध्ययोः । दृक्कर्णयोजनैर्भक्तो दृग्गोले क्षेप इष्यताम् ॥ ४५ ॥ केवलादेव दृक्क्षेपात् भूव्यासार्धेन ताडितात् । विधीयोजनदृक्कर्णभक्तान्नतिरिलिप्तिकाः ॥ ४६ ॥ तद्वदेव च दृक्क्षेपात् स्फुटदृक्क्षेपेन3 भास्वतः । रवीन्द्रोर्नतिभेदः स्यात् सर्वदैव4 नतिर्विधोः ॥ ४७ ॥ तद्बूपृष्ठोदितक्षेपयुतिः साम्येऽन्यथान्तरम् । एवं भूपृष्ठगां नीत्वा5 नतिं बिम्बद्वयं तथा ॥ ४८ ॥ सर्वग्रासो विनिर्णैयो नाम्ना मध्यतमस्तथा । ग्रहणं वाप्यभावो वा वाच्यो मानैः स्फुटैरिति ॥ ४९ ॥

chunks.text: स्पर्शे मध्ये च मोक्षे चाप्यन्यत्रेष्टेऽपि वा पृथक् ॥ ५७b ॥ वलनद्वयमानीय प्राग्वत् तद्योगभेदजात् । $$191$$ गुणादेकाङ्कभूभक्तं वलनं स्यात् स्फुटं त्विह ॥ ५७ ॥ $$18$$ वृत्तं धृतिमितास्येन कर्कटेन लिखेत्6 क्षितौ । दिशौ पूर्वापरे व्यस्तं लेखने फलके यदि ॥ ५९ ॥ वलनं पूर्ववन्नीत्वा रवेः पन्थाश्च तद्वशात् । नतेर्दिशि विधोस्तस्मात् स्फुटान्त्यन्तरे परः ॥ ६० ॥ कार्यस्तद्वृत्तमध्येऽथ रविबिम्बं स्फुटं लिखेत् । मात्वा तत्केन्द्रगाबाग्रबिम्बान्तरशलाकया ॥ ६१ ॥ बिन्दुं कृत्वा विधोर्मार्गे तद्विम्बं तत्र संलिखेत् । स्पर्शे प्रत्यङ्मुखीं मोक्षे शलाकां प्राङ्मुखीं नयेत् ॥ ६२ ॥ एवमेवेष्टकालेऽपि प्राक् पश्चाद् ग्रासमध्येतः । चन्द्रबिम्बाद् बहिर्भूतो भागो दृश्योऽर्कमण्डले । तदन्तर्गतभागस्तु ग्रस्तस्तेनासितः सदा ॥ ६३ ॥ [ ॥ इति तन्त्रसंग्रहे रविग्रहणप्रकरणं नाम पञ्चमोऽध्यायः ॥ ] 1: 1. $C{1-8.10}$ चैक्यम् 2: 2. $C{1-8}$ खण्डक: 3: 3. chunks.text: बिम्बान्तरसमेनादौ लिखेत् सूत्रेण मण्डलम् ॥ ४६b ॥ बिम्बान्तरं तु सम्पर्कदलं स्यात् स्पर्शमोक्षयोः । शलाकाङ्कितमध्या या2 वलनद्विगुणांयता ॥ ४७ ॥ प्राग्रेखागतमध्याङ्कनेमिस्पृष्टोभाग्रया । वलनं नीयतां स्पष्टं यथादिशमथानया ॥ ४८ ॥ प्रत्यग्रेखास्थ३ मध्याङ्कन्यस्तया व्यस्तमेव च । रेखां पूर्वापरां कुर्यात् तद्वशादपि चेतराम् ॥ ४९ ॥ छायामार्गोऽनयोः पूर्वो विक्षेपान्तरिता विधोः । रेखाविक्षेपदिक्स्थाहो४ मार्गो तत्कालज्ञौ तु तौ ॥ ५० ॥ लिप्ताव्यासहलेनेन्दोः स्वमार्गे परिधौ लिखेत् । पौर्णमास्यां प्रतीच्यां तु प्रागेव प्रतिपद्यपि ॥ ५१ ॥ वृत्तममध्ये तमोबिम्बं स्वमार्गे सर्वदा लिखेत् । तमोबिम्बाद् बहिर्भूतं दृश्यमिन्दौ न तद्गतम् । हनुपार्श्वादिभेदादि दृश्यतामत्र सुस्फुटम् ॥ ५२ ॥ [ ॥ इति तन्त्रसंग्रहे चन्द्रग्रहणप्रकरणं नाम चतुर्थोऽध्यायः ॥ ] 1: C. घातत्रिज्याप्त तस्य 2: C. मध्याया ३: C. प्रत्यग्रेखास्त ४: A. विक्षेपान्तरितं --- S 96 V. chunks.text: द्रष्टुर्भूपृष्ठगस्येन्दुबिम्बोऽर्कच्च महान् भवेत् । नानात्वात् प्रतिदेशं तन्नेयं बिम्बं स्वदेशजम् ॥ ३४ ॥ मध्यकालभुजाज्यायाः प्राग्वद् दृक्क्षेपमानयेत् । भानोर्दृक्क्षेपलग्ना ज्या हता दृक्क्षेपशङ्कुना ॥ ३५ ॥ त्रिज्याप्ता दृग्गतिर्भानोर्यत्तद्वद् दृक्क्षेपवर्गयोः । योगात् पदं तदैक्योनं त्रिज्यावर्गच्च यत् पदम् ॥ ३६ ॥ 1: C. 1-5, 8, 10 काले विशेषतः 2: B. तद्युक्ते S 109 TANTRASAMGRAHA OF NĪLAKANṬHA SOMAYĀJI [ बिम्बमानादीनां दृक्साम्यपरीक्षणम् ] चक्रांशाद्यङ्किते1 वृत्ते तन्मध्यासक्तचक्षुषा ॥ ३८b ॥ ज्ञेयं ग्रहान्तरं बिम्बदृग्ज्याचापादिकं स्फुटम् ॥ ३९a ॥ [ ग्रन्थोपसंहार: ] गोल: काल: क्रिया चापि द्योत्योऽत्र मया स्फुटम् ॥ ३९b ॥ लक्ष्मीनिहितध्यानैरिश्र्वं सर्वं हि लभ्यते ॥ ४० ॥ [ इति तन्त्रसंग्रहे शृङ्गोन्नतिप्रकरणं नाम अष्टमोऽध्याय: ॥ ] 1: B. शक्रांशाद्यंशिते CHAPTER - IV Lunar Eclipse Moment of conjunction in Lunar Eclipse : 1, 2. The true value of earth's shadow is said to be the sum of the true position of the sun and half the Circle (i.e. $180^\circ$), storing the values of the shadow and the moon at the time of sunset or sunrise whenever they are close to each other, the time of their conjunction is to be determined. It is to be understood that if the longtitude of the moon is greater, the conjunction has already taken place, if it is less then it is yet to take place. 3. The difference (in their longitudes) is multiplied by sixty, and is divided by the difference in their daily motions. The result in the same order gives the time in $ghaṭis$ of either the interval that had elapsed after conjunction or the interval that is required for the conjunction yet to take place. True sun and moon at sysygey (end point of full or new moon): 4, 5a. The mean and true positions of the sun and moon are again obtained at the determined instant, of conjunction. If the time of conjunction is found from the position of the sun and moon at sun-rise, then as indicated earlier, the correction for $cara$ at that time is to be obtained. 5b. (If the time of conjunction is found out from the position of sun and moon) at sun-set, then the $cara$ correction is to be found out as stated before for sun-set, If the value obtained from the $cara$ is varying, (then the following successive approximation is given). 6. From the value of the sun at the calculated time of conjunction, the difference in $prāṇas$ in minutes is obtained, using this and also the difference in the $dohphala$ (equation of centre of the sun) corrections are to be done to sun and moon as stated earlier to obtain the true values. 7. The time of conjunction is once again calculated, using the time elapsed from sunrise (or yet to elapse to sun rise). This is multiplied by the true motion and divided by 60. The results are added or subtracted (to the time of conjunction) according as the conjunction had already occured or yet to occur. 8a. The two longitudes will become identical even in seconds at the end of a new moon or full moon. ** S 112 V. S. NARASIMHAN Radius of the orbit of the sun and moon in yojanas 8b, 9a. The Radius of the orbit of the moon is R multiplied by 10 in $yojanas$ (i.e. 34380 $yojanas$). That multiplied by the number of revolutions of the moon and divided by the revolutions of the sun gives the radius of the orbit of the sun. Determination of the linear diameter of the discs of the earth, sun and moon. 9b, 10a. From the value of the circumference of the earth mentioned earlier calculate its diameter. The diameter of the sun's disc is 4410 $yojanas$ and that of the moon's disc is 315 $yojanas$. Note: The commentator states thus: 'Earth's circumference is 3300. Multiply this by 113 and divide by 354. That gives the diameter'. Hence $\text{Diameter} = \frac{3300 \times 113}{354}$ is taken to be equal to $\frac{354}{113}$ To find the true hypotenuse in yojanas of sun and Moon. 10b, 11. The radius in $yojanas$ of the orbits of each (the sun and the moon) is multiplied by the $manda\ karṇa$ in minutes (the $aviśiṣṭakarṇa$ obtained in chapter II) and divided by R. The result is the true distance in $yojanas$ of the distance between the centres of earth and sun at the desired instant. Note: In Trivandrum Sanskrit series edition śloka 10b is given as कालकर्णहतं । But Punjab University Indological series edition gives it as कालकर्णहतं । The commentator observes कलारूपेणविशिष्ट मन्दकर्णेन निहत्य ......... Hence the correct reading is कालकर्णहतं only. To find the second true hypotenuse in yojanas of sun and moon. 12. The true position of the moon is diminished by its higher apsis and the remainder is obtained, half of this value is subtracted from the true hypotenuse (calculated earlier) in $yojanas$, if the remainder at the end of the $parva$ (new moon/full moon) is in the six signs starting from cancer. (It is to be added if otherwise). 13, 14a. The result is the distance between the centres of moon and earth. From that the value of the moon's disc in minutes is to be obtained. To find the distance between the centres of the sun and earth, at the end of the month ($amāvasyā$ or solar eclipse), using the first $sphuṭa\ karṇa$ of the sun, follow the same process as for the moon. At the end of the $śukla\ pakṣa$ ($pūrṇima$, lunar eclipse) the reverse process is to be followed. Angular diameters of the orbs of the sun and moon 14b, 15a. The diameters of the discs in $yojanas$ of the sun and moon (4410 - sun; 315 - moon, śloka 10a Ch. IV) are multiplied by R and divided by the distances between them and the earth (using the second $sphuṭa\ yojana\ karṇa$). The results in minutes are their angular diameters. TANTRASAMGRAHA OF NĪLAKANṬHA SOMAYĀJI S 113 Diameter of the shadow of the earth :* 15b, 16a. The distance between the centres of the sun and earth is multiplied by 1050 (Diameter of earth) and then divided by 3360. The result is the length of the shadow in $yojanas$ from the centre of the earth.

Both the latitude and the true motion of the moon are multiplied by the $bhagola$ $candra$ $karṇa$ (the first $sphuṭa$ $yojana$ $karṇa$) and divided by the distance between the earth and moon. (second $sphuṭa$ $yojana$ $karṇa$). The results are to be taken as the true latitude and true daily motion. The result is multiplied by 60, and divided by the difference between the true daily motions of sun and moon. The result gives half the duration of the eclipse in $nādikas$. The two values got by adding and subtracting the same, (to the middle of the eclipse) give respectively the time of release and of contact, of the eclipse. These two values obtained after interation give the two true values.

The two results in minutes are subtracted from the positions of the sun and moon. The two results give their positions at the time of contact. In the case of the node, its position is obtained in the reverse manner. Thus the values for that instant are obtained. 25. From the position of the moon (the shadow and node obtained) at the time of contact, the latitude and duration of the eclipse and the motion of the sun are found as per the process described earlier, till a value (time of contact) that does not vary (or that which is steady) is obtained. 26. Obtain the sun and moon at the time of release by adding (instead of subtracting) their motion from the time of conjunction, for obtaining time of release, the duration of the eclipse by the process of iteration - everything else is the same (as in the case of time of contact).

When the sun is setting (and the moon is about to rise), the doubt arises whether the contact is noticed (seen) or not, at that place. If the contact takes place before the rising of the sun, that is seen; if the release takes place after the setting of the sun, then also it is seen. (otherwise it is not seen).

heading_path: Determination of the visibility of sparśa and mokṣa
chunks.text: 29b. (In order to determine whether the eclipse is visible) The zenith - distance of the nonagesimal ($drkkṣepa$) and latitude of the moon are to be calculated. --- S 116 V. S. NARASIMHAN 30a. The true latitude (of the moon) is multiplied by $R$ and divided by half of the sum of the diameter of the moon and shadow ($samparka$ $ardha$ :). (This value is kept separate as $K$). 30b. The value of the latitude in arc, is subtracted from the arc value of the $drkkṣepa$, if their directions are the same; otherwise the two are added. 31. The result is then diminished from three $rāśis$ (i.e. $90^\circ$) and then sine of the balance is found. This is multiplied by the radius of the shadow and divided by $R$. The result obtained in minutes is to be added to the $lambana$ for obtaining the $śaṅku$ of earth’s shadow. 32a. Here $lambana$ is the result obtained by dividing by fifteen the true motion of the moon (in minutes, by finding the $dvitiyasphuṭa$ $bhukti$). 32b, 33. If the value obtained (by adding) the latitude and $drkkṣepa$ is more than three $rāśis$ ($90^\circ$), from the $R sine$ value of the arc that is in excess of $90^\circ$, the result is obtained as explained earlier (in $śloka$ 31). This is subtracted from the $lambana$. The balance then becomes $tamas$ $śaṅku$. This is multiplied by the square of $R$. 34, 35a. The result is divided by the product of $dyujyā$ of the sun and $lambaka$. The value is obtained in $prāṇas$. If these $prāṇas$ show that the contact occurred in the night i.e. before sun-rise, then the eclipse is visible, otherwise it is not visible. 35b. In the same way we take $kṣepa$ etc. at the time of sunset and calculate $tamaśaṅku$. From that calculate the $prāṇas$. If they indicate that the release is after sunset, then the eclipse is visible. If the release occurs before sunset it is not visible.

chunks.text: 37, 38a. Or alternately, at the time (of first or last contact, desired immersion) find the true longitudes of the sun, moon and node. Therein the difference in minutes of (the longitudes of) the moon and the earth's shadow is multiplied by the difference in the corrected daily motions (of the sun, moon) and divided by the difference in the corrected daily motions as determined at first. The result is to be taken as their true differences in the longitudes. 38b, 39. To the sum of the squares of that difference and the latitude of moon, add the square of the difference of their $śaras$. The square root of the result is the subtle value of the distance between the two discs (the distance between the centres of the shadow-disc and that of moon-disc). For finding the desired immersion also, the same distance is used. 40. $Śara$ is obtained by dividing the square of the (above) $sphuṭāntara$ by the total diameter. For the latitude also, the $śara$ is obtained in the same manner. For a better --- TANTRASAMGRAHA OF NĪLAKAṆṬHA SOMAYĀJĪ S 117 value of $śara$ an iterative process is adopted to the sum of the square of the $śara$ (calculated earlier) and the $sphuṭāntara$ (or $kṣepa$). S. NARASIMHAN $$= \frac{x^2 - \frac{1}{3} \frac{R^4 \theta^4}{4R^2}}{2R}$$ $$= \frac{x^2 - \frac{1}{3} \left(\frac{x^2}{2R}\right)^2}{2R}$$ 41b. When the calculated value of $Bimbāntara$ is subtracted from the $sampark\text{-}ardha$, we get the extent of obscuration always.

chunks.text: Parallax in longitude (Lambana) and in latitude (Nati) are of importance in solar eclipse. Hence these are explained in the beginning itself. 1. When the planet is in the middle of the visible hemisphere (i.e. Dṛkṣepa vṛtta, vertical circle passing through the pole of the ecliptic) there is no parallax in longitude (lambana). Then the planet is said to be in Dṛkṣepa lagna. When the planet is to the east or west of Dṛkṣepa lagna (Nonagesimal) then there will be lambana. 2a. (when the planet) lies on the ecliptic and also at the Zenith, then there is no nati also. ![[Spherical diagram showing parallax components]](media/p32page.png) $$ \begin{aligned} SŚ &= \text{Parallax} \\ SM &= \text{Lambana} \\ ŚM &= \text{Nati} \\ \text{Great Circle ZVK} - Dṛkṣepa\ vṛtta. \end{aligned} $$ 2b, 3a. When the planet in the Dṛkṣepa vṛtta, lies at a place which is different from Centre of samamaṇḍala (Zenith), then there will be no nati. 3b, 4a. From the rise time of 1/8th of the rāśis given (in prāṇas) for an observer at Lanka, and the hour angle (of the sun, i.e. natāsava:) by subtracting and adding the hour angle from or to the half-duration of the day, obtain the true value of the madhya lagna. ** TANTRASAMGRAHA OF NĪLAKAṆṬHA SOMAYĀJĪ | S 121 ![[Spherical diagram showing Madhyalagna and Madhyajyā]](media/p33page.png) $$ \begin{aligned} M &- \text{Madhyalagna} \\ R \sin ZM &= \text{Madhyajyā} \\ R \sin EA &= \text{Udayajyā} \\ rQR &- \text{Equator} \\ rMA &- \text{Eclipse} \end{aligned} $$ 4b. From the madhya lagna, find the declination of the same in arcs with respect to the equinoxes. 5. The sum or difference of this (declination of Madhya lagna) and the arc length of the latitude of the place are found according as the directions are the same or different. Its R Sine is called madhyajyā. The jyā of the Agra of the praglagna (point of the ecliptic at the eastern point of horizon) is called a Udaya jya. 6. Their product (madhya jyā and Udaya jyā) divided by R is called Bāhujyā. Subtract its square from the squares of the madhyajyā and R. 7. Of their square roots, the first is multiplied by R and divided by the other. Then Dṛkṣepajyā is obtained. Its complement (Koṭi) is known as Dṛggati. ![[Spherical diagram showing components for Dṛkṣepajyā]](media/p33_page.png) S 122 | V. S. NARASIMHAN $Bhujyā = R \sin \theta = \frac{R \sin ZM . R \sin EA}{R}$ $Dṛkṣepajyā = R \sin ZV = R . \frac{\sqrt{(R \sin ZM)^2 - (R \sin \theta)^2}}{\sqrt{R^2 - (R \sin \theta)^2}}$ i.e. According to modern notation: $\sin ZV = \sqrt{\frac{(\sin ZM)^2 - \sin^2 \theta}{\cos \theta}}$ where $\sin \theta = \sin ZM \sin EA$ --I Proof: Now A is the pole of ZV and E that of ZM $EA = x = mzv$ In $\Delta MZV$, $\frac{\sin MV}{\sin x} = \frac{\sin ZM}{1}$ Hence $MV = \theta$ $\sin ZM . \cos x = \cos MV . \sin ZV + \sin MV . \cos ZV . \cos 90^\circ$ $= \cos \theta . \sin ZV$ Hence LHS $= \sin ZM \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 x} = \sin ZM \sqrt{1 - \frac{\sin^2 \theta}{\sin^2 ZM}}$ $= \sqrt{\sin^2 ZM - \sin^2 \theta}$, which is I. 8. The Divisor is obtained by dividing the square of the first Jyā by the Jyā of Dṛggati, Cheda : is $\frac{(R \sin 3 \iota)^2}{R \sin ZV}$ The Bahujyā of the difference between the sun and Dṛkṣepalagna is divided by this Divisor. The result in Nāṭika gives the Lambana (parallax in longitude). 9. At the end of the parva, if the longitude of the sun is less than that of the Dṛkṣepa lagna, it is added; if it is more then subtracted. This parvānta (apparent instant of conjunction) is to be obtained by method of iteration thus. 10. From the Dṛkṣepajyā ($R \sin D$) this obtained after iteration, multiply the same by the true daily motion of the sun (determined at the parvānta which itself is obtained by iteration), divide (the product) by $51570 (= 15 \times R)$. The result gives Nati (parallax in latitude in minutes). Its direction is to be determined like that of Dṛkṣepajyā (If R sin D is less than lambana direction is northern, otherwise southern). ** TANTRASAMGRAHA OF NĪLAKAṆṬHA SOMAYĀJĪ | S 123

heading_path: Parallax in latitude of the moon in minutes :
chunks.text: 11. The true latitude is calculated from the true position of the moon at that instant (parvānta) as before (i.e. by multiplying by first sphuṭa karṇa and dividing by second sphuṭa karṇa). The arcs of the latitude (thus obtained) and the Dṛkṣepa are added if the directions are the same, if not their difference is taken. 12. The sine of the result is multiplied by the second true (daily) motion (in minutes) and divided by $51570$ (- $15$ R). The result is the nati (parallax in latitude of the moon). The sum of the nati and the corrected Vikṣepa (described in verse 11) is taken if their directions are the same, otherwise, their difference is taken. 13. Of that and the value of the nati of the sun in minutes the difference is obtained if their directions are the same (both to the South of ecliptic); if the directions are opposite (moon lies to the south and sun to the north), their sum is taken. (The result) is the true Nati during the solar eclipse. 14. If the nati of the sun is substratible from the difference of the natis of the sun and moon, then the direction of the difference is taken oppositely; otherwise it is taken along the direction of the moon.

chunks.text: 16. (As in the case of lunar eclipse) from the sum of the semi-diameters of the sun and moon, and the sphuṭa nati, the half-duration has to be obtained. The lambana (parallax in longitude) is also to be obtained. 17a. For obtaining half the duration of the eclipse, the difference of the lambanas is to be added when (the sparśa madhya and mokṣa take place) in the same hemisphere. (To the time of contact, (sparśa) add the difference between the lambanas at the time of sparśa and madhya. Similarly for the time of release, add the difference of the lambanas between madhya and mokṣa to it. Commentator). 17b. When (the sparśa madhya, mokṣa are in) different hemispheres, the sum of the lambanas is to be added to half the duration of the eclipse (for obtaining the true value). 18. In the eastern hemisphere, the values of the lambana (at the times of contact etc., (i.e. contact, middle and release) become lesser and lesser in order; their lambanas increase in order when the sun is in the western hemisphere. 19a. Whenever the situation is found to be opposite, then the difference in lambana is to be subtracted. 19b. (In the eastern hemisphere) in the proximity of the rising (of the sun) if at the time of release the lambana is more (than that of contact). 20. During night, if the lambana at the time of the middle of the eclipse is more than at the time of release then the madhya lambana is to be subtracted from the mokṣa lambana. 21, 22a. The difference in lambanas is to be subtracted from the second half duration. Thus if the lambana at contact is more than that at the middle, in the proximity of sun-set, the difference between the two lambanas is to be subtracted from the first half duration.

chunks.text: 27b, 28. To the time of syzygy (parvānta) which is obtained by iteration, add the half-duration of the eclipse (This will give the approximate value of mokṣa-kāla. At the mokṣa kāla found thus determine lambana, nati etc., with this sphuṭa nati, the half-duration is again found). To the half-duration determined with sphuṭa nati, the sum or difference of lambanas is applied and the result (which is taken as new half-duration) is added to the parvānta. This process is repeated as done earlier (for sparśa kāla to get consecutive constant value). 29a. The interval (second half-duration) added to the time of the middle of the eclipse (sphuṭa parvānta) is to be taken as the time of release of the eclipse of the sun. 29b, 30a. (If the angular diameter of the moon is greater than that of sun), then subtracting the angular diameter of the sun from that of the moon, take half the value of the balance. If the true value of the nati is less than this value, then a total eclipse takes place. 30b, 31a. (If the angular diameter of the sun is greater than that of moon), deduct the angular diameter of the moon from that of the sun and take half the value of the balance. If the nati is less than this value, the circumference of the sun will then be visible (i.e. the eclipse in annular). 31b, 32a. Take square root after subtracting the square of the nati from the square of the difference of the angular semi-diameters (of the sun and moon). Multiply by 60. Divide by the difference in the daily motions of the sun and moon (dvitiya sphuṭa bhukti antaraṇa). The result gives the half duration of the observation of the sun. 32b. If the angular diameters of the moon is less (than that of the sun) it is an annular eclipse. Here too the process of iteration should be done as explained earlier (to determine the half-duration of totality or annularity of the eclipse). 33. The half-duration of totality determined thus if deducted from the instant of the middle of the eclipse, that gives the instant of nimīlana (beginning of the totality of eclipse). If it is added then it gives the instant of unmīlana (end of the totality of the eclipse). S 126 | V. S. NARASIMHAN In the same way if it is deducted or added in the case of the annular eclipse, then these are to be understood as the instants of beginning of annularity (poorti) and end of annularity (chedha) of the circumference of the disc of the eclipsed body. 34. For an observer on the surface of the arth, the disc of the moon is larger (greater) than that of the sun. It also varies from place to place. Hence the value of the disc at one's own place is to be obtained. 35. Calculate the Dṛkkṣepa as earlier from the R sine of the madhya kāla. $$R \sin ZV = \frac{R \sin \phi R \cos w}{R} \pm \frac{R \cos \phi R \cos \gamma E}{8442}$$ Fig. 38. Celestial diagram showing Z, P, V, S, M arcs Fig. 38. Celestial diagram showing Z, P, V, S, M arcs (Refer: Ch. III 104b-105) S - Sun - V- Vitribhālagna M- Madhyalagna 35b, 36. The R sine of the Dṛkkṣepa lagna of the sun (R sin SV) multiplied by the R Cosine of Dṛkkṣepa (R cos ZV) and the result divided by R is the Drggati of the sun, $$\{ \text{Drggati, } x = \frac{R \sin SV \cdot R \cos ZV}{R} \}$$ The sum of the squares of that (x) and the Dṛkṣepa jyā (is taken). Its square root (is obtained) and that which is the square root of their sum diminished from the square of R, are the chāyā and śaṅku of the sun. Note: $Chāyā, R \sin ZS = \sqrt{x^2 + (R \sin ZV)^2}$ $R \cos ZS, Śaṅku = \sqrt{R^2 - \{ x^2 + (R \sin ZV)^2 \}}$ S 127 | TANTRASAMGRAHA OF NĪLAKAṆṬHA SOMAYĀJI According to modern notation, the result given is $(\sin ZS)^2 = (\sin ZV)^2 + (\sin SV \cos ZV)^2$ Fig. 39. Geometric arc diagram ZVS showing 90 degree angle Fig. 39. Geometric arc diagram ZVS showing 90 degree angle In $\Delta$ ZVS, $\cos ZS = \cos ZV \cdot \cos SV$ $\therefore (\sin ZS)^2 = 1 - (\cos ZV \cdot \cos SV)^2$ $= 1 - (\cos ZV)^2 \{ 1 - \sin^2 SV \}$ $= (\sin ZV)^2 + (\cos ZV \cdot \sin SV)^2$ 37. These two (chāyā and śaṅku) are multiplies by the radius of the earth in yojanas and (divided) by R. The result are respectively the Doḥphala and Koṭiphala in yojanas. $(Doḥphala) := a \cdot \frac{R \sin ZS}{R}$, and $Koṭiphala = a \cdot \frac{R \cos ZS}{R}$ where $a = \text{Radius of earth}$. 38. The koṭiphala is subtracted from the dvidiya sphuṭayojana karṇa of the sun (x). The square root of the sum of squares of that and the bāhu (doḥphala) becomes the Dṛkkarna in yojanas of the sun. i.e. $Dṛkkarna = \sqrt{(x - \frac{a R \cos ZS}{R})^2 + (\frac{a R \sin ZS}{R})^2}$
