chunks.title: Intercalation in the Vedic Texts
chunks.text: Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, one of the six disciplines (aṅgas/limbs) studied by Vedic priests, provided the priests with the means to compute the prescribed times for performing sacrifices. It is one of the two Vedic texts that is not devoted to the description and exposition of the rituals. The date of composition of this text is not known; astronomical data in the text suggest composition sometime between 1370 BC and 1150 BC1 but a later date of approximately 500 BC has also been suggested2. This is the only text of astronomy available from the Vedic period and it is likely to be the culmination of a process of identification and classification of calendric concepts that must have started at a much earlier age. This earlier period can be explored with the aid of Vedic texts (i.e. the Saṃhitās, the Brāhmaṇas and the Sūtras); these texts are devoted to the description, exposition and justification --- 496 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE of various Vedic rituals and ceremonies. The date of composition of these texts is also not known; the oldest text, Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, is believed to have been composed between 1700 BC and 1200 BC3 and the consensus of opinion is that most if not all of the other texts were composed before 500 BC. From these texts following elements of a calendar can be identified; The seasons – in Ṛgveda Saṃhitās ($RV$) three, five and six seasons have been mentioned. In the post-$Ṛgvedic$ texts there are five or six (and rather infrequently, seven) seasons in a year. The tropical or the seasonal year – this can be inferred from a number of verses in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitās and in other Vedic texts, in which the age of a person etc. is given by the number of elapsed seasons (usually autumn/śarad) e.g. $RV$. X.85.394. The synodic year – this can be inferred from verses like "the moon is the one that shapes the years" e.g. $RV$. X.85.55. The month – the canonical length of a Vedic month was 30 days, this is the rounded-up mean synodic month of 29.53 days; the moon is often referred to as māsakṛt (month maker) also the word māsa means both the moon and the month. In the post-$Ṛgvedic$ texts each season was assigned two months, sometimes two seasons were combined. A ritual year – the length of this year was 360 days (i.e. 12 months of 30 days each) e.g. $RV$. I.164.116. An intercalary month – a thirteenth month (adhimāsa) is often mentioned and the phrase "with the thirteenth month you obtain the year" occurs frequent in the Vedic texts. The earliest reference to a thirteenth month is in $RV$. I.164.157. A period of intercalation – in the post-$Ṛgvedic$ texts a group of five years is frequently mentioned but (with one exception, as discussed below) no specific role is identified for this group. In the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa a five year period of intercalation is used. It is obvious that both the synodic year (of 354.36 days) and the ritual year (of 360 days) will lag behind the tropical (seasonal) year (of 365.24 days) after the fiducial year and a scheme of intercalation would have been essential for the Vedic priests to perform their rituals and ceremonies at the --- INTERCALATION IN THE VEDIC TEXTS 497 proper time. The Vedic priests are frequently enjoined to keep the "ordained order" of the twelve months and sacrifice at the proper season e.g. $RV$. VII.103.98. The Vedic priests were also aware that the tropical/seasonal year was at least 365 days long as they point out in Taittirīya Saṃhitā ($TS$. VII.1.10)9 that the year (saṃvatsara), in order to create the seasons "saw this five-night rite ........the four-night rite is incomplete; the six-night rite is redundant, the correct sacrifice is the five-night rite". This need to correct the ritual year was recognised in the oldest Vedic texts available to us; in $RV$. I.25.8. it is noted that "Dhṛtavrata (Varuṇa) has knowledge of the productive twelve months, he knows, that which is extra". The nature of "that which is extra" is not stated but the productive twelve months refers to a ritual year of twelve months (each of thirty days) and it is reasonable to assume that the "extra" refers to the days required to match the length (in days) of ritual year and the tropical year. The addition of extra days (five) to a ritual year of 360 days was practised by ancient Iranians and is mentioned in Avestan10. Similarly, for many centuries ancient Egyptian priests added extra days to their ritual year to bring it closer in length to the tropical year. Apart from the few statements like those quoted above, the Āryas have left us no clues to reconstruct the procedure(s) they may have used to synchronise the tropical year and the ritual year. Perhaps the first (in the South Asian cultural sphere) reference to intercalation is in Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa. This has encouraged the belief that "no systematic intercalation scheme can be attributed to this (Vedic) period"11. And yet the Āryas performed their rites and ceremonies, both simple and intricate, over hundreds of years. The Vedic texts give times when some of these rituals should be performed and a sacrificer is constantly urged (and warned) that the full efficacy of a ritual is only accrued by following the procedures of a ritual ‘to the latter’. The ceremonies like Darśapūrṇamāsa (new and full moon) and Cāturmāsya (four monthly or the three seasons) would have required the ability to forecast and identify appropriate days for performance of ceremonies. It is inconceivable that these ceremonies and rituals would not have been performed at the appointed and proper times. A closer look at the Vedic texts indicates that the Āryas were aware of problems encountered in getting the time right for their rituals. For example, Aitareya Brāhmaṇa ($AB$. VII. 11; XXXII. 10) and Kauṣītaki Brāhmaṇa ($KB$. III.1)12 describe ceremonies to be performed at new-moon. But in Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa ($SB$.XI.1.5.1)13 the sacrificer is --- 498 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE warned that when he thinks that it "is the day of the new moon the moon is seen" i.e. the moon rises a day earlier than the calculated day. Similarly, $SB$.XI.1.4.114 recommends expiation rituals if the moon is seen on a new-moon day "on account of not having ascertained properly" i.e. the moon rises when new(no)-moon was expected. Passages like this suggest that the Āryas were aware that there could be discrepancies between the calculated and observed times of astronomical events. Starting with the nineteenth century pioneer Weber15,16, the Vedic texts have been studied and analysed (to various depths) by Thibaut17,18, Tilak19 and Dikshit20 to identify the calendar of this period. In the twentieth century this topic has been examined by Saha and Lahiri21, Pingree22,24, Jaggi23, Ōhashi25, Narahari Achar26,28, Abhyankar27 and Balachandra Rao29. These works address the problem of intercalation but analyse and discuss only the simplest and inadequate scheme (Section 2). Different and more detailed schemes for intercalation in the Vedic texts have identified and investigated by Faddegon30 and Chakravarty31. In Section 2 the intercalation schemes which can be inferred from the Vedic texts and may have been followed by the Āryas are analysed and discussed. The results of these procedures are compared with the best known intercalation scheme of Meton. In Section 3 it is shown that some salient features of the calendar of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa* are similar to those that are given or can be derived from the Vedic texts. The conclusions are given in Section 4.

chunks.title: Intercalation in the Vedic Texts
chunks.text: A number of early civilizations timed their ritual and social ceremonies by the synodic month. It was also recognised that a synodic year of 12 months and about 354 days did not ‘keep pace’ with the tropical year of about 365 days. In the Middle East the attempts to synchronise the synodic and the tropical years can be traced back to about eighth century BC32, but the best known early attempt to synchronise the synodic calendar and the tropical calendar is the Metonic cycle. This was devised (more likely adopted from the Babylonians) around 432 BC by the astronomer Meton of Athens. This scheme is based on the observation (known to the Babylonians) that after 19 years (235 lunations or synodic months) the moon’s phase recurs on the same day of the tropical year. The Metonic cycle is an arithmetic rule to --- INTERCALATION IN THE VEDIC TEXTS 499 synchronise the synodic and tropical years by adding an extra month to seven years in a nineteen-year cycle. The rationale of this scheme is as follows; $$ \text{Mean length of the synodic month} = 29.5306 \text{ days} $$ $$ \text{Mean length of a synodic year } (12 \times 29.5306) = 354.3672 \text{ days} $$ $$ \text{19 synodic (lunar) years with 7 additional months } = 6939.6910 \text{ days} $$ $$ \text{Mean length of the tropical year is } = 365.2422 \text{ days} $$ $$ \text{19 tropical years } 19 \times 365.2422 = 6939.6018 \text{ days} $$ Traditionally a month was added to the years 3, 6, 8, 11, 14, 17 and 19 of the Metonic cycle. More practically the cycle of 19 years was approximated to a whole number of 6940 days by 125 long months of 30 days and 110 short months of 29 days. Starting from a fiducial year, the difference (in days) between the accumulated number of days in the tropical years and in the corresponding synodic years, intercalated according to the Metonic cycle, is shown in Fig. 1 for a period of 500 years. The difference is obtained at the end of each tropical year. Although every year the (corrected) Fig. 1. Metonic Cycle. The difference, every year, between the accumulated number of days in the tropical years and in the corresponding intercalated synodic years. --- [^] Stoke Lodge, 10 Royal Crescent, Sandown, Isle of Wight, PO36 8LZ. Email: p.gondhalekar@btinternet.com <<<CONTINUE>>> synodic year differs in length from the corresponding tropical year, this difference does not diverge over hundreds of years. The greatest advantage of the Metonic cycle was that it offered a lunar calendar with a definite rule for inserting intercalary months to keep in step with the cycle of seasons. It also gave an accurate average length of the tropical year: 365.25 days. The scheme was so successful that it formed the basis of the calendar adopted in the Seleucid Empire (Mesopotamia) and was used in the Jewish calendar and the calendar of the Christian Church. It is not known if the Āryas also had developed an arithmetic procedure for synchronising their ritual year and the tropical year. As mentioned above, the thirteenth month can be traced back to Ṛgveda Saṃhitā and a thirteenth month is mentioned, either explicitly or implicitly, in all post-Ṛgvedic Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas. Unfortunately the Āryas have not left us the algorithm they might have used for intercalation. It has been assumed that the Āryas would have followed the arithmetic approach typified by Meton and other ancient Greek calendar makers. In the simplest application of such a scheme a month of 30 days could be intercalated after ‘$n$’ years to synchronise the tropical year of 365.24 days and the ritual year of 360 days, that is; $$365.24 \times n = 360.0 \times n + 30$$ $$n = 5.73$$ The tropical and the ritual years would be perfectly synchronised if a thirty day month is intercalated after five years and (about) nine months. The Vedic texts have no references to this form of intercalation. But a group of five years is frequently mentioned, in calendrical context, in the post-Ṛgvedic Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas. In the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa a group of five years is called a yuga and is the period of intercalation (see below). Guided by Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa rather than by the Vedic texts, it has been assumed that the Āryas may have intercalated a thirteenth month every fifth year. That is; $$Tropical\ year;\ 5 \times 365.24 = 1826.20$$ $$Ritual\ year;\ 5 \times 360 + 30 = 1830.00$$ $$Difference\ (Tropical - Ritual)\ year = -3.8\ days$$ This scheme of intercalation results in an average year of 366 days. In this scheme, after five years, the tropical year would have lagged behind the ritual year by 3.8 days and this would accumulate to thirty days after about thirty-nine years and six months. The ‘shift in the seasons’ would have been noticed long before thirty-nine years. The annual difference between the accumulated number of days in the tropical years and in the ritual years, over five hundred years, is shown in Fig. 2. The difference between the intercalation scheme of the Metonic cycle and the ‘five-year-yuga’ cycle is dramatic and it should be obvious that the Āryas could not have followed this rather crude scheme of intercalation. Fig. 2. The annual difference in the accumulated number of days in the tropical years and the intercalated ritual years. The ‘simple’ intercalation in which a month of 30 days is added every fifth ritual year is shown in Curve #1. For Curve #2 the same correction is made every fifth year except every fortieth year no correction is made i.e. the 30-day month is not added. The Āryas could have used a ‘six-year-yuga’ for intercalation i.e. added a (thirteenth) month of 30 days in every sixth year. The only reason for considering this scheme is a reference, in calendrical context, to a group of six year in Taittirīya Brāhmaṇas (TB.III.10.4).33 That is; $$6 \times 365.24 = 2191.44\ days$$ $$6 \times 360 + 30 = 2190.00\ days$$ $$Difference\ (Tropical - Ritual)\ year = 1.44\ days$$ After six years the tropical year would have gained 1.44 days on the ritual year and this would have accumulated to thirty days after one hundred and twenty five years. This scheme of intercalation results in an average year of 365 days. This scheme is far more stable than the ‘five-year-yuga’ scheme nevertheless it is not particularly satisfactory over long periods. Two possible schemes of intercalation after six years are suggested in SB. In SB. IX 1.1.43. and SB. IX 3.3.18. a thirteenth month of thirty-five days is suggested and in SB. X. 4.3.8. SB. X. 4.3.19. and SB*. X 5.4.5., a thirteenth month of thirty-six days is suggested. The reasoning behind these two schemes could be as follows; $$7 \times 365.24 = 2556.68\ days$$ $$6 \times 360 + 360 + 35 = 2555.00\ days$$ $$6 \times 360 + 360 + 36 = 2556.00\ days$$

chunks.title: Intercalation in the Vedic Texts
chunks.text: The result of intercalating a thirteenth month of thirty-five days in the seventh year is very similar to that of intercalating a thirteenth month of thirty days in the sixth year, that is, the difference (in the number of days in the tropical year and the ritual year) of 1.68 days will accumulate to thirty days after one hundred and twenty five years and the average length of the year would be 365 days. But in the scheme of intercalating a thirteenth month of thirty-six days in the seventh year the difference (in the number of days in the tropical year and the ritual year) of 0.68 days will accumulate to thirty days after three hundred and eight years and ten months and the average length of the year would be 365.14 days. The intercalation of thirty-five and thirty-six days were identified by Weber34 but he erroneously assumed an intercalation period of six years. It is possible to make a very simple amendment to the ‘five-year-yuga’ scheme of intercalation to obtain a very satisfactory synchronisation of the tropical year and the Vedic ritual year. This is achieved by omitting the intercalary thirteenth month (of 30 days) in every eighth yuga i.e. every forty years.35 The results of this scheme of intercalation over five-hundred years are shown in Fig. 2. and it is obvious that this is an exceptionally stable scheme. And yet there is no evidence in the Vedic texts that the Āryas followed this scheme of intercalation. This cannot have been due to their lack of ability to perform simple arithmetic operations because in the construction of their ritual fire-altars, the Āryas demonstrate a high degree of mathematical skill. The only Vedic text that describes an intercalation scheme is Maitrāyaṇīya Saṃhitā (MS.I.10.8).36 In this text two type of ritualists can be identified; the $ṛtu-yājins$ and the $cāturmāsya-yājins$. The $ṛtu-yājins$ celebrated the three seasonal sacrifices ($cāturmāsya$) on the first full-moon day that followed the beginning of spring, summer and autumn. These yajins were not concerned with the number of days between the seasons or the length of the lunation but relied entirely on observations to perform the required rituals. The $cāturmāsya-yājins$, on the other hand, performs the seasonal sacrifices at fixed number of lunations. But these yajins had to follow (arithmetic) rules to keep in step with the seasons. The scheme suggested is as follows: the yajins celebrated the $cāturmāsya$ ceremonies for three years (of thirty-six synodic months) at fixed intervals and followed this by an intercalated thirteenth month, the ceremonies were then performed for further two years (of twenty-four synodic months) followed by another intercalated thirteenth month. Both intercalated months were of thirty days. A possible scheme of alternate lunations of thirty and twenty-nine days respectively is as follows; $$18 \times 30 + 18 \times 29 + 30 = 1092\ days$$ $$12 \times 30 + 12 \times 29 + 30 = 738\ days$$ $$Total = 1830.00\ days$$ $$Tropical\ year:\ 365.24 \times 5 = 1826.20\ days$$ This scheme can be improved slightly (that is, reduce the difference between the number of days in five tropical years and the number of days in five intercalated years) by altering the number of months with lunations of thirty and twenty-nine days. But a (near) perfect match is not possible. As discussed above, in this scheme the ritual year (of the $cāturmāsya-yājins$) would have gained on the tropical year and would have required additional correction. MS.I.10.8. is the only Vedic text that has unambiguously identified the purpose of grouping five years in a calendar but in this Saṃhitā this five year period is not called a ‘yuga’. This Saṃhitā has not told us why a period of five year was used for intercalation, for this we have to turn elsewhere. The daily observances of the sattra of Gavām ayana follow the apparent annual motion of the sun. This sattra has two foci, the Viṣuvant and Mahāvrata days and these correspond respectively to the summer and the winter solstice as explained in KB. XIX.3.37 The day of the start of the sattra is not given in KB. XIX.3., but AB. IV.26; XIX.4) prescribe that the sattra should commence in the cool season ($śiśira$ in the months of $māgha$ or $phālguna$), this passage also enjoins against starting the sattra in any other season. More definite information on the day of the start of the sattra is given in TS.VII.4.8.38 and with minor variations in the wording and with additional information, in Pañcaviṃśa Brāhmaṇa (PB.V.9).39 The importance of these passages has been recognised for a long time and these passages have been discussed extensively by mīmāṃsakas and Sāyaṇa (fourteenth century, died about 1387). In the nineteenth century the passages again came under scrutiny, this time of Weber40 and Tilak.41 More recently the passage has been discussed by Chakravarty.42 The mīmāṃsakas attempted to interpret the passages and understand their implications and these have been used by the nineteenth and twentieth century scholars to discuss the New Year Day of the Vedic calendar. From these texts no single chronological marker can be identified for the start of the ritual year. According to KB. XIX.3. “on the new moon of $māgha$ he (sun) rests, being about to turn north....” and the Mahāvrata would have been performed on this day and the ceremony concluding Gavām ayana (Udayanīya Atirātra) would have been performed on the following day. Thus the new ritual year must have started (soon) after the winter solstice and this is in agreement with AB. IV.26; XIX.4. It is however unlikely that the new cycle of the sattra was started two days after the Mahāvrata as the start of the Vedic ceremonies was usually on either the day after the new moon or on the full moon day. It is also impossible for the winter solstice to coincide with a new moon (of any month) every year and the requirements of KB. XIX.3. are unrealistic. The conclusion of the discussion of the mīmāṃsakas43 is that the start of the sattra was on the full moon following the ekāṣṭakā immediately after the winter solstice. This would be the full moon of the month of $māgha$. Śabara44 (approximately 1 BC) points out that “every eighth day of every month is ekāṣṭakā” (sūtra 33). The (Vedic) month starts on the day after the new-moon, (that is why the waxing phase is called purvapakṣa), thus according to Śabara, ekāṣṭakā would be the first quarter. Guided by the mīmāṃsakas (the first half of) TS.VII.4.8., ***

Jha, op. cit. (ref. 42), p. 1132. INTERCALATION IN THE VEDIC TEXTS 505 could be interpreted to mean – the sattra of Gavām ayana ends on the winter solstice (which could be the new-moon of māgha, but not every year), (re)initiation is on the (following) first quarter and the new sattra starts on the following full-moon which can be designated as the full-moon of māgha. The ekāṣṭakā-period is described as ‘distressed/pained (ārtam vā)’ and has been explained as the period when one sattra has ended but a new one has not started45 i.e. an ‘interregnum’. This period has also been described as being ‘reverse (vyastaṃ vā)’; Śabara46 explains this as the period when the ayana has changed or the sun has ‘reversed’ its course. Both explanations are consistent with the interpretation proposed above. The crucial point is that the start of the sattra is locked to the winter solstice, that is, to the start of the tropical year (the tropical year, by definition, is from solstice to solstice or from equinox to equinox). The stability of this calendar can be tested; the essential steps are as follows; Find the date of the winter solstice; this is the end of the tropical year and the end of the sattra and the next day is the start of the new tropical year. Find the date of the following first quarter. Find the date of the following full-moon, the new sattra starts on this day. The date of the winter solstice is determined by computing the minimum value (around -23.5°) of the declination of the sun. This is followed by computing the angle of separation between the sun and the moon, the date of the first quarter is when this angle is 90°. Only the date that is after the winter solstice is retained. The date of the following full-moon is when the angle of separation between the sun and the moon is 180°. The length of the tropical year is the separation (in days) between two consecutive dates of the winter solstice. The start of two consecutive sattras is separated by the number of days between the two full-moon days determined by the above procedure. This is the ritual or sattra year that is, a synodic year corrected by intercalation. A sample of data obtained is given in Table 1. The start of a new ritual year is not determined by the number of lunations in the previous ritual year but by the relative position of the sun and the moon after the winter solstice. As will be shown below, the second 506 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Table 1. The difference every year between the accumulated number of days in the tropical years and in the corresponding sattra years over a period of five hundred years is shown in Fig. 3. These results have been calculated from 1500 BC to 1000 BC but the epoch of calculation is not important, any other epoch would have similar results. This difference is as stable as that achieved by the Metonic cycle (Fig. 1). A closer look at these results reveals a number of interesting features. The length (in days) of the sattra* years in a fifty year interval is not same but in an interval of five years the total number of days is 1830 and this is true for five (sometimes six) consecutive periods of five years, the sixth period of five years is 1800 days long. chunks.text: Labels in Fig 4: $5(2 \times 6 \times 30) + 30 = 1830$; $5(2 \times 6 \times 30) = 1800$ 508 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE the data for first twenty years (Table 1) of the interval shown in Fig. 4. To simplify discussion all dates are Gregorian dates (that is the calendar dates currently used internationally). The tropical year 1931 ends on 21 December i.e. the winter solstice. The 1931 sattra ends on the following day. The tropical year 1932 starts on 22 December. The first quarter (ekāṣṭakā) after the winter solstice is on 15 January 1932 and the ritual year 1932 starts on the following full-moon on 24 January. Similarly the tropical year 1932 ends on the 21 December and the sattra ends on the following day. The following first quarter is on 4 January 1933 and the ritual year 1933 starts on the full-moon of 11 January 1933 or the ritual year 1933 starts twelve lunations after the ritual year 1932 has ended. The tropical year 1933 ends on 21 December and the sattra ends on the following day. The first quarter after the winter solstice is on the following day and the ritual year 1934 starts on 1 January 1934 also twelve lunations after the end of 1933 ritual year. This ritual year ends the day before 19 January 1935 that is thirteen lunations later. The 1935 ritual year ends after twelve lunations. The 1936 sattra starts on the full-moon of 9 January and ends on the day after the winter solstice on 21 December 1936. This is also the first quarter and the next sattra cannot start on the full-moon of 28 December 1936 because the ekāṣṭakā condition is not fulfilled, that is, the ekāṣṭakā is not after the winter solstice. Thus the new sattra will start on 26 January 1937 or thirteen lunations later. This pattern of two (synodic) thirteenth months in every five year period is repeated and leads to 1830 days in a five year period as shown in Table 1 and Fig. 4. As discussed above, this five year period is 3.8 days longer than five tropical years. This ‘error’ accumulates and in the sixth (sometimes seventh) five year period there is only one thirteenth month because of the ekāṣṭakā condition and the total number of days in this five year period is 1800. The 1830 days in a five year interval can be resolved into six seasons of two months, each of thirty days and a thirteenth month (as shown in Fig. 4.). This is entirely consistent with the Vedic texts and (as shown below) with Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa. The scheme is also in agreement with the practice of the cāturmāsya-yājins of MS.I.10.8., who attempted to ‘maintain the order of the seasons’ by adding two intercalary months in a five year period. In the scheme described here the thirteenth (intercalary) month does not have to be added (as in the Metonic cycle or MS.I.10.8.) or dropped ‘manually’. The thirteenth month appears to be added rather randomly but as explained above INTERCALATION IN THE VEDIC TEXTS 509 the thirteenth month is a consequence of the (apparent) relative motion of the sun and the moon and the condition imposed by TS.VII.4.8 (and PB. V.9). This may explain why majority of Vedic texts do not enjoin a ritualist to add (or subtract) a thirteenth month (to a year), the texts only state that there is a thirteenth month. This scheme introduces period(s) of ‘interregnum’ in the Vedic calendar because the sattra of Gavām ayana ends the day after Mahāvrata and the following sattra does not start till the full-moon of māgha (or phālguna) which will not always be on the second day after a winter solstice. This may explain why the thirteenth month is variously referred to as aṃhasaspati (lord of distress), saṃsarpa (creeping or sliding along), and malimluca (a thief, a demon or a Brāhmin who omits the five devotional acts) and why no religious observances are allowed during this month. In the Vedic texts there are no explicit statements regarding the period between the end of a sattra in one year and the beginning of the next sattra. But the Āryas may not have been unfamiliar with the concept of interregnum. Both TS.VII.5.7.1 and PB V.10. propose schemes for ‘dropping days’ but the implications of dropping these days is not clear from these lessons. Similarly, Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra (LŚS. IV.8.8-21)47 propose various schemes for dropping days in a ritual year. In LŚS. IV.8.1-7,48 ritual years longer or shorter than the canonical 360 days are mentioned, not unlike the length of the years obtained in the scheme proposed here. These passages from the Vedic texts do not have a direct bearing on the present scheme but they demonstrate that the Vedic ritualists were familiar with years of different lengths and the need to adjust the length of their ritual year. Within a sattra, different groups of ritualists may have followed their own particular ways of timing the start (or the end) of rituals and ceremonies, as was done by the ṛtu-yājins and cāturmāsya-yājins of MS.I.10.8.

chunks.text: It is not the intention here to give a full exposition of the calendar of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, the aim here is to present a limited discussion of the similarities (and differences) between the calendar of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa and the calendars described and deduced from the Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas. Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa has survived in two recensions – a Ṛgveda recension called 34: A. Weber, op. cit. (ref. 15), p.298. 35: B. Faddegon, op. cit. (ref. 30), p.125. 45: A.K. Chakravarty, op. cit. (ref. 31), p. 13. 46: B. G. Tilak, op. cit. (ref. 19), p. 51. 47: H. G. Ranade, Lāṭyāyana Śrauta Sūtra, (New Delhi, 1998), pp. 409-415. 48: H. G. Ranade, op. cit. (ref. 46), pp. 407-408. 510 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Arca Jyotiṣa and a Yajurvada recension called Yājuṣa-Jyotiṣa. There are minor differences between the two recensions; the Ṛgvedic recension is smaller, it has thirty six verses. Thirty of these are repeated in the Yajurvedic recension and this recension has thirteen additional verses. The Ṛgvedic recension is considered to be much earlier than the Yajurvedic recension and is attributed to Lagadha, unfortunately nothing else is known about him. The author of the Yajurveda recension is not known. In the following discussion all references to Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa are to the translation and interpretation of Kuppanna Sastry49. The intercalation period of the calendar of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa is (approximately) five tropical years and it is called "yuga". The verses RJ. 5-6 (i.e. the $5^{\text{th}}$ and $6^{\text{th}}$ verse of Arca Jyotiṣa) and YJ. 6-7 (i.e. $6^{\text{th}}$ and $7^{\text{th}}$ verse of Yājuṣa-Jyotiṣa) state that "When the sun and the moon occupy the same region of the zodiac (sky) together with the asterism of Śraviṣṭhā, at that time begins the yuga, the (synodic) month of māgha, the (solar seasonal) month of tapas etc., .........the sun and the moon begin to move north.........". That is, the intercalation period starts when the star (or star group) Śraviṣṭhā rises helically at winter solstice. Apart from identifying the epoch (via the helical rising of Śraviṣṭhā) when this scheme of intercalation was formulated or more likely formalized, the start of a yuga in the Jyotiṣa is same as that inferred from TS.VII.4.8. Also the season and the month at the start of the year are same as those prescribed in AB. IV.26; (XIX.4). But the composer(s) of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa cannot have meant the start of the month māgha or the season tapas every year as the Vedic month starts the day after a new moon and it is impossible to have a new moon at winter solstice every year. This anomaly is also similar to that encountered in the calendar based on TS.VII.4.8. A yuga is $1830$ sāvana (civil) days or the mean length of a sāvana (tropical) years is $366$ sāvana days (YJ. 28). The length of $1830$ sāvana days of a yuga is fundamental to Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa; almost all parameters and algorithms of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa are based on this number. This is not a naturally occurring number like a month or a year. It seems improbable that the author(s) of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa simply made-up this number for their intercalation scheme. As shown above this period of intercalation follows from the mathematical interpretation of TS.VII.4.8 (and PB.V.9.). It is possible that the author(s) of the Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa were familiar with the scheme of TS.VII.4.8 that required observations of the solstice and INTERCALATION IN THE VEDIC TEXTS 511 the phases of the moon and reduced it to an arithmetic rule based on an intercalation period of $1830$ sāvana days. The Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa notes that the lack of synchronization between the tropical and the synodic years is due to the difference in the length of the lunar day and the solar day and it recommends that in order to synchronise the two years an extra month should be added at half yuga and another at the end of the yuga (YJ. 37). This is similar to the scheme of intercalation adopted by the cāturmāsya-yājins as described in MS.I.10.8. and that which follows from TS.VII.4.8. What is perhaps surprising is that the surviving recensions of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa do not mention the correction that is necessary every eighth yuga to stop the runaway accumulation of the difference between the number of days in five tropical years and a yuga (see above). This correction is so glaringly necessary and obvious that it is inconceivable that the composers of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa would have missed it. Is it possible that this vital passage was lost between Lagadha, the putative composer of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa, and Śuci the redactor? We may never know. In spite of this lacuna the similarities between these crucial aspects of the calendar of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa and the calendar in Maitrāyaṇīya Saṃhitā and that which can be derived from Taittirīya Saṃhitā are so striking that the conclusion that the origins of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa are in the earlier Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas is inescapable.

chunks.title: Intercalation in the Vedic Texts
chunks.text: The five year intercalation scheme (yuga) is unique to South Asia. This scheme is first explicitly mentioned in Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa but its origins have baffled Ideologists for over hundred years. The concept of intercalation can be traced back to Ṛgveda, the earliest Vedic text available to us. A number of intercalation schemes can be inferred from post-Ṛgvedic Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas. These schemes would have synchronised the synodic or the ritual year and the tropical year over short periods (ten to twenty years) but failed over longer periods. An algorithm for intercalation is given in Maitrāyaṇīya Saṃhitā and this scheme of intercalation is based on an intercalation period of five (tropical) years although this period is not called a yuga. This Saṃhitā does not mention the correction that is necessary to the five year intercalation scheme to keep the synodic year synchronised with the tropical year over extended periods. A 'perfect' scheme of intercalation can be obtained from mathematical expression of passages in Taittirīya 512 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Saṃhitā that describe the start of the tropical year and the ritual year. This scheme has the five year intercalation period built into it and the correction that this scheme requires. This scheme also includes all the calendrical features that can be traced back to the earliest Vedic texts and are important to the Vedic culture, namely, six seasons of two months each, a canonical month of thirty days, a canonical (ritual) year of $360$ days, a thirteenth month and the number 'five' (through the five year period) which plays an important part in Vedic thinking. The scheme would keep the synodic year and the tropical year synchronised over hundreds of year. Far from "no systematic intercalation scheme" the Āryas appear to have 'experimented' with a number of schemes. They may even have discovered a perfect scheme. A number of features of the calendar of Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa can be traced back to the Saṃhitās and the Brāhmaṇas and is possible that in Vedāṅga Jyotiṣa (whenever it was composed) the Āryas were only formalizing a calendar that had been in use for decades earlier.

chunks.text: *S. BALACHANDRA RAO\, S.K. UMA\\ AND PADMAJA VENUGOPAL\\\** (Received 17 August 2007; revised 15 February 2008) The exciting phenomenon of the transit of Venus on June 8, 2004 was observed with great interest the world over. A recent transit after that was of Mercury on the night (in India) between 8th and 9th of November 2006. The transits of Mercury and Venus occur when either of them is in conjunction with the Sun as observed from the Earth provided these are within the prescribed “ecliptic limits.” The transit of Venus is a less frequent phenomenon than that of Mercury. For example, after the transit of Venus in June 2004, the next occurrence will be in June 2012. After that, the subsequent Venus transit will be about 105.5 years later. In Indian classical astronomy, the siddhāntic texts have discussed in detail the phenomenon of conjunctions of the Sun, the Moon and the planets, between any two of them as also with some important visible stars like Rohiṇī (Aldeberan), Tiṣya or Puṣya ($\delta$ Cancri), Citrā* (Spica) etc. In the present paper, we have discussed the actual working procedures, based on siddhāntas, of not only transits of Venus and Mercury but also of the occultations of planets and stars. The results are compared with those of modern astronomical procedures.

Director, Gandhi Centre of Science & Human Values, Bharatiya Vidya Bhavan, 43/1, Race Course Road, Bangalore - 560 001. \\ Senior Lecturer, Department of Mathematics, Sir M. Visvesvaraya Institute of Technology, Hunasamaranahalli, Bangalore - 562 157. \\\ Professor and Head, Dept. of Mathematics, SJB Institute of Technology, Kengeri, Bangalore - 560 060. 516 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE phenomena of eclipses and planetary conjunctions. Āryabhaṭa I (b. 476 AD) in his Āryabhaṭīyam1,2 explains how some of the parameters of the Sun, the Moon and the planets have to be corrected periodically by observing the eclipses (uparāga) and conjunctions (grahayuti). This tradition of updating the parameters by constant observation of astronomical phenomena was rigorously followed throughout. It is well known that remarkable contributions to mathematics and astronomy were made from the 14th century onwards by the astute Kerala astronomers. Among the prominent ones was the great Parameśvara (1360-1455). He was responsible in popularizing the observation based on astronomical computations called Drggaṇita system. In fact, paying rich tribute to Parameśvara, his grand student (praśiṣya), Nīlakaṇṭha Somayājī says: पञ्चपञ्चाशतं वर्षाकालं निरीक्ष्य ग्रहण ग्रहयोगादिषु परीक्ष्य समदृग्गणितं करणं चकार । — (Parameśvara) having observed for 55 years the eclipses and planetary conjunctions, and examined them, composed his handbook, Samadrggaṇitam. While detailed working of planetary conjunctions is discussed in the siddhāntic texts under the chapter Grahayuti, it has to be noted that the transits of Mercury and Venus are not explicitly mentioned. This is mainly because when a planet is close to the Sun it is said to be “combust” (asta) and hence not visible to the naked eye. In a transit of Mercury or Venus, the concerned tiny planet passes across the bright and wide disc of the Sun as a small black dot.

chunks.text: Among the planets (tārāgraha), conjunction (yuti) takes place between any two of them and also with the Moon or the Sun. This phenomenon takes place when the longitudes of the two concerned bodies are equal and their latitudes are within permissible limits of difference even as in the case of the eclipses of the Sun and the Moon. तारा ग्रहाणामन्योऽन्यं स्यातां युद्धसमागमौ । समागमः शशाङ्केन सूर्येणास्तमनं सह ॥ Sūrya Siddh. Ch. 7. śl.1 CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULTATIONS 517 If the conjunction is (i) between two planets it is called yuddha (encounter) (ii) between a planet and the Moon, then it is called samāgama. In modern parlance it is called ‘occultation’. (iii) between a planet and the Sun, it is called astamana or astaṅgata (heliacal setting) In particular if Mercury or Venus is in conjunction with the Sun, such an alignment is called ‘transit’. The recently witnessed transit of Venus on June 8th 2004 was truly spectacular.

4. THE INSTANT OF CONJUNCTION OF TWO BODIES
chunks.text: The famous Indian astronomer of the early 16th century, Gaṇeśa Daivajña (epoch: March 19, 1520) describes the method of determining the instant of conjunction and also whether it is past or yet to occur in his Grahalāghava (GL): ऋजुगतिखगयोस्तु वक्रयोर्वा विवरकला गतिजान्तरेण भक्तः । गतिजयुतिहृता यदैकवक्री युतिगता प्रगताप्तवासरैः स्यात् ॥ Grahalāghavam, Ch. 13, śl. 3\ --- \ See Grahalāghavam English Exposition with Notes etc. by S. Balachandra Rao and S.K. Uma, INSA, New Delhi, 2006 518 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE This śloka explains how to obtain days (and ghaṭīs etc) of gata or gamya instant of conjunction. (i) If both the bodies are in direct motion or in retrograde motion then divide the difference between their positions by the difference between their daily motions, both the values expressed in the same unit of angle viz., kalā (minute) or aṃśa (degree). The result will be in days, ghaṭīs etc. This gives the time in days etc of the gata (elapsed) or gamya (to be covered). (ii) Of the two bodies if one is in direct motion and the other in retrograde motion then divide the difference between their positions by the sum of their daily motions. Example: On May 2, 1610(G), Sunday (Cakras = 8, Ahargaṇa = 778) at the sunrise the true longitude of Kuja, $P1 = 10^R \ 6^\circ \ 35' \ 9''$ and the true longitude of Śani, $P2 = 10^R \ 2^\circ \ 58' \ 44''$ and both are in direct motion. The number of days for yuti is given by $$\frac{P1 - P2}{DP1 - DP2}$$ the difference between the longitudes of Kuja and Śani: $$P1 - P2 = 3^\circ 36' 25'' = 216' 25''$$ and the difference between their daily motions $$DP1 - DP2 = 42' 50'' - 3' 3'' = 39' 47''.$$ $$\therefore \text{Days for } yuti = \frac{216' 25''}{39' 47''} = 5^d 26^h 23^{vig}$$ Since the longitude of Kuja is greater than that of Śani, the yuti is over by $5^d 26^h 23^{vig}$ before the given date.

chunks.text: The mean diameters (MD) of the planets Kuja, Budha, Guru, Śukra and Śani, though extremely small, are given respectively as 5, 6, 7, 9 and 5 CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULTATIONS 519 minutes of arc (kalās) in the two popular karaṇa texts, Karaṇakutūhalam3 (KK), (epoch 1183 A.D.) and Grahalāghavam4,5 (epoch 1520 AD). The following is the procedure to get the true angular diameter (TD) of a planet: $$TD = \frac{1}{3} \left[ MD \pm (11 - SK2) \times \frac{MD}{n} \right] \text{ aṅgulas}$$ where $n = 21, 12, 6, 24 \text{ and } 3$ for Kuja, Budha, Guru, Śukra and Śani respectively (1 $aṅgula = 3 \ kalās$). The śīghrakarṇa ($SK2$) will have been obtained earlier while finding the true position of the planet. However, in “Grahalāghavam” the method of obtaining $SK2$ is not explained explicitly in the chapter on true positions. The author Gaṇeśa Daivajña has described the procedure clearly in the chapter Udayāstādhikāraḥ (Rising and Setting of planets). According to Bhāskara II, the following śloka : पञ्चाङ्गसप्ताङ्कशराः पृथक्स्थैस्त्रिज्याकृणान्तर साङ्गुणास्ताः । परधिजैः ख्योर्विहृत्वाः फलोनयुक्ताः पृथक्स्थशास्त्रै भमौविकायाः । कणेहिधिकोने त्रिहृता भवन्ति बिम्बाङ्गुुलानीति कुजादिकानाम् । Karaṇakutūhalam, Grahayuti śl 1 & 2 gives the true angular diameter (TD) as $$TD = MD + \frac{(120 - SK1)MD}{3p} \ kalās$$ where the parākhya (or parasaṅkhyā) $p$ are prescribed constants for different planets as given in Table 1.

According to him the result is obtained by the rule of proportion: If the planet has its maximum śīghra correction, the excess over the (mean) diameter is its one-third (i.e. $\frac{MD}{3}$) then what is the excess (over the mean diameter) for $(R - SK1)$. This gives the excess over the mean diameter $\frac{(R - SK1) \times MD}{3p}$. Here $SK1$ is the śīghrakarṇa and $p$ is the parākhya i.e. the śīghra periphery. In GL, Gaṇeśa Daivajña has taken his śīghrakarṇa as 11 times the value given by Bhāskara II. i.e. $SK2 = 11 SK1$. Bhāskara II’s formula reduces to $$ \text{True diameter, } TD = \frac{1}{3} \left[ MD + \frac{(120 - 11 SK1) MD}{3p} \right] aṅgulas $$ $$ \approx \frac{1}{3} \left[ MD + \frac{11(11 - SK1)}{3p} MD \right] \approx \frac{1}{3} \left[ MD + \frac{11(11 - SK1)}{11n} MD \right] $$ $$ = \frac{1}{3} \left[ MD + \frac{(11 - SK_1)}{n} MD \right] $$ taking $\frac{3p}{11} = n$. For different planets $n$ has different values. The values of $n$ are obtained as follows: The antyaphalajyā i.e. Rsine of the critical value of the śīghra* anomaly for Kuja, Budha, Guru, Śukra and Śani are respectively about 77, 43, 22, 86, 12. Multiplying these by 33 and dividing by 120 ($R=120$), we get $n = 21, 12, 6, 24, 3$ (to the nearest integer). CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULATIONS 521

chunks.text: Definition: The nodes (pātas) of a planet are the points of intersection of its orbit with the ecliptic (as seen from the earth). Heliocentrically, the nodes $V1$ and $V2$ are the points of intersection of the planet’s orbit with the plane of the earth’s orbit (Fig. 1). $E1 V1 S V2 E2$ is the line of nodes. The latitude of a planet is a function of the sum of the planet’s mean longitude and its pāta. Here it should be noted that Bhāskara II uses the word pāta to mean ($360^\circ$ - the ascending node). However Gaṇeśa Daivajña calls the ascending node itself as pāta. ![The orbital plane of Venus is inclined to that of the earth. The points, $V1$ and $V2$ are called nodes. The line joining them is called the line of nodes. [Courtesy: Transit of Venus by Dr B.S. Shylaja]](media/p07_page.png) The pātas of different planets as in Grahalāghavam and Karaṇakutūhalam are listed in Table 2: Table 2. Nodes (pātas) | Planets | Grahalāghavam : Node | Karaṇakutūhalam: $360^\circ$ – Node | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | Kuja | $40^\circ$ | $11^R \text{ } 8^\circ = 338^\circ$ | | Budha | $20^\circ$ | $11^R \text{ } 9^\circ = 339^\circ$ | | Guru | $80^\circ$ | $9^R \text{ } 8^\circ = 278^\circ$ | | Śukra | $60^\circ$ | $10^R \text{ } 0^\circ = 300^\circ$ | | Śani | $100^\circ$ | $8^R \text{ } 17^\circ = 257^\circ$ | 522 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Remark In GL, (longitude - pāta) is the argument for the latitude whereas in KK the argument is (longitude + pāta). As explained earlier, the word pāta connotes differently in the two texts. According to KK: (i) The above pātas of the superior planets are combined with the śīghraphalas of the respective planets to get corrected pāta i.e., corrected pāta = pāta - śīghraphala (ii) In the case of inferior planets corrected pāta = pāta + mandaphala

chunks.text: Bhāskara II explains the method of obtaining the latitudes of planets in his KK as follows: मन्दाभ्यां बुधशुक्रयोरथ कुजादिक्षेपका: खेश्वरा । द्वीपक्ष्मा: षडगा: षडग्निशशिन: खत्रीन्द्रवो लिप्तिका: ॥ खेटात्पातयुतात्तथा ज्ञसितयो: शीघ्रोच्चतो दोर्ज्यका । क्षेपघ्नी चलकर्णहृत्त्रि विहता स्यादङ्गुलाद्य: शर: ॥ Karaṇakutūhalam, Ch. 6, śl. 10 Fig. 2. The perpendicular $PM = \beta$ from the position $P$ of a planet on its orbit to the ecliptic is the planet’s latitude. Here $N$ is the node and $i$ is the inclination of the planet’s orbit. Fig. 2. The perpendicular $PM = \beta$ from the position $P$ of a planet on its orbit to the ecliptic is the planet’s latitude. Here $N$ is the node and $i$ is the inclination of the planet’s orbit. CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULATIONS 523 (i) The (maximum) vikṣepas (śaras) of Kuja, Budha, Guru, Śukra and Śani are respectively 110, 152, 76, 136 and 130 kalās. (ii) (a) In the case of Kuja, Guru and Śani i.e., superior planets consider the true planet and add its corrected pāta to it. In the case of inferior planets Budha and Śukra add pātas to their respective śīghroccas. (b) Consider the bhujajyā of the sapātagraha (i.e. planet + pāta), obtained in (ii) (a). Multiply this bhujajyā by its mean śara and divide by its śīghrakarṇa. The result gives the śara of the concerned planet in kalās. Dividing the śara in kalās by 3, we get the same in aṅgulas. The śara is north or south according as (planet + pāta) is less or greater than $180^\circ$. Note: Comparative values of orbital inclinations, angular diameters, and nodes (pātas) are provided in the Appendix. Example: On a certain day suppose we have true Budha = $37^\circ 27' 5''$. Budha śīghrocca’s daily motion = $103' 28''$ Budha’s śīghrocca = $94^\circ 57' 16''$, śīghrakarṇa = $145 | 15$ Mandaphala = $+ 0^\circ 15' 07''$, Mean pāta = $11^R 9^\circ = 339^\circ$ Corrected pāta = Mean pāta + Mandaphala $= 339^\circ + 0^\circ 15' 07'' = 339^\circ 15' 7''$ Sapātagraha = Budha’s śīghrocca + Corrected pāta $= 94^\circ 57' 16'' + 339^\circ 15' 7'' = 74^\circ 12' 23''$ Bhujajyā of Sapātagraha $\approx 115' 6''$ $$ \text{śara of Budha} = \frac{Bhujajyā \times \text{Mean śara}}{śīghrakarṇa} \text{ kalās} $$ $$ \text{i.e. Budha’s śara} = \frac{115 | 6 \times 152}{145 | 15} \approx 120' 27'' $$ Dividing by 3, $\text{śara} = 40 | 9 \text{ aṅgulas}$. 524 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE

chunks.text: Even as in the cases of solar and lunar eclipses, two bodies may have the same longitude but those may not form technically a “bhedayuti” in the sense of one body eclipsing the other. At the instant of conjunction if the mānaikyakhaṇḍa i.e. sum of the semi-diameters of the planets, is less than the algebraic difference of their latitudes there is no “bheda yoga.” What is of interest for further computations and observations is the bheda yoga – one planet “piercing” the other. This happens when the sum of the semi-diameters of the bodies is greater than the algebraic difference of their latitudes. In case there is bheda yoga, the planet which is “lower” is treated as Moon and the “higher” one as the Sun. In that case the effects of parallax on the longitude and latitude namely lambana and nati are determined as in the case of a solar eclipse. Note: Between two conjuncting bodies the higher and the lower between them are decided as follows: (i) If both bodies have northern latitudes then the one with the higher latitude is considered as higher. (ii) If both the bodies have southern latitudes then the one with numerically lesser latitude is considered as the higher body. (iii) If the two bodies have their latitudes in opposite directions then the one with the northern latitude is the higher body. In general, the body towards the north is considered as the higher body. Remark: While the conjunctions in longitudes of any two planets occur frequently, in the special sense of one “eclipsing” the other, such occurrences are extremely rare. This is so because the angular diameters of the planets are very small and therefore the sum of their semi-diameters is rarely greater than the difference between their latitudes. However, the commentator of Karaṇakutūhalam, Sumatiharṣa works out in detail the conjunction of Guru and Śukra which took place on Śālivāhana śaka 1541, Vaiśākha kṛṣṇa 14, Sunday. Though it was a case of a perfect conjunction (bheda yoga) it was not visible at the given place since the planets were below the horizon. CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULATIONS 525 Therefore it is more meaningful to consider situations where one of the conjuncting bodies is either the Sun or the Moon.

chunks.text: We provide below a procedure, evolved by us based on our traditional siddhāntas and inspired by the collected papers of the late Prof. T. S. Kuppanna Sastry.⁷ This algorithm is specially designed for transits of Śukra and Budha. This procedure is different from the one adopted in modern astronomy. It is important to note that for a transit the concerned inferior planet is always retrograde (vakra) and in inferior conjunction. (i) The true instant of conjunction in longitudes of the true Sun and the true planet is determined. Note: In what follows, the parameters are represented by convenient-to-remember multi-letter notations like SDIA, PAR, HDUR etc. for the advantage of computer programming. (ii) At the instant of true conjunction, the following parameters are computed: (1) True positions of the Sun and the planet (2) True daily rates of motion of the two bodies (SDM and PDM) (3) The geocentric latitude of the planet $\beta$ (BETA) (4) The horizontal parallaxes of the two bodies ($PAR1$ and $PAR2$) (5) Rate of change of planet’s latitude per $nāḍī$, $P$ (6) Angular diameters of the bodies (SDIA and PDIA) [Note: Items (2) to (6) are in minutes of arc (kalās)] (7) The rate of motion of (planet $-$ Sun) per $nāḍī$: $vyarkagraha\ nāḍīgati = (PDM - SDM)/60$ (8) Let the combined parallax, $PAR = PAR1 - PAR2$ (9) The sum of the combined parallax and the semi-diameters $$D = PAR + \frac{SDIA + PDIA}{2}$$ --- 526 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE (10) The sum of the parallax with the difference of the semi-diameters $$D' = PAR + \frac{SDIA - PDIA}{2}$$ (11) The conditions for the occurrence of a transit and its totality: (i) If $|\beta| < D$, the transit occurs. (ii) If $|\beta| < D'$, the transit is total. (12) The middle (MIDDLE) of the transit is obtained by applying a small correction to the instant of conjunction. This correction is given by $$\frac{-pP}{\dot{m}^2 + P^2}\ nāḍī \text{ or approximately } \frac{99}{100} \frac{|\beta|}{\dot{m}}\ nāḍī$$ where $p = \beta$ and $P = d\beta$, the rate of change in planet’s latitude per $nāḍī$ (see Appendix) (13) Half duration of the transit is given by $$HDUR = \frac{\sqrt{D^2 - \beta^2}}{\dot{m}}\ nāḍī$$ (14) Half duration of the totality is given by $$THDUR = \frac{\sqrt{(D')^2 - \beta^2}}{\dot{m}}\ nāḍīs$$ Summary of the transit: (i) Beginning of transit (External Ingress) : $BEGG = MIDDLE - HDUR$ (ii) Beginning of totality (Internal Ingress) : $BEGGT = MIDDLE - THDUR$ (iii) Middle of the transit (greatest obscuration) : $MIDDLE$ (iv) End of totality (Internal Egress) : $ENDT = MIDDLE + THDUR$ (v) End of the transit (External Egress) : $TREND = MIDDLE + HDUR$ --- CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULATIONS 527 The tracks of Venus’ transits across the Sun’s disc over a period of seven centuries from 1388 to 2011 AD are shown in Fig.3. Fig. 3. Tracks of Venus during transits from 1388 to 2012 A.D.⁶ Fig. 3. Tracks of Venus during transits from 1388 to 2012 A.D.⁶ Table 3. Venus' transits from 1388 to 2012 AD occurring in June and December | December transits | June transits | Interval | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | 1388 (?) | | | | 1396 | 1518 | 121.5 | | | 1526 | 8 | | 1631 | | 105.5 | | 1639 | | 8 | | | 1761 | 121.5 | | | 1769 | 8 | | 1874 | | 105.5 | | 1882 | | 8 | | | 2004 | 121.5 | | | 2012 | 8 | \The transit in 1388 did not occur. The track of Venus was outside the Sun's disc.⁶ Example 1 : Venus transit of June 8, 2004 We illustrate the above procedure by applying the same to the latest Venus transit for the centre of the earth. --- 528 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE (1) Instant of conjunction (in longitude) of the Sun and Venus : $14^h\ 8^m$ (IST) At the instant of conjunction: (2) True Sun = True Venus $= 77^\circ 53' 32"$ (Sāyana, tropical) (3) (i) Sun’s true daily motion, $SDM = 0^\circ 57' 23"$ (ii) Venus’ true daily motion, $PDM = -37' 36"$ (4) Latitude of Venus, $\beta = -11'$ (5) Sun’s parallax, $PAR1 = 8".659262$ (6) Venus’ parallax, $PAR2 = 30".44077$ so that $PAR = PAR2 - PAR1 = 21".781508$ (7) Venus’ ascending node $= 76^\circ 43' 12"$ (Sāyana) (8) (i) Sun’s angular semi-diameter: $\frac{SDIA}{2} = 946".8672$ (ii) Venus’ angular semi-diameter: $\frac{PDIA}{2} = 28".86874$ (9) Rate of motion of (Venus $-$ Sun) per $nāḍī$, $$VRKNG = \frac{57' 23" + 37' 36"}{60} = 1'.5830556$$ (10) The sum of the resultant parallax with the semi-diameters: $$D = PAR + \frac{SDIA + PDIA}{2} = 16'.625$$ (11) The sum of the resultant parallax and the difference of the semi-diameters: $$D' = PAR + \frac{SDIA - PDIA}{2} = 15'.663$$ --- CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULATIONS 529 (12) Since $|\beta| < D$, the transit is possible. (13) Since $|\beta| < D'$, the transit is total. (14) True Venus $-$ Node $= 1^\circ 10' 19" \equiv VPG$ (15) The rate of motion of (Venus $-$ Sun) per $nāḍī$, $\dot{m} = VRKNG \approx 1'.5831$ (16) Correction to the instant of conjunction for the middle of the transit : $$\frac{99}{100} \left[ \frac{|\beta|}{10 \dot{m}} \right] = 0.68789\ nāḍī = 16^m.5$$ Since $VPG$ is in the $1^{st}$ quadrant, the above correction is subtractive. Therefore Middle of transit $= 14^h\ 8^m - 16^m.5 = 13^h\ 51^m.5$ (17) Half duration of the transit $= \frac{\sqrt{D^2 - \beta^2}}{\dot{m}} \approx 3^h\ 9^m$ (18) Half duration of totality $= \frac{\sqrt{(D')^2 - \beta^2}}{\dot{m}} = 2^h\ 49^m$ Summary of the transit (i) Ext. Ingress, $BEGG = 10^h\ 42^m$ (IST) (ii) Int. Ingress, $BEGGT = 11^h\ 02^m$ (IST) (iii) Middle $ = 13^h\ 51^m$ (IST) (iv) Int. Egress, $ENDT = 16^h\ 40^m$ (IST) (v) Ext. Egress, $TREND = 17^h\ 00^m$ (IST) Note: According to the Indian Astronomical Ephemeris the transit of Venus was visible in India between $10^h 44^m$ and $16^h 56^m$ (IST).

10. SUPERIOR CONJUNCTION OF AN INFERIOR PLANET WITH THE SUN
chunks.text: The transits of the inferior planets, Venus and Mercury discussed in the previous section occur when these planets have an inferior conjunction with the Sun. Of course these are subject to their respective transit limits. An interesting situation, rarely discussed, is when an inferior planet has a superior conjunction with the Sun. In the case of a transit the inferior planet comes in between the earth and the Sun. This is the case of an inferior conjunction of the planet. On the other hand, in the case of a superior conjunction the Sun hides the inferior planet i.e. the Sun lies between the earth and the planet. In Indian classical astronomical texts, the two situations are not explicitly discussed. However, their circumstances can be worked out by the general classical method of planetary conjunctions (grahayuti) discussed in this paper earlier. In fact, the cases of inferior and superior conjunctions of an inferior planet can be easily determined from the Indian siddhāntic procedure. In the case of an inferior conjunction the śīghrakendra of the planet is $180^{\circ}$ whereas for the superior conjunction the śīghrakendra vanishes. More interestingly, for an inferior conjunction the śīghrakarṇa of the planet is the difference between the heliocentric distances of the earth and the planet. On the other hand, for a superior conjunction the śīghrakarṇa is the sum of the heliocentric distances. In fact for an inferior planet the śīghrakarṇa is a measure of its geocentric distance. We have considered a modern example of superior conjunction of Venus with the Sun in what follows. 532 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Example : Superior conjunction of Venus with the Sun dated 2008 June 9. The instant of the superior* conjunction in longitude is $9^h7^m.5$ (IST). This is not a transit of Venus since in this case the planet comes behind the Sun and hence the phenomenon is referred to as an "occultation" by the Sun. The duration of the occultation is quite long and extends to the previous day as well as to the following day of the day of conjunction.

12. CONDITION FOR OCCULTATION OF CITRĀ STAR
chunks.text: In the nirayaṇa system, longitude of $Citr\bar{a} : 180^{\circ}$; latitude, $\beta1 = -2^{\circ}3'18''$. Moon’s diameter is minimum for its anomaly from perigee, $m = 180^{\circ}$. In fact, Moon’s minimum diameter is about $29'16''$. Then the Moon’s horizontal parallax is also minimum and its value is about $53'43''$. In that case, the sum of the semi-diameter and the parallax, $$D = \frac{29'16''}{2} + 53'43'' = 68'.358333 = 1^{\circ}8'21''.5$$ This is the minimum value of $D$. If $\beta$ is the difference between the latitudes $\beta1$ and $\beta2$ of the Moon and Citrā, then the condition for the occurrence of the occultation is $$|\beta| < D \text{ i.e., } |\beta| < 1^{\circ}8'21''.5 \text{ i.e. } |\beta1 - \beta_2| < 1^{\circ}8'21''.5$$ this leads to the condition that the Moon’s latitude should lie between $-3^{\circ}11'39''.5$ and $-0^{\circ}54'56''.5$. ** 534 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Interestingly the above condition prescribes the range for the position of the Moon's node (Rāhu) for the occultation of Citrā. The resulting condition, using the traditional expression for the Moon's latitude, $\beta = 270' \sin(M - R)$, is : $$314^{\circ}46'40'' < Rāhu < 348^{\circ}15'33''$$ where $M$ and $R$ are respectively the true positions of the Moon and its node and $M = 180^{\circ}$ (for conjunction with Citrā). However, considering the modern expression for the Moon's latitude, the range for the position of $R\bar{a}hu$ is between $321^{\circ}31'$ and $349^{\circ}43'$ approximately. In the traditional language this means that $R\bar{a}hu$ should lie between the first pāda of Pūrvābhādrā and the first pāda of Revatī*. In the example, True $R\bar{a}hu = 340^{\circ}25'$ in the Uttarā-bhādra nakṣatra.

chunks.text: The Rohiṇī śakaṭa bheda (RSB) is an interesting configuration in which an eligible heavenly body enters the region marked by a group of stars including and very close to the yogatāra (junction star) Rohiṇī (Aldebaran). In Indian astronomical literature we find frequent references to RSB. The phrase śakaṭa bheda means “piercing the cart” (of Rohiṇī). The eligible stake-holders of the RSB phenomenon are the Moon, Mars and Saturn. Among the traditional texts, it is the Grahalāghavam (GL) --- 536 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE of Gaṇeśa Daivajña (1520 A.D.) that is the most explicit in giving the details for RSB event, particularly by the Moon. Gaṇeśa prescribes the following4 $^{,}$5: गवि नगकुलवे खागोऽस्य चेद् यमदिग्निषुः खशराङ्गुलाधिकः । कभशकटमसो भिनत्यसृक् शनिरुडुपो यदि चेज्जनक्षयः ॥ GL, Ch. 11, śl. 7 “If a planet is at $17^\circ$ of Vṛṣabha having its latitude southern and greater than 50 aṅgulas (i.e. $150' = 2^\circ 30'$ south) it is said to break (pierce) the Rohiṇī cart (wain).......” The texts mention the Moon, Mars and Saturn as the possible stakeholders of RSB. Gaṇeśa Daivajña further prescribes the condition for the Moon to hit the Rohiṇī cart: स्वर्भानवदितिभतोष्ट्र ऋक्षसंस्थे शीतांशुः कभशकटं सदा भिनत्ति । भौमार्क्सोः शकटभिदा युगान्तरे स्यात् सेदानीं न हि भवतिदृशि स्वपाते ॥ GL, Ch. 11, śl. 8 “As long as Rāhu is in the eight nakṣatras from Punarvasu (upto Citrā) the Moon breaks the Rohiṇī cart. . . .” He further points out that the RSB by Mars and Saturn take place after very long period (thousands of years) and that the event does not take place now. In fact for Moon’s RSB event, which takes place more frequently, while the Moon must be around Nirayaṇa $47^\circ$, its node Rāhu must lie between $80^\circ$ and $186^\circ 40'$.

chunks.text: The Rohiṇī asterism, according to Indian traditional texts, comprises five visible stars with southern latitudes in the constellation of Vṛṣabha (Taurus). The celestial (sidereal) longitudes of the stars in the above group range from $45^\circ 46'$ to $49^\circ 45'$ of which the central longitude is about $47^\circ$. The latitudes of these stars vary from $2^\circ 36'$ to $5^\circ 47'$ to the south of the ecliptic considering the measure of one aṅgula as 3 arc-minutes, the above range comes to 52 to 116 aṅgulas. Therefore for a body to enter the cart of Rohiṇī it must have its southern latitude more than about $2^\circ .5$ i.e. 50 aṅgulas. --- CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULATIONS 537 We have the traditional expression for the southern latitude (śara) of the Moon : $$\beta = -270' \sin(M - R) = 270' \sin(R - M)$$ This gives the range for Moon’s node Rāhu from about $80^\circ .4$ to $193^\circ .6$ i.e. from the beginning of Punarvasu to the middle of Svātī. However from the modern expression for the Moon’s latitude the leading term is $18461'' \sin F$ where $F = M - R$, the mean distance of the Moon from its ascending node. Taking the sidereal longitude of the Moon $M = 47^\circ$, the range for sidereal Rāhu is from $77^\circ .47$ to $196^\circ .53$. The Moon’s sidereal period is about 27.32166 days. Rāhu’s sidereal period being 6793.47 days, it takes about 2246.74 days to cover the above prescribed range which is of length $119^\circ .06$. During this period of Rāhu’s stay in that range, the sidereal Moon comes to $47^\circ$ about 82 times. This means that in the course of Rāhu’s sidereal period of about 18.6 years, the maximum number of times the Moon enters the Rohiṇī cart is 82 times successively. Now, out of Rāhu’s sidereal period of 6793.47 days (18.6 years) the remaining part during which the Moon does not hit the Rohiṇī śakaṭa is about 12.45 years. However, the RSB by the Moon with Rāhu at a particular position, in the prescribed range repeats once in about 55.8 years.

chunks.text: As discussed earlier, besides the Moon, the other participating bodies of RSB are Mars and Saturn. Using the modern astronomical software it is estimated by Mahajani et al9 that the last RSB by Mars occurred around 5284 B.C. and also more repeatedly in the $10^{th}$ millennium B.C. Further it is concluded that this event will not repeat till about 10,000 A.D. So far as Jupiter is concerned its maximum orbital inclination with the ecliptic is about $1^\circ 18'$ and hence Jupiter never participates in RSB.

chunks.text: We have discussed in the preceding chapters how the Indian astronomers classified the different types of conjunctions between two heavenly bodies. The conjunction of a star or a planet by the Moon is called samāgama. This phenomenon is referred to as lunar “occultation.” Modern Indian authors, in Indian languages, call the phenomenon “saṅkramaṇa” and “ācchādana” (covering). We shall illustrate our improved procedure, within the siddhāntic framework, with a few interesting examples. Example 1: Occultation of Venus on July 12, 1996 According to Ind. Ast. Eph. we have the following. Time of conjunction of Moon with Venus : $14^h 04^m$ IST Moon’s latitude at conjunction, $\beta1 = -4^\circ 23' 11''.1$ Venus’ latitude at conjunction, $\beta2 = -4^\circ 46' 58''.52$ Moon’s daily motion, $MDM = 12^\circ 8' 26''.1$ Venus’ daily motion $VDM = 0^\circ 21' 17''.7$ --- CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULATIONS 539 Daily change in Moon’s latitude $= -0^\circ 28' 28''.3 \equiv D\beta1$ Daily change in Venus’ latitude $= -0^\circ 01' 17''.1 \equiv D\beta2$ Parallax of the Moon $= 54' 41''.63 \equiv PAR1$ Parallax of Venus $= 21''.25 \equiv PAR2$ Moon’s diameter $= 2 \times 14' 53''.9 \equiv MDIA$ Venus’ diameter $= 2 \times 20'' \equiv VDIA$ (1) $PAR = PAR1 - PAR2 = 54' 20''.38$ (2) $D = PAR + \frac{(MDIA + VDIA)}{2} = 69.571333$ (3) $\dot{m} = \frac{(MDM - VDM)}{60} = 0^\circ .1964277 = 11' 47''.1 \text{ per } nāḍī$ (4) Correction to conjunction time for the middle $= \frac{-pP}{\dot{m}^2 + P^2}$ where $p = \beta1 - \beta2 = 23' 47''$ and $P = d\beta1 - d\beta2 = -27' 11''.2$. The correction to the conjunction time $= +1^m 51^s.55$ $\therefore$ Middle of occultation $= 14^h 05^m 51^s.55$ (5) Half duration $= \frac{\sqrt{D^2 - p^2}}{\dot{m}}$ where $p = 23' 47''$ and $D = 69'.5717333$ $\therefore$ Half duration $= 5.5477166 \ nāḍīs = 2^h 13^m 8^s.71$ 4: Grahalāghavam of Gaṇeśa Daivajña, with com. of Mallāri and Viśvanātha and Hindi com. by Kedarnath Joshi, Motilal Banarsidass, Varanasi, 1981 5: Grahalāghavam of Gaṇeśa Daivajña, with Eng. Exposition & Math. Notes by Balachandra Rao, S. and Uma, S.K., INSA, New Delhi, 2006 8: N.M. Swerdlow and O. Neugebauer, Mathematical Astronomy in Copernicus's De Revolutionibus, Ed. G. J. Toomer, Springer-Verlag, New York, 1984 9: Parag Mahajani, M.N. Vahia, Mohan Apte and A.P. Jamkhedkar, Dating of Rohiṇī Śakaṭa Bheda (To be published) 540 | INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE Summary of the Occultation (IST) Beginning : $11^h 52^m 42^s.84$ Middle : $14^h 5^m 51^s.55$ End of occultation : $16^h 19^m 0^s.26$ According to Indian Astronomical Ephemeris, we have IST Beginning : $11^h 54^m$ Middle : $14^h 6^m$ End : $16^h 18^m 32^s$ Example 2: Double Occultation We now consider a very interesting occurrence of a "double occultation" and a conjunction. On April $23^{rd}$ 1998 there was a double occultation of Guru and Śukra (by the Moon) and a conjunction between themselves. We shall work out the circumstances of this phenomenon. (i) Occultation of Guru (Jupiter) Instant of Guru’s conjunction with the Moon: $12^h 33^m$ IST At the instant of conjunction, following the earlier notations, we have $p = 13'$, $P = -77'$, $\dot{m} = 867'.3$ per day $$D = PAR + \frac{MDIA + JDIA}{2} = 77'.117359$$ where $PAR = \text{difference of the parallaxes of the Moon and Guru} = 60'.4$ --- CONJUNCTIONS, TRANSITS AND OCCULATIONS | 541 Fig. 4. 18. CONJUNCTION OF GURU WITH TIṢYA NAKṢATRA
chunks.text: In the Ṛgveda saṃhitā (ṚV), hailed as the most ancient literary work, and also in the Atharvaveda (AV), Jupiter’s conjunction with the Tiṣya (Puṣya i.e. $\delta$ Cancri) nakṣatra is mentioned in the following mantra: बृहस्पतिः प्रथमं जायमानो महो ज्योतिषः परमे व्योमन् । सप्तस्यस्तु विजातो रवेण सप्तरश्मिर्धमत् तमांसि ॥ ṚV, 4.50, 4; AV, 1088.4 “Bṛhaspati, when being born in the highest heaven of supreme light, seven-mouthed multi-form (combined) with sound and seven-rayed, has subdued the darkness.” There is a more specific reference to the location of Jupiter in the following mantra from the Taittirīya saṃhitā: बृहस्पतिः प्रथमं जायमानस्तिष्यं नक्षत्रमभिसम्बभूव Tai. Saṃ. 3.1.5 “Bṛhaspati, when first appearing, rose in front of the Tiṣya (Puṣya) asterism.” Again, the conjunction of Guru with Puṣya nakṣatra ($\delta$ Cancri) being a rare event, it is worth investigating when this special conjunction took --- 544 | INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE place so that on that basis the date of the Ṛgveda can be fixed. The latitude of Puṣya is $0^\circ 04' 37"$ north, very close to the ecliptic. The sidereal longitude is about $104^\circ 52'$. The inclination of Jupiter’s orbit with the ecliptic being about $1^\circ 18'$, the said conjunction is feasible. S.D.Sharma $^{11}$ has tried to find out when such a conjunction occurred in the past. We will now consider a rare “close conjunction” of Venus and Jupiter. Example: Conjunction of Guru and Śukra on January 3/4, 1818 A.D. The instant of conjunction (in longitude) $T0$ of Guru and Śukra: $3^h 21^m.53$ a.m. (IST). At the instant of conjunction, we have Sāyana Guru = Sāyana Śukra = 266°34'48" Śukra’s latitude, $\beta1 = 17'.54709$ and Guru’s latitude, $\beta2 = 17'.24695$ Therefore, the difference in their latitude, $p = \beta1 - \beta2 = 0'.30034 \approx 18"$ Parallax of Śukra, $PAR1 = 5".452357$ Parallax of Guru, $PAR2 = 1".4164$ $\therefore$ Difference of the parallaxes, $PAR = PAR1 - PAR2 = 4".036257$ Semi diameter of Śukra, $d1 = 5".170786$ Semi diameter of Guru, $d2 = 14".82752$ The sum of the semi-diameters and the resultant parallax $$D = PAR + d1 + d2 = 24".034563$$ The instants of beginning (sparśa) and the end (mokṣa), as in an eclipse, are given by $$T0 - \frac{pP}{\dot{m}^2 + P^2} \mp \frac{\sqrt{D^2 - p^2}}{\dot{m}} \dots(1)$$ --- 10: Courtesy: B.S.Shylaja & H.R.Madhusudan 11: S.D. Sharma, Conjunction of Jupiter $\delta$ Cancri, IJHS, 31.3 (1996) 269-74. where (i) $P = (D\beta1 - D\beta2)$, the difference in the daily rates of change in latitudes of the two bodies; and (ii) $\dot{m} = VDM - JDM$. Here $VDM$ and $JDM$ are respectively the true daily motions of Venus and Jupiter. In the example considered, we have $$D\beta1 = -5'.05634, \quad D\beta2 = -0'.15717, \quad VDM = 2^\circ30'34", \quad JDM = 0^\circ26'47"$$ $$\therefore P = -5'.05634 + (0'.15717) = -4'.89917$$ $$\dot{m} = 2^\circ30'34" - 0^\circ26'47" = 2^\circ3'47" = 123'.78333$$ In expression (1), if $T_0$ is taken as the instant of conjunction, then the second term $\frac{-pP}{\dot{m}^2 + P^2}$ is the time interval from the instant of conjunction to the "middle" of conjunction i.e. of maximum obscuration. This term can be called "correction" to get the middle. The third term in (1) gives the half-duration. When this value is subtracted from and added to the "middle" we get the beginning and the end of the conjunction respectively. In the current example, from (1) we have "correction" $= +8.28$ sec. and half-duration $= 3^m5^s.28$ Therefore, the instant of beginning ($sparśa$) is $3^h18^m34^s.8$ (IST). The end of the conjunction ($mokṣa$) is $3^h24^m45^s.36$ (IST) on January 4, 1818 A.D. The middle is $3^h21^m40^s.08$. Remark: It is important to note that conjunctions of planets take place quite often in the sense of their longitudes being equal. But the difference in their latitudes most often exceeds the sum of their semi-diameters which are very small as compared to those of the Sun and the Moon. However once in a way, though rarely as in the case of the example considered above, a "close" conjunction as in the case of an eclipse can take place. Such a phenomenon is called $bheda\ yoga$, i.e. "piercing" conjunction.

chunks.text: We have discussed at length in the preceding sections, conjunctions, transits and occultations between the heavenly bodies, by the Indian classical astronomical procedures. For this purpose we have explained the $siddhāntic$ algorithms for computing the important parameters like the angular diameters ($bimba$), the nodes ($pātas$), the latitudes ($śaras$), distinction between the $bheda$ and $abheda$ conjunctions and then finally the circumstances of the phenomena of transit and occultation. We have observed that the Indian classical procedures, with necessary but minimal modifications, yield results which are comparable to those obtained by modern procedures.

Latitudes, Inclinations and Nodes of Planets
chunks.text: In section 7, the determination of the celestial latitude ($śara$) according to the Indian classical texts has been presented and an example is also worked out. Essentially, the geocentric latitude is given by $$Śara = \frac{\text{Maximum } śara \times Bhujajy\bar{a}}{Ś\bar{i}ghrakar\d{n}a} kal\bar{a}s$$ (cancelling the $trijy\bar{a}\ R$ both in the numerator and the denominator). It is interesting to note that among Indian astronomers the Kerala astronomer, Nīlakaṇṭha Somayāji (1500 A.D.) was the first to explain clearly the geocentric latitude of a planet (see M.S.Sriram12). In his cited paper M.S.Sriram has clearly explained the relation between the heliocentric and the geocentric latitudes of a planet considering the Keplerian model. ![Fig. 5. Heliocentric and geocentric latitudes of a planet.12](media/p33page.png) If $\betaS$ and $\betaE$ are respectively the heliocentric and the geocentric latitudes of a planet and $ih$ is the inclination of the planet’s orbit with the ecliptic then $\betaS \approx ih \sin(\lambdaP - \lambdaN)$ where $\lambdaP$ and $\lambdaN$ are respectively the true heliocentric longitudes of the planet and the node. If $SP$ and $EP$ are respectively the heliocentric and the geocentric distances of the planet, then the geocentric latitude $\betaE$ is given by $$\betaE = \frac{ih SP \sin(\lambdaP - \lambdaN)}{EP}$$ In the traditional texts, before Nīlakaṇṭha Somayāji, the expression for the latitude provided an approximate value for the geocentric latitude. While their values for the inclination ($paramaśara$) were reasonably good (except for Mercury) their values for the nodes ($pātas$) were not that correct. Further, in the expression for the geocentric latitude, $\lambdaP$ is the true heliocentric longitude of the planet. For the inferior planets, Budha and Śukra, $\lambda_P$ is the planet's $ś\bar{i}ghrocca$ (mean heliocentric planet) to which the $mandaphala$ is added. But the $mandaphala$ is itself calculated using the mean Sun (and not the mean planet) as the $madhyagraha$. We provide below tables of comparative values for the inclinations, nodes and the mean diameters of the planets. We observe, from Table 4, that Brahmagupta’s values for the inclinations of the orbits of Kuja and Guru are closest to the modern values. Ptolemy’s values for those of Budha, Śukra and Śani are closest to the modern ones.

Maximum obscuration and half-duration of the phenomenon
chunks.text: Suppose the conjunction (in longitude) of two heavenly bodies occurs at time $T0$. Let $p$ be the difference in their latitudes and $P$ the hourly rate of change in the difference in their celestial latitudes. If $\dot{m}$ is the hourly rate of change in the difference of the two celestial bodies, then after $t$ hours from the instant of their conjunction $T0$, the distance between the centres of the two bodies is $$\sqrt{(\dot{m}t)^2 + (p + Pt)^2}$$ Now, the phenomenon (eclipse, transit or occultation) commences ($sparśa$) and ends ($mokṣa$) when the rims of the two bodies just touch each other. At these two instants the distance between their centres equals the sum of their "apparent" semi-diameters. Here, the word "apparent" means the appearance of the discs affected by parallax. Thus, at the commencement of the phenomenon, we have $$(\dot{m}t)^2 + (p + Pt)^2 = d^2 \qquad \dots(1)$$ 12: M.S. Sriram, Planetary Models in Indian and Greek Astronomical Traditions, 500 Years of Tantrasangraha, IIAS, Shimla, 2002. 550 INDIAN JOURNAL OF HISTORY OF SCIENCE where $d$ is the sum of the "apparent" semi-diameters of the two bodies, that is $$d = PAR + \frac{1}{2}(SDIA + PDIA) \qquad \dots(2)$$ $$\text{or} \qquad d = PAR + \frac{1}{2}(MDIA + PDIA) \qquad \dots(3)$$ Here, (2) and (3) apply respectively for the transit (of Venus or Mercury across the Sun) and the occultation (by the Moon). The angular diameters (bimba) of the Sun, the Moon and the planet are denoted respectively by $SDIA$, $MDIA$ and $PDIA$. The difference in parallaxes of the two bodies is denoted by $PAR$. The time $t$ in hours (from $T_0$) at which the phenomenon commences or ends is given by the solution of the quadratic equation (1). Solving (1), we get $$t = -\frac{pP}{\dot{m}^2 + P^2} \mp \sqrt{\frac{p^2 P^2}{(\dot{m}^2 + P^2)^2} + \frac{(p^2 - d^2)}{(\dot{m}^2 + P^2)}} \qquad \dots(4)$$ In the expression (4), the second term (with square-root) gives the half-duration of the phenomenon and the first term is the "correction" to the instant of conjunction (longitude) to get the instant of maximum obscuration. The negative and positive signs in (4) are used respectively for the beginning and the end of the phenomenon. It is important to note that in (4), all the quantities have the same angular unit (say arc-minutes) and the rates of change $\dot{m}$ and $P$ are per hour.
